A logic instructor correctly explains to students that knowing something about an individual under one description does not create a different individual when the same person is described another way. (Quine, 1956) https://doi.org/10.2307/2182308
A journalist confirms that two organizations with different names share the same executive director and correctly treats their policies as reflecting one person's leadership. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A patient who recognizes their doctor outside the clinic correctly acknowledges it is the same person and interacts accordingly rather than treating them as a stranger. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
An audience member who learns that the confident performer on stage is actually very anxious backstage correctly updates their view of the performer's inner experience rather than treating the descriptions as contradictory. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A sports analyst confirms that the same player's on-field statistics and off-field behavior belong to the same individual and evaluates both when forming an overall assessment. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A forensic linguist correctly concludes that stylistic patterns shared across two documents attributed to different authors reveal a single authorship and integrates both sets of evidence. (Quine, 1956) https://doi.org/10.2307/2182308
A referee correctly identifies a player wearing an unusual number as the same athlete who received a warning in a previous match and enforces the cumulative consequence. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5

column3: false belief that something you just recently noticed is a brand-new phenomenon
column4: Believing something is new because it's new to you.
column5:
A language columnist declared that using 'hopefully' as a sentence adverb was a recent degradation of English, when corpus records show the same usage dating to the 17th century. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
People in the 1990s complained that 'I could care less' was a new error invented by careless young speakers, when the same phrasing appears in print from several decades earlier. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
A grammar blogger insisted that starting sentences with 'And' or 'But' was a modern mistake, even though this usage appears throughout the King James Bible and centuries of formal prose. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
Many people believe that using 'they' as a singular pronoun is a new invention driven by recent social changes, but writers including Shakespeare used the singular 'they' four centuries ago. (Zimmer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933
A TV pundit claimed that using 'contact' as a verb was a brand-new Americanism ruining the language, though that verb form appears in print from the 1800s. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
People commonly believe that using 'literally' as an intensifier is a new misuse invented by the internet generation, but critics were complaining about this same usage in the early 1900s. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
A linguist coined the term 'recency illusion' after observing that even professional grammarians routinely declare constructions new when historical corpus searches disprove the claim. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
Commenters online declared that the word 'selfie' represented a uniquely narcissistic new behavior, not recognizing that self-portraiture has a centuries-long tradition in fine art and photography. (Oxford University Press, 2013) https://public.oed.com/blog/november-2013-update-new-words/
A parent complained that teenagers today use 'awesome' to mean anything good and that this represents a new dumbing-down of English, even though the word's semantic drift from extreme reverence began in the 19th century. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A grammar teacher marked a student wrong for ending a sentence with a preposition, believing this was an eternal rule, when the prohibition was invented by 17th-century prescriptivists and has no basis in earlier usage. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
People regularly assume that abbreviating words in text messages is a new invention of smartphones, when abbreviations and phonetic shortcuts appear in personal letters and telegrams from the 1800s. (Zimmer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933
A critic argued that using 'gift' as a verb was a new and irritating business-speak coinage, when the verb 'gift' appears in 16th-century English writing. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
Many believed that using 'impact' as a verb was a recently invented corporate buzzword, even though the verb form dates to at least the early 1800s. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
Readers complained that using 'fun' as an adjective was a brand-new generation's innovation, when the adjective use is documented in 19th-century texts. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
A language teacher told students that splitting infinitives was a modern trend degrading formal English, when the prohibition itself is a Victorian-era prescriptive invention with no ancient authority. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
People assumed that calling food 'plant-based' was a new marketing term invented in the 2010s health food movement, when similar framing appears in vegetarian literature from decades earlier. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A language columnist complained that 'between you and I' was a new hypercorrection invented by people who watched too much prestige TV, when Shakespeare used the same construction in The Merchant of Venice. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
People in the early 2000s believed that the concept of tagging content was a revolutionary internet innovation, when librarians had been using formal classification and subject-heading tags for over a century. (Oxford University Press, 2013) https://public.oed.com/blog/november-2013-update-new-words/
An editor believed that the word 'snark' meaning a sarcastic remark was a new internet-era coinage, not knowing the word appeared in print with similar meaning in the late 19th century. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
Many people believed that youth slang changes faster today than it did in previous generations, when historical records show each generation has always perceived contemporary slang as uniquely fast-moving and new. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
column6:
A lexicographer correctly identified that the word 'selfie' was coined around 2002 and was genuinely new to the language when it entered widespread use. (Oxford University Press, 2013) https://public.oed.com/blog/november-2013-update-new-words/
A corpus linguist searched historical databases and confirmed that a particular slang term first appeared in writing within the past five years, with no earlier instances in any available text. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A researcher correctly verified through newspaper archives that the phrase 'social distancing' was rarely used before 2020 and was genuinely not in common everyday usage before that year. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
An etymologist correctly traces a recently added dictionary entry to its first recorded use within the last decade and confirms no earlier unrecorded history of the word. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
A teacher correctly explains to students that the term 'crowdsourcing' was coined in 2006 and is a genuinely new word formed to describe a genuinely new technological phenomenon. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
A journalist correctly notes that a newly coined political term did not exist before a specific election cycle and provides corpus evidence confirming its first appearance. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A dictionary editor adds a new word to the reference work only after confirming that the term has no substantial history of earlier use under the same meaning. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
A language blogger verifies through the Oxford English Dictionary that a usage a reader complained about as new actually has citations going back 400 years, correctly identifying the recency illusion rather than a new word. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A historian of technology correctly documents that the word 'podcast' is genuinely new, first appearing in the early 2000s alongside the technology it describes. (Oxford University Press, 2013) https://public.oed.com/blog/november-2013-update-new-words/
A grammar expert correctly informs students that singular 'they' is not a recent invention but has historical precedent, while also confirming that some specific pronoun combinations used today are genuinely new. (Zimmer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933
A prescriptivist who searches a historical corpus before publishing a complaint correctly discovers that the construction has centuries of use and withdraws the complaint rather than spreading a recency illusion. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
A writing teacher correctly informs students that ending sentences with prepositions has always been natural in English, citing historical examples rather than assuming the usage is new. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
A linguist studying language change correctly traces precisely when a new meaning for a word emerged and provides dated corpus evidence rather than relying on their subjective sense that the usage is recent. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
An OED editor adding a new word this year notes that the entry has a clear and genuinely recent origin, unlike many words that appear new but turn out to have long documented histories. (Oxford University Press, 2013) https://public.oed.com/blog/november-2013-update-new-words/
A reader who fact-checks a complaint about a supposedly new grammatical trend confirms via Google Ngrams that the usage has been common in print for over 150 years, identifying the recency illusion in action. (Liberman, 2003) https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=653
A textbook author correctly describes the origin of a newly coined technical term to a specific decade, with documented evidence of its first use in a scientific paper. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A copy editor correctly verifies before flagging a word as new slang that it is absent from all reference works and corpora predating the current decade. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives
A documentary filmmaker correctly describes a new type of viral content format as genuinely new, supported by clear records of the specific platform's launch date. (Oxford University Press, 2013) https://public.oed.com/blog/november-2013-update-new-words/
A language researcher correctly attributes a new sense of an existing word to a specific recent period, providing dated citation evidence rather than relying on their personal impression. (Zwicky, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110220933.19
A word nerd who looks up the word 'awful' in a historical dictionary correctly discovers it once meant 'inspiring awe' and recognizes this as genuine semantic change rather than recency illusion, because the shift is well documented over time. (Merriam-Webster, n.d.) https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/to-boldly-split-infinitives

column3: Overweighting recent events over earlier ones.
column4: Giving more importance to recent events
column5:
Judging a student by recent grades only.
 Assuming a stock is strong due to recent gains.
 Thinking a friend's recent behavior defines them.
 Judging a restaurant by the last visit only.
 Believing a team is great after a short streak.

An investor who saw the stock market drop sharply last week sells all their holdings even though the market has returned positive gains over the past decade. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A hiring manager rates a candidate as excellent primarily because they gave an impressive answer to the final interview question, even though earlier answers were weak. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A teacher gives a student a high grade on a report card based mainly on their strong performance in the last two weeks of the semester, ignoring months of poor work. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A sports fan declares their team is championship-worthy after a three-game winning streak, forgetting the team lost twelve of their previous fifteen games. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A doctor orders an unnecessary battery of tests because the last three patients with similar symptoms turned out to have a rare disease, even though base rates make this highly unlikely. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
Consumers rated a product as low quality primarily because a friend complained about it last week, despite the product having hundreds of positive reviews over several years. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
An employee who had an excellent performance review for five straight years is passed over for promotion after one difficult quarter, with the manager focusing almost entirely on recent results. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
Research participants asked to judge the likelihood of a flood in their town gave much higher estimates the week after a heavy rainstorm than they did six months later, even though actual flood risk had not changed. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037743
A judge gives a harsher sentence to a defendant whose crime was reported in the news last month compared to an identical crime committed two years ago, reflecting greater salience of recent events. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A financial analyst upgrades a company's stock rating solely because it beat earnings expectations in the most recent quarter, ignoring a five-year pattern of declining revenue. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
Voters rated a candidate more favorably after hearing their most recent speech, even though the candidate's policy record over the past four years remained unchanged. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A person decides a neighborhood is dangerous after hearing about two incidents in the past month, despite crime statistics showing it is safer than average over the past five years. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037743
A mutual fund that outperformed the market for the last six months attracted large inflows of investor money, even though research shows short-term performance does not predict future returns. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A manager rates a long-term employee's overall performance as poor because of a single mistake made the week before the annual review, discounting years of strong contributions. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
Experimental participants who learned information in a sequence gave substantially more weight to items presented last when making a final judgment, a pattern that held across multiple studies. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A person who had a bad meal at a restaurant last month tells friends never to go there, despite having eaten there happily twenty times before. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
After a run of sunny weekends, a family books an outdoor wedding venue without checking the venue's historical weather patterns, assuming recent conditions will continue. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A coach benches a reliable starting player after two poor games, overlooking the player's strong season-long statistics that far outperform the available replacement. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
Public support for climate change policy rose sharply immediately after a major hurricane but returned to baseline within months, showing that recent extreme events temporarily dominate long-term statistical reasoning. (Weber, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-006-9060-3
A loan officer approved a small business application primarily because the business had a strong last quarter, without adequately weighting the company's three-year history of inconsistent cash flow. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
column6:
Evaluating performance over long-term trends.
 Considering full history instead of recent events.
 Avoiding snap judgments based on short-term changes.

An investment committee reviews a fund's full ten-year return history before making an allocation decision, explicitly discounting the most recent quarter as insufficient evidence of a trend. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A teacher calculates a student's final grade using a weighted average of all assignments across the entire semester, giving equal credit to work completed in September and work completed in December. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A hiring panel scores each interview question independently using a rubric and averages all scores before making a decision, so that a strong final answer cannot override a weak early one. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A doctor evaluates a patient's cardiovascular risk using a standardized calculator that incorporates ten years of cholesterol readings, blood pressure history, and lifestyle data rather than only the most recent values. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A sports analyst correctly identifies that a team's three-game winning streak falls within the normal range of variance for their season-long win rate, and does not revise their overall assessment of the team. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A research team explicitly uses pre-registered hypotheses and multi-year datasets to evaluate a policy intervention, preventing recent headlines from influencing their analytical framework. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A city council evaluates a neighborhood's safety using five years of crime statistics rather than reacting to a cluster of incidents reported in the past month. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0037743
An HR manager conducting an annual review uses behavioral anchors collected throughout the year, ensuring that performance documented in January carries the same weight as performance in November. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A climate scientist presenting findings on sea level rise uses a 30-year temperature average rather than the most recent year's data, explicitly noting that single-year readings are insufficient to draw conclusions. (Weber, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-006-9060-3
A restaurant critic who had a poor experience on their most recent visit checks their own notes from four prior visits before publishing a review, and concludes the kitchen is generally strong despite the recent off night. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
An investor who saw the market drop last week checks the 20-year historical return data before deciding to stay in index funds, recognizing that a single week's movement is not meaningful evidence. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A coach keeps a reliable starter in the lineup despite two poor recent games because the player's season-long statistics remain the best on the team. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A voter researches a candidate's full legislative record over four years before deciding how to vote, rather than basing the decision on the candidate's most recent speech. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A loan officer flags a business application for further review because despite a strong last quarter, the company's three-year cash flow trend shows persistent instability. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
Participants in a decision-making study who were trained in base rate reasoning correctly discounted recent vivid examples and based their probability estimates on long-run statistical data. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A doctor evaluating whether to prescribe a medication consults the full body of clinical trial evidence spanning fifteen years rather than being swayed by a single recent case study. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A mutual fund selector ignores last year's top-performing funds and instead selects based on ten-year risk-adjusted returns, consistent with research showing short-term performance does not persist. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A public health agency sets vaccination targets based on multi-year disease burden data rather than adjusting policy every time there is a spike or drop in weekly case counts. (Weber, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-006-9060-3
A couple who had a single difficult argument chooses to attend relationship counseling that reviews their full relationship history before drawing conclusions, rather than treating the recent conflict as definitive. (Hogarth & Einhorn, 1992) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(92)90002-J
A judge uses structured sentencing guidelines calibrated to long-term crime data rather than adjusting sentences upward because a similar crime was in the news recently. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697

column3: Believing past random events influence future ones.
column4: Thinking the past changes future luck
column5:
Expecting tails after many heads.
 Thinking roulette is due for black.
 Believing a losing streak must end soon.
 Assuming a slot machine will pay out soon.
 Thinking future exam questions might be similar.

A roulette player bets heavily on black after red has come up five times in a row, believing black is now overdue even though each spin is independent. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
Lottery players systematically avoided numbers that had won recently, believing those numbers were less likely to be drawn again in subsequent drawings. (Clotfelter & Cook, 1993) https://doi.org/10.2307/2117560
A person who has flipped heads seven times in a row is certain the next flip must come up tails, even though the coin has no memory of previous flips. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
Asylum judges who had granted two applications in a row were significantly more likely to reject the third application, as if they were correcting for a streak. (Chen et al., 2016) https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw016
Baseball umpires were measurably less likely to call a third consecutive strike in a row even when the third pitch was clearly in the strike zone. (Chen et al., 2016) https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw016
Casino gamblers placed larger bets on roulette after long runs of the same color came up, expecting the pattern to break soon. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A slot machine player insists a machine that has not paid out in several hours is overdue for a jackpot, even though each spin is determined independently by a random number generator. (Wagenaar, 1988) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315542409
Loan officers who had approved several loans in a row were significantly more likely to reject the next application even when it was objectively creditworthy. (Chen et al., 2016) https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw016
A parent who has had three daughters in a row becomes convinced their next baby is much more likely to be a boy, misunderstanding how biological probability works. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
Students asked to produce a random sequence of coin tosses instinctively avoided long runs of the same outcome, making their sequences less random than true random sequences. (Wagenaar, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01766763
A gambler who has lost four consecutive hands of blackjack doubles their bet again, believing the law of averages must soon favor them. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
Investors sold winning stocks too early because they believed a run of price increases could not continue much longer, despite no fundamental reason for a reversal. (Odean, 1998) https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072
A couple who has been trying to conceive for six months begins to feel their chances must be higher now simply because of how long they have been trying, even though monthly probability is unchanged. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
Participants shown a sequence of random coin flip outcomes showed a clear tendency to switch their prediction after a run of the same result, expecting alternation. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A poker player who has not been dealt a good hand in an hour starts calling with weaker cards, believing a strong hand must be coming soon. (Wagenaar, 1988) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315542409
Sports fans believe a losing team is statistically overdue for a win after a long losing streak, even in sports where each game outcome is largely independent of the last. (Gilovich, 1991) https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780029117064
A person playing a number-generation game insists a number that has appeared three times recently cannot reasonably come up again so soon. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A quality inspector notices three defects in a row on an assembly line and becomes certain the machine must now produce good items, treating the defects as if they drew from a limited quota. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A weather forecaster showed a tendency to predict rain after several consecutive dry days, as if dry weather created a deficit that rainfall would soon correct. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A person driving to work believes they are unlikely to hit a red light again soon after hitting four in a row, not understanding that each traffic light cycle is independent. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
column6:
Recognizing each event is independent.
 Using probability theory to judge randomness.
 Accepting that streaks don't change future odds.

A probability professor correctly explains to a class that seven heads in a row does not change the 50/50 probability of the next coin flip, because each event is statistically independent. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A casino dealer correctly explains to a patron that the roulette wheel has no memory and that previous outcomes cannot make any particular number more or less likely on the next spin. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A statistician trained in probability correctly evaluates each loan application on its individual financial merits without considering how many applications they have recently approved or denied. (Chen et al., 2016) https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw016
A lottery player who understands probability correctly recognizes that last week's winning numbers are just as likely to appear again this week as any other combination. (Clotfelter & Cook, 1993) https://doi.org/10.2307/2117560
A doctor correctly explains to a couple that having had three daughters does not make a son more statistically likely in the next pregnancy, as each conception is an independent event. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A research participant who completed a module on probability correctly treats each draw in a random sequence as independent and does not switch predictions after a run of the same outcome. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
An investor correctly does not sell a stock simply because it has risen for several days in a row, recognizing that past price increases do not make a decline any more probable in the near term. (Odean, 1998) https://doi.org/10.1111/0022-1082.00072
A baseball umpire who attended a decision-making workshop correctly calls pitches based on their actual location in the strike zone regardless of how many consecutive calls of the same type they have recently made. (Chen et al., 2016) https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw016
An asylum judge trained in debiasing techniques evaluates each application based solely on the individual case facts without adjusting their decision based on their recent approval or rejection streak. (Chen et al., 2016) https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw016
A slot machine manufacturer correctly informs players that each spin is generated by an independent random number process, meaning previous spins provide no information about future outcomes. (Wagenaar, 1988) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315542409
A sports analyst correctly notes that a team's losing streak does not make them statistically due for a win and that the probability of winning depends on the matchup, not the streak length. (Gilovich, 1991) https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780029117064
A gambler who has studied expected value correctly decides that doubling their bet after losses is not a valid strategy because each game round is independent of the previous one. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A card player correctly notes that in a well-shuffled deck with replacement, drawing ten low cards in a row does not increase the probability that the next card will be high. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A quality engineer uses statistical process control charts to distinguish genuine machine faults from random variation rather than treating a cluster of defects as evidence that a run of good parts must follow. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A driver correctly recognizes that hitting four red lights in a row provides no information about whether the next light will be red or green, as each light cycle runs on its own timer. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A weather forecaster correctly bases tomorrow's rain probability on current atmospheric data rather than on how many consecutive dry days have occurred. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A nurse correctly explains to a patient that having recovered from an infection twice before does not make recovery from a third infection more or less likely, as each immune response depends on current health factors. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3
A poker player correctly understands that not receiving a good hand for an hour reflects normal variance and that the deck has no memory of how long it has been since they were last dealt a strong hand. (Wagenaar, 1988) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315542409
A child correctly answers a probability question in class by stating that past coin flips cannot influence the next flip, demonstrating that the concept can be learned and correctly applied. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.185.4157.1124
A couple correctly understands that the monthly probability of conception does not increase because of how many months they have been trying, and they consult a physician to evaluate biological factors rather than waiting for odds they imagine must be building in their favor. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(72)90016-3

column3: Believing success streaks will continue.
column4: Believing luck comes in streaks
column5:
Thinking a basketball player will keep scoring.
 Believing a trader on a streak will keep winning.
 Assuming a student will keep answering correctly.
 Thinking a gamer on a streak is unbeatable.
 Expecting a salesperson to keep closing deals.

Basketball fans and players believed that a shooter who had made three shots in a row was significantly more likely to make the next shot, even though statistical analysis of actual shooting data showed no such pattern. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A poker player who wins three hands in a row starts betting more aggressively on weaker cards, convinced they are on a hot streak that makes future wins more likely. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
Casino gamblers who observed another gambler winning several bets in a row placed larger bets on that person's next outcome, treating the streak as evidence of continued success. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A sales manager gives the month's biggest accounts to the salesperson who closed the most deals last week, assuming their recent streak predicts continued superior performance. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A volleyball coach consistently passed the ball to a player who had just scored twice in a row, even though controlled data showed no actual increase in that player's success probability after prior scores. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
An investor who sees a fund manager outperform the market for three straight quarters puts all their savings into that fund, believing the manager has a hot hand in stock picking. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A sports commentator declares that a pitcher is unhittable tonight after retiring the first six batters, framing the streak as evidence of an elevated performance state rather than normal variance. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A darts player who hits the bullseye twice in a row aims for a more difficult target on the next throw, confident that their current streak means they are in an unusually accurate state. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
Researchers found that participants shown a sequence of made and missed basketball shots rated shooters who had just made several shots as significantly more likely to make the next one, despite the shots being randomly ordered. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A tennis player who wins the first two sets takes more risks than usual at the start of the third, believing momentum from the streak makes bold play more likely to succeed. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A startup investor continues funding a founder after two early product successes, attributing the wins to a hot-hand quality in the founder rather than to market timing or luck. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A gambler who correctly guesses the color of five roulette spins in a row believes they are on a hot streak and increases their bet, even though each spin is independent. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A basketball coach draws up a play to get the ball to the player who scored the last four times down the court, convinced that player is currently in a hot scoring state. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
An author who publishes two bestselling novels in a row believes their next manuscript will also be a hit because they are on a creative hot streak, ignoring the high base rate of publishing failures. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
Professional sports bettors placed higher bets on athletes who had won their last three events, treating the streak as predictive of continued success even when underlying skill levels had not changed. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A hiring manager who makes three successful hires in a row becomes overconfident in her next hiring decision, attributing the streak to a hot hand in candidate evaluation rather than to good luck or a strong applicant pool. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A student who scores well on three consecutive pop quizzes goes into the midterm exam without studying, believing their streak signals they are in an unusually sharp academic state. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
Fans in a study were willing to pay significantly more for a ticket to watch a player who had scored in the last three games compared to an equally skilled player who had not, reflecting belief in a hot hand. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A day trader who has made profitable trades for five days straight increases their position sizes, believing they are currently in a state of elevated market insight rather than experiencing a lucky run. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A football coach benches a reliable field goal kicker in favor of a backup who has made his last four kicks, treating the backup's short streak as evidence of superior current form. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
column6:
Evaluating performance using long-term averages.
 Recognizing streaks can be random.
 Checking actual skill metrics instead of streaks.

A sports statistician analyzes a baseball pitcher's performance across an entire season and finds that success in one game has no predictive relationship with performance in the following game, correctly ruling out a hot hand. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A basketball coach uses season-long shooting percentages to decide which player takes a critical shot, explicitly ignoring which player happened to make the last two baskets. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A casino manager correctly explains to a patron that each spin of the roulette wheel is independent, and that winning several bets in a row does not increase the probability of winning the next one. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
An investor selects a mutual fund based on its ten-year risk-adjusted return history rather than its recent three-month performance streak, recognizing that short runs do not predict future results. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A baseball analyst presents data to coaches showing that players who hit home runs in consecutive games perform at exactly their career average in the following game, confirming no hot-hand effect. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A poker player who has won the last four hands correctly recognizes that each hand is determined by the cards dealt and their decisions, not by any streak-based momentum, and continues to bet based on hand strength alone. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A sports analytics department advises coaches that giving the ball to the most recently successful player rather than the statistically best player results in worse outcomes over a season. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A startup mentor advises a founder that early product successes do not guarantee the next product will succeed and encourages ongoing rigorous market testing regardless of the recent streak. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A teacher assigns the next challenging problem set based on students' average scores over the semester rather than on which students happened to do best in last week's quiz. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A researcher who reviews the controlled shooting study data finds no significant serial correlation between consecutive shot outcomes, confirming that the hot hand in basketball is a statistical illusion. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A fund manager who has outperformed the market for two quarters in a row correctly attributes the success to favorable market conditions and does not increase risk, recognizing the pattern is likely to revert. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A gambler who has studied probability correctly treats each casino game as independent of previous outcomes and does not change their strategy based on a recent winning streak. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A hiring manager who has made three good hires in a row continues to use the same structured interview and scoring rubric for the next candidate rather than becoming overconfident and skipping steps. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
An athlete who has scored in the last four games correctly attributes her form to consistent training and preparation rather than a hot streak, and continues the same approach for the next match. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A day trader who has been profitable for a week correctly recognizes that streaks in noisy markets are consistent with random outcomes and does not increase position sizes beyond their tested strategy rules. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A volleyball coach keeps the same rotation throughout the match rather than adjusting to feed a player who just scored twice, correctly treating short streaks as statistically uninformative. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A writer who has published two successful books submits the next manuscript through the same careful editing and beta-reading process, recognizing that past success does not guarantee the next project will work without the same rigor. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A student who scored well on three quizzes correctly attributes the results to good study habits and maintains the same preparation routine for the midterm rather than becoming complacent. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
A sports betting analyst correctly identifies that a team on a five-game winning streak is no more likely to win the next game than their season-long win rate would predict, and prices the odds accordingly. (Croson & Sundali, 2005) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joep.2004.12.002
A tennis player who wins the first two sets maintains their standard tactical approach for the third set rather than taking uncharacteristic risks, knowing that the streak does not change the underlying probabilities. (Gilovich et al., 1985) https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6

column3: Perceiving relationships between unrelated variables.
column4: Believing unrelated things are connected
column5:
Believing full moons cause strange behavior.
 Thinking certain clothes predict personality.
 Linking unrelated events as cause and effect.
 Assuming two random trends are connected.
 Believing lucky charms influence outcomes.


Clinicians who used projective tests believed that patients who drew large eyes were more likely to be paranoid, even though controlled studies found no actual relationship between drawing features and diagnosis. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A nurse on a hospital ward became convinced that more patients deteriorated on nights with a full moon and began tracking the pattern carefully, even though controlled studies found no statistical lunar effect on patient outcomes. (Rotton & Kelly, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.97.2.286
Participants in an experiment overestimated how often minority group members appeared alongside negative behaviors in a list, even when the actual pairing rates were equal to those of the majority group. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A person who gets a headache every time they eat a specific food concludes that the food causes headaches, even though they get headaches equally often without eating it and simply do not notice those cases. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A student believes they always do poorly on tests when they forget their lucky pencil, even though their scores are unrelated to which pencil they use. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
Police officers in a study overestimated the correlation between certain demographic characteristics and criminal behavior based on a few salient cases, a pattern not supported by the underlying crime statistics. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A trader believes a specific technical chart pattern reliably predicts market movements, even though systematic backtesting shows the pattern performs no better than chance. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
A parent is convinced their child's behavior is always worse after eating sugar, even though double-blind studies consistently find no causal relationship between sugar consumption and children's activity levels. (Wolraich et al., 1995) https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199502023320503
Participants shown descriptions of rare group members paired with negative traits remembered those pairings at far higher rates than their actual frequency, creating a false impression of a strong group-trait correlation. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A hiring manager incorrectly believes candidates from a particular university consistently underperform, based on two or three salient negative examples that stand out in memory more than the many successful hires from the same school. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
An elderly patient is certain their arthritis pain is always worse before it rains, even though a controlled diary study shows no significant relationship between their pain levels and actual weather changes. (Redelmeier & Tversky, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.93.7.2895
Clinicians given consistent personality test results felt confident in diagnosis-personality links that were statistically invalid, because the pairing of certain test signs with certain diagnoses felt intuitively coherent. (Chapman & Chapman, 1969) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0027889
An investor believes a specific news anchor's appearance on television reliably predicts a market drop that week, noticing the coincidences and forgetting the many times no drop followed. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A person notices that their sports team loses every time they wear a particular shirt and concludes the shirt is bad luck, ignoring the many games they lost while wearing other shirts. (Gilovich, 1991) https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780029117064
Research showed that people infer a correlation between two rare events simply because both are unusual and distinctive, making them cognitively grouped together even when they co-occur no more than chance would predict. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A manager concludes that team morale is always low on Fridays after noticing it twice in a month, ignoring the many Fridays where morale was normal and the other days when morale was also low. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
People exposed to news that disproportionately covered violent acts by members of a particular group developed an overestimated perceived correlation between that group and violence that was not supported by base rate data. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A cook becomes convinced that a certain brand of salt makes their food taste better, even though blind taste tests show no difference between their dishes made with that brand versus a generic alternative. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A doctor over-orders a specific diagnostic test because two patients who had unusual presentations last month both tested positive, perceiving a diagnostic link that is not supported by the broader clinical evidence. (Redelmeier & Tversky, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.93.7.2895
An employee believes the printer always breaks when they are in a hurry, noticing and remembering these coincidences while forgetting the many times the printer broke without time pressure or worked fine when they were rushed. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
column6:
Testing correlations statistically.
 Rejecting associations without evidence.
 Recognizing coincidences as random.

A researcher runs a contingency table analysis on projective test data and confirms there is no statistically significant relationship between any drawing features and clinical diagnosis before making any interpretations. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A meteorologist uses thirty years of data and a controlled time-series analysis to confirm there is no significant relationship between lunar phase and emergency room admissions. (Rotton & Kelly, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.97.2.286
A parent who suspects sugar makes their child hyperactive agrees to participate in a double-blind challenge study and correctly finds they cannot identify which days their child consumed sugar versus a placebo. (Wolraich et al., 1995) https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199502023320503
A rheumatologist explains to a patient that their perceived correlation between weather and pain has been formally tested with prospective diary studies and found to be illusory, then reviews the actual data with them. (Redelmeier & Tversky, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.93.7.2895
An epidemiologist correctly identifies that the apparent disease cluster near a facility disappears after controlling for age, socioeconomic status, and population density, confirming the initial perceived correlation was spurious. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A data analyst runs a regression on years of hiring data and finds that university attended has no significant relationship with job performance after controlling for relevant competency scores. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A nurse who suspects a lunar effect on patient behavior systematically records outcomes across six months and finds the rate of incidents is identical across all phases of the moon. (Rotton & Kelly, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.97.2.286
A trading algorithm backtests a chart pattern across ten years of market data and confirms it has no predictive value beyond chance before the company decides not to trade on it. (Barberis & Thaler, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1016/S1574-0102(03)01027-6
Participants trained in contingency analysis correctly identified that two variables in an experiment co-occurred no more than chance predicted, resisting the tendency to perceive a relationship. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A psychologist who uses a structured validity-based test battery rejects informal test sign interpretations that have not been empirically verified as predictive, relying only on validated score relationships. (Chapman & Chapman, 1969) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0027889
A journalist includes base rate statistics in a story about crime to show readers that the perceived link between a demographic group and criminal behavior in local news is not supported by population-level data. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A sports fan who tracks all their team's results over two full seasons correctly concludes that wearing the lucky shirt has no relationship with the team's win rate. (Gilovich, 1991) https://www.hup.harvard.edu/catalog.php?isbn=9780029117064
A hiring committee that uses blind scoring rubrics and structured panel interviews finds no difference in long-term performance between candidates from different universities when evaluated on the same criteria. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
A doctor who suspected a medication caused a side effect reviews all patient records for the past year and finds the rate of the side effect is the same in patients who took the medication and those who did not. (Redelmeier & Tversky, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.93.7.2895
A researcher correctly calculates the phi coefficient for two variables and finds it is near zero, confirming that the intuitive sense of a relationship between them is not supported by the data. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A cook conducts a properly blinded taste test with independent tasters and finds no difference in ratings between dishes made with the premium salt and the generic alternative. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697
A manager who tracks team morale scores every day for a full quarter finds that Friday morale is not statistically different from morale on other days of the week. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A police department analyzes its own stop-and-frisk data and finds that after controlling for neighborhood crime rates, the perceived correlation between demographic characteristics and likelihood of carrying contraband disappears. (Hamilton & Gifford, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(76)90049-X
An employee who tracks printer failure events and their own schedule over three months finds no relationship between time pressure and printer malfunction rate. (Chapman & Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024964
A student who keeps a detailed study log finds that their test scores are unrelated to which pencil they used and stops attributing any predictive power to the lucky pencil. (Kahneman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.58.9.697

column3: Seeing meaningful images in random stimuli.
column4: Seeing faces in random objects
column5:
Seeing faces in clouds.
 Seeing animals in rock formations.
 Seeing shapes in tree bark.
 Seeing figures in shadows.
 Seeing patterns in static.

A person looking at a cloud formation clearly sees the face of a lion staring down at them, even though the cloud is simply the result of random atmospheric turbulence. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
Someone staring at wood grain on a cabinet door perceives the face of an elderly man looking back at them from the natural pattern of the wood fibers. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
Thousands of people reported seeing the face of the Virgin Mary in the burnt pattern on a grilled cheese sandwich, treating the random result of uneven heat as a meaningful image. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
Neuroscientists found that face-selective brain regions activated when participants viewed objects that only vaguely resembled human faces, showing that face detection runs ahead of conscious recognition. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A driver glances at a rust stain on a concrete wall as they pass and briefly perceives a grinning skull before recognizing it as a random corrosion pattern. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
Scientists photographing the Martian surface in 1976 released an image that appeared to show a humanoid face carved into the rock, which later high-resolution imaging confirmed was a natural landform shaped by erosion and lighting angle. (Sagan, 1995) https://archive.org/details/demonhauntedworl00saga
Participants in an experiment who were told to look for faces in noisy grayscale images reported seeing faces at much higher rates than those given no such instruction, showing that expectation amplifies pareidolia. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
People who heard backward recordings of rock songs reported hearing hidden messages specifically when they had been told in advance what the alleged message said, demonstrating expectation-driven auditory pareidolia. (Vokey & Read, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.40.11.1231
Researchers found that infants as young as a few months old preferentially tracked face-like arrangements of dots over scrambled versions, suggesting that face detection and its associated pareidolia tendency are deeply built into human perception. (Johnson et al., 1991) https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-835X.1991.tb00892.x
Automobile designers deliberately shape the front ends of cars with headlights and grille features that resemble a face, knowing that consumers unconsciously perceive and respond emotionally to the face-like appearance. (Windhager et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1068/p5996
A child looking at the full moon perceives a smiling human face in the pattern of dark maria and lighter highlands, a perception that persists even after being told the marks are geological features. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
Participants who were exposed to scrambled noise images and primed to think about faces reported seeing faces in the static at rates significantly higher than those in a control condition. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A person looking at the random pattern of water stains on a bathroom ceiling begins to see the profile of Abraham Lincoln and cannot unsee it once perceived. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A study found that people with higher anxiety levels were more likely to perceive faces in ambiguous noise images, suggesting that threat sensitivity amplifies the brain's tendency toward face-based pareidolia. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
Someone listening to white noise through headphones at night becomes convinced they can hear a voice whispering their name, even though the sound is simply random acoustic variation. (Vokey & Read, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.40.11.1231
A hiker notices that a rocky cliff face looks strikingly like a stern human profile from a certain angle and posts a photo online, where thousands of viewers also perceive the face despite knowing it is natural rock. (Sagan, 1995) https://archive.org/details/demonhauntedworl00saga
Participants shown Rorschach inkblots universally reported seeing faces, animals, and figures in the symmetrical abstract shapes, demonstrating how strongly the human perceptual system imposes meaningful forms onto ambiguous stimuli. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A piece of toast with an irregular burn pattern is submitted to an online auction after the owner reports seeing Jesus in the surface, attracting bids from thousands of people who also perceived the face. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
fMRI imaging studies showed that when people perceive a face in an object that is not a face, the fusiform face area activates in a pattern similar to viewing an actual human face, confirming the neural reality of pareidolia. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A person watching shadows move on a bedroom wall at night repeatedly perceives crouching human figures, even after realizing rationally that the shapes are caused by tree branches moving in the wind. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
column6:
Identifying objects only when evidence is clear.
 Recognizing random shapes as meaningless.
 Using instruments instead of intuition to interpret images.

A geologist correctly identifies the Martian Face as a mesa shaped by natural erosion and differential lighting after reviewing high-resolution images taken from multiple angles and publishes a detailed geological explanation. (Sagan, 1995) https://archive.org/details/demonhauntedworl00saga
An acoustics researcher plays backward recordings to participants without telling them what to listen for, and they report hearing only unintelligible noise rather than any meaningful message. (Vokey & Read, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.40.11.1231
A photographer who deliberately sets up lighting to make a cliff face look like a human profile acknowledges in their caption that the face-like appearance is an artifact of the shooting angle and does not exist from any other viewpoint. (Sagan, 1995) https://archive.org/details/demonhauntedworl00saga
A scientist who sees a face-like rock formation from one angle checks additional perspectives and correctly concludes the resemblance is angle-specific and not a real face. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A control group participant shown noisy grayscale images with no prior instruction reports seeing only abstract shapes and not faces, confirming that expectation is a key driver of pareidolia in other participants. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A parent correctly explains to a child that the man-in-the-moon appearance is caused by ancient volcanic plains and impact craters rather than an actual face carved into the lunar surface. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A product designer creates a household appliance with a purely geometric front panel, specifically avoiding any face-like arrangement of elements to prevent users from forming emotional anthropomorphic attachments to the device. (Windhager et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1068/p5996
A neuroscientist correctly notes that fusiform face area activation during pareidolia confirms a perceptual mechanism rather than actual face detection, and explains this distinction in a public lecture. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A person who briefly sees a face in wood grain correctly identifies it as a pattern projection and immediately moves on, rather than treating it as a meaningful or significant image. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A low-anxiety participant shown the same ambiguous noise images as high-anxiety participants correctly reports fewer perceived faces, consistent with research showing that threat sensitivity moderates face pareidolia. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A skeptic who is shown the grilled cheese sandwich image correctly identifies the pattern as a random burn mark produced by uneven heat and does not interpret it as a meaningful face. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
An artist who deliberately arranges geometric shapes to create a face in an abstract painting is intentionally exploiting face detection rather than experiencing pareidolia, because the face-like quality is designed rather than perceived in a random stimulus. (Windhager et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1068/p5996
A person who listens to white noise after reading about pareidolia correctly attributes their momentary sense of hearing a voice to a well-understood perceptual tendency rather than an actual external sound. (Vokey & Read, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.40.11.1231
A science teacher correctly informs students that Rorschach inkblots are symmetrical abstract shapes designed to elicit projection rather than images that contain hidden pictures to be found. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A hiker who notices a rock formation that resembles a face correctly describes it as a geological coincidence in their blog post and does not attribute any cultural or spiritual significance to the shape. (Sagan, 1995) https://archive.org/details/demonhauntedworl00saga
A psychologically trained observer correctly identifies that perceiving a skull in a rust stain is an instance of normal pattern-completion by the visual system rather than evidence of anything supernatural. (Shermer, 2011) https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195397697.003.0001
A team of NASA image analysts correctly applies image enhancement and terrain modeling to the Face on Mars photograph and confirms it is a natural landform before the findings are released to the public. (Sagan, 1995) https://archive.org/details/demonhauntedworl00saga
An infant who preferentially tracks a face-like dot pattern over a scrambled one is demonstrating an evolved perceptual bias rather than pareidolia, because the face-like stimulus is structurally face-like by design. (Johnson et al., 1991) https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2044-835X.1991.tb00892.x
A participant shown a photograph of a genuinely human face correctly perceives a real face rather than experiencing pareidolia, because the stimulus is actually a face rather than an ambiguous pattern onto which a face is being projected. (Liu et al., 2014) https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1400991111
A car owner who finds the front of their vehicle friendly-looking correctly recognizes this is because designers intentionally shaped the headlights and grille to suggest a face, not because they are projecting a face onto a random pattern. (Windhager et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1068/p5996

column3: Attributing human traits to non-human entities.
column4: Giving things human feelings
column5:
Talking to a pet as if it understands language.
 Naming a car and treating it like a person.
 Assuming a robot has emotions.
 Thinking weather is intentional.
 Believing a plant is 'happy' or 'sad.'

People who owned Roomba robotic vacuums described them as having distinct personalities, gave them names, and reported feeling guilty leaving them to clean alone, even knowing the devices were running preprogrammed instructions. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
Dog owners consistently interpreted their dogs' submissive body posture after a misdeed as a guilty expression, even though researchers showed the posture was a learned fear response to the owner's tone rather than an emotion-based display. (Horowitz, 2009) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.beproc.2009.03.002
A child who bumps into a chair scolds it for hurting them, treating the inanimate object as if it had acted with intention and is therefore responsible for the pain. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Stock market commentators routinely described the market as nervous, hopeful, fearful, or relieved, attributing emotional states to a statistical abstraction produced by millions of independent transactions. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Participants who felt socially isolated assigned significantly more human traits, including intentions, consciousness, and feelings, to a robotic weather forecasting system than participants who felt socially connected. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Users of the early chatbot ELIZA became emotionally attached to the program, disclosed personal information to it as if confiding in a therapist, and resisted being told it had no understanding of what they were saying. (Weizenbaum, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168
Ancient peoples attributed earthquakes, floods, and volcanic eruptions to the anger or punishment of humanlike gods rather than to geological and atmospheric processes. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Participants rated the front end of a car with wide round headlights as friendly and approachable, responding emotionally to the face-like configuration as if the vehicle had a personality. (Windhager et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1068/p5996
A person who regularly talks to their houseplants explains that the plants seem to enjoy the conversation and respond better when spoken to kindly, attributing comprehension and social responsiveness to organisms without nervous systems. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Lonely individuals in a study were significantly more likely to attribute human mental states and intentions to pet animals, believing their pets understood their emotions and deliberately acted to comfort them. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
An astronaut who worked closely with a specific robotic arm during a space mission reported feeling reluctant to hand it off to another crew, describing a sense of partnership and even affection for the machine. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
Children in an experiment assigned moral intentions and emotions to simple animated shapes, blaming a triangle for chasing a circle and praising a smaller shape for helping, based entirely on the movement patterns. (Hamlin et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1038/nature06288
A company ran an advertising campaign that gave their cleaning product a face, a name, and a friendly backstory, resulting in higher consumer trust and sales than versions of the product with purely functional packaging. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A person who loses a game of chess against a computer program accuses the program of playing dirty, attributing strategic malice and competitive gloating to a system executing mathematical search algorithms. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Participants in a charitable giving study donated significantly more money to help a single named and photographed child than to help a statistical description of thousands of unnamed children, responding to the identifiable individual as a fully human agent deserving of personal concern. (Slovic, 2007) https://doi.org/10.1007/s11211-007-0058-0
A person caring for a dying car that has served them for many years feels genuine grief at the thought of scrapping it, attributing loyalty and a life history to the machine as if it were a longtime companion. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A weather reporter described the approaching hurricane as angry and targeting coastal communities, using language that implied intention and agency in an atmospheric pressure system. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
Participants who interacted with a social robot that made eye contact, used gestures, and spoke in a warm tone reported that the robot was genuinely curious about them and seemed to care about their wellbeing. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
A toddler who drops their toy accidentally scolds the floor for making the toy fall, assigning blame and intention to the physical surface as if it had acted against them. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
People who played against a humanoid robot in a game showed clear signs of social comparison, including embarrassment when they lost and satisfaction when they won, treating the robot's performance as personally meaningful rather than as mechanical output. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
column6:
Recognizing machines lack emotions.
 Understanding animal behavior scientifically.
 Avoiding human-like interpretations of natural events.


A robotics engineer correctly reminds users in the product manual that the robot's movements and responses are the output of programmed instructions and sensor data, with no inner experience, intention, or personality. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
A dog behavior researcher correctly explains to a pet owner that the expression they interpret as guilt is a conditioned appeasement behavior triggered by the owner's tone rather than an emotion reflecting self-awareness of wrongdoing. (Horowitz, 2009) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.beproc.2009.03.002
A meteorologist correctly describes a hurricane using atmospheric pressure gradients, wind speed, and storm surge projections rather than using language that implies the storm has intentions or emotions. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A scientist who hears about ELIZA correctly notes that users' emotional attachments to the chatbot reflect a human tendency to project meaning onto pattern-matching outputs rather than evidence of machine understanding. (Weizenbaum, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168
An adult who accidentally bumps into a table correctly attributes the pain they feel to physics and their own lack of attention rather than to any intent on the part of the furniture. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A geologist correctly describes seismic activity in terms of tectonic plate movement and fault line stress rather than attributing the earthquake to the anger or intention of any supernatural force. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A financial analyst correctly describes market movements using supply, demand, and investor positioning data rather than attributing fear, greed, or hope to the market as if it were a single sentient actor. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A plant biologist correctly explains to a gardening enthusiast that plants respond to CO2 in exhaled breath, not to the words or emotional tone of the speaker, meaning talking to plants has no social dimension from the plant's perspective. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A developer who builds a conversational AI explicitly discloses in the interface that the system has no feelings, intentions, or inner life, and designs the interaction to avoid fostering emotional attachment. (Weizenbaum, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168
A participant in a study who was given a mechanistic explanation of robot behavior before interacting with it showed significantly reduced anthropomorphism scores compared to participants given no such explanation. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
A chess player who loses to a computer program correctly attributes the loss to the program's exhaustive search of move possibilities and their own error, rather than to the program playing with competitive intent. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A charity researcher notes that while individual victim stories increase donations, this response reflects a cognitive shortcut rather than a rational assessment of comparative need, and advocates for supplementing stories with statistical framing. (Slovic, 2007) https://doi.org/10.1007/s11211-007-0058-0
A car owner who feels affection for their old vehicle correctly identifies the feeling as nostalgia tied to memories of experiences had in the car rather than evidence of the car having any form of loyalty or reciprocal relationship. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A socially connected participant in the isolation study showed no significant increase in human trait attribution to machines, confirming that the anthropomorphism tendency is modulated by social need rather than being a fixed trait. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A toddler who has been gently corrected learns to say the toy fell rather than the floor did something mean, beginning to distinguish intentional agents from physical causes with parental guidance. (Epley et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864
A product designer who wants a device to appear purely professional and functional deliberately avoids face-like element arrangements, knowing that these would trigger anthropomorphic responses in users. (Windhager et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1068/p5996
A cognitive scientist correctly explains that children's tendency to assign intentions to animated shapes reflects their developing theory of mind rather than the shapes having any actual agency or inner states. (Hamlin et al., 2007) https://doi.org/10.1038/nature06288
An animal behavior expert correctly tells a pet owner that their cat knocking items off a table is likely driven by predatory instinct and exploratory behavior rather than by spite or a desire to get attention. (Horowitz, 2009) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.beproc.2009.03.002
A space mission controller correctly describes a robotic rover's decision-making as algorithmic path planning based on sensor input rather than as the rover choosing or wanting to explore a particular area. (Šabanović et al., 2006) https://doi.org/10.1109/ROBOT.2006.1642311
A user who has been educated about AI systems correctly describes a chatbot's responses as pattern matching trained on text data rather than as the chatbot thinking, understanding, or caring about what they said. (Weizenbaum, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168

column3: Assuming an individual's traits reflect their group, or a group's decisions reflect each member.
column4: Judging a whole group by one person's behavior
column5:
Believing a coworker is organized because their team is known for efficiency.
 Assuming a student is athletic because their school excels in sports.
 Thinking a neighbor is wealthy because their neighborhood is upscale.
 Believing a club member shares all the club's values.
 Assuming a colleague is introverted because their department is quiet.


After learning that a country's government voted against a trade deal, a citizen assumes that the entire population of that country must be opposed to free trade, ignoring the diversity of individual opinions within the nation. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A manager who attended a meeting where the marketing team collectively proposed a risky campaign assumes every individual on that team is personally reckless, ignoring that group decisions rarely reflect each member's private views. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A voter assumes that because their political party passed a controversial bill, every member of that party personally supports the bill, not recognizing that many legislators voted along party lines under pressure. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A student who hears that a sports team was fined for misconduct concludes that every player on the team must be dishonest, attributing the group's collective penalty to the character of each individual member. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
