A person reads that a company donated to a controversial political cause and immediately assumes all employees at that company personally support the cause, not considering that most had no input in the decision. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
Research participants who were told that a group voted in favor of a policy rated individual members of that group as personally more supportive of the policy than participants who were given no group information. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A customer who receives poor service from one employee of a company concludes that all employees of that company must be unfriendly and incompetent, extending an individual's behavior to the whole organization. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A spectator watching a country's athletes compete assumes the athletes personally endorse the policies of their government, attributing national political decisions to the traits of individual citizens who represent the country. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A jury member assumes that because a defendant belongs to an organization with a controversial reputation, the defendant personally holds all the views associated with that organization's leadership. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A neighbor learns that a religious congregation made a collective charitable donation and concludes that every individual congregant must be generous, attributing a group action to the personal traits of all members. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
Experimental studies showed that observers who learned a group had made a decision consistently rated individual group members as personally endorsing that decision at higher levels than the decision actually warranted. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A reader who sees that a university's faculty senate voted to adopt a new policy assumes every professor at the university personally supports the policy, not recognizing that many faculty were not involved or disagreed. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A journalist writes that a community group's official statement opposing a development project means residents in the neighborhood are united against it, when in fact many residents have mixed or supportive views. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
Research found that people attributed the characteristics of a group's formal negotiating position to each individual member of the group, assuming personal conviction where only collective strategy existed. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A patient who has a negative experience with one nurse at a hospital concludes that the entire nursing staff of that hospital must be poorly trained, using one person's behavior to characterize the group. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A person who learns a union voted to strike assumes every union member personally wanted to strike, ignoring the fact that strike votes are often close and reflect group decision rules rather than unanimous personal desire. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A traveler who is overcharged by one vendor in a foreign market concludes that merchants from that culture are universally dishonest, attributing one person's behavior to a shared trait across all members of the group. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A news consumer who reads that a political party blocked a piece of legislation assumes that every individual member of that party personally opposes the bill's goals, rather than recognizing that party votes involve complex strategic considerations. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
An employer who learns that graduates from a particular program performed poorly on average assumes any individual graduate from that program will be a poor employee, applying group-level statistics to individual-level hiring decisions. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A child who sees that a rival school's team cheated in a competition concludes that all students at that school are cheaters, using a group's behavior to infer the personal character of every member of the group. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
column6:
Evaluating a coworker solely on their individual performance.
 Asking a student about their own interests instead of assuming them.
 Recognizing that people in the same group can have very different views.


A manager who learns that a marketing team collectively approved a risky campaign interviews each team member individually before drawing conclusions about their personal risk tolerance, correctly distinguishing group decisions from individual attitudes. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A diplomat negotiating with a foreign delegation correctly notes that the group's official position may not reflect each delegate's personal views and privately consults individual members to understand the range of opinion. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A voter who disagrees with their party's platform on one issue correctly recognizes that their individual views can diverge from the group's official stance, demonstrating awareness that group membership does not determine personal opinion. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A researcher correctly notes in their analysis that group-level voting behavior cannot be used to infer individual-level attitudes, which is a textbook example of the ecological fallacy rather than the group attribution error. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A customer who receives poor service from one employee correctly files a complaint about that individual rather than concluding that all employees of the company must share the same shortcoming. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
An HR manager who reviews a department's collective performance metrics correctly recognizes that individual employees within the department may vary significantly and evaluates each person separately before making promotion decisions. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A journalist correctly distinguishes between an organization's official statement and the personal views of its members, noting in the article that internal disagreement on the issue is widespread among those within the group. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A traveler who is treated kindly by one person in a new city correctly notes the interaction as a positive individual experience rather than drawing conclusions about the character of all people from that city or culture. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A social psychologist correctly explains to students that a group decision reflects the aggregation of individual inputs under social influence and structural rules, not the unanimous personal preferences of all members. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
An employer who learns that graduates from a particular program performed below average on a test asks follow-up questions about individual candidates rather than automatically rejecting all applicants from that background. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A jury member who hears that a defendant belongs to an organization with a controversial reputation is instructed by the judge to evaluate only the defendant's individual actions and not infer personal beliefs from group membership. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A parent correctly tells their child that even though one player on a rival team cheated, it would be unfair to conclude that all students at that school are dishonest since people within a group can behave very differently. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A patient who has a bad experience with one nurse explicitly tells the hospital administrator that their complaint is about that individual and should not be taken as a judgment of the nursing staff as a whole. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A consumer who reads that a company donated to a political cause correctly recognizes that the decision was made by a small group of executives and does not reflect the personal views of the company's thousands of employees. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A student who learns that a university faculty senate adopted a new policy correctly asks whether the vote was unanimous or contested, recognizing that a group decision may not represent the views of every individual within it. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A union member who voted against a strike correctly points out to friends that the strike vote result does not mean every member personally wanted to stop working, and that many like herself voted no. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A sociologist correctly explains in a lecture that attributing a group's collective behavior to the shared personal traits of all its members is a logical error, and distinguishes between group dynamics and individual disposition. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A reader who sees a news story about a congregation's collective charitable gift correctly notes that not every individual in the congregation may be personally generous, since group participation does not guarantee individual motivation. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A political scientist correctly explains that a legislative party's bloc vote reflects institutional coordination and loyalty rather than the uniform personal policy preferences of each legislator. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A spectator watching an international sports competition correctly separates their admiration for an individual athlete's performance from any assumptions about that athlete's personal political views or endorsement of their government's policies. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466

column3: Explaining out-group failures as internal flaws and in-group failures as external circumstances.
column4: Blaming bad behavior on the group someone belongs to
column5:
Excusing your team's loss as bad luck but blaming the rival team's loss on incompetence.
 Assuming your group's mistake was due to pressure but another group's mistake was due to laziness.
 Believing your political group acted under constraints but the other acted maliciously.
 Explaining your culture's problems as situational but others' as inherent.
 Seeing your friend's failure as circumstantial but a stranger's as personal.


After a Black student wins a math competition, white classmates assume he must have gotten lucky or had extra help, but when a white student wins the same competition they credit his natural intelligence. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A sports fan whose team loses blames the referee for bad calls, but when the rival team loses the same fan says their opponents just weren't good enough. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
When a member of a rival political party makes a mistake in a speech, people say it proves the whole party is incompetent, but when their own party makes the same mistake they say it was just a bad day. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A manager assumes that when her team misses a deadline it was because of difficult circumstances, but when the competing department misses a deadline she concludes they are disorganized and lazy. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
Research found that people consistently explained negative behavior by out-group members as reflecting their bad character, while explaining the same behavior by in-group members as caused by bad luck or outside pressure. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
When a woman CEO's company fails, observers in a study were more likely to say she lacked leadership ability, but when a male CEO's company failed they were more likely to blame the economy. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A student who cheats on a test is seen by a rival classmate as proof that his whole friend group has no integrity, but when the classmate's own friend cheats it is explained away as stress from a tough semester. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
White participants in a study rated identical aggressive behavior as more threatening and intentional when the person acting was Black, attributing it to character rather than to the situation. (Duncan, 1976) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.34.4.590
A neighbor assumes that when a family from a different ethnic background has a noisy party it reveals something about their culture, but when their own family does the same thing they say it was just a one-time celebration. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
When a foreign country's economy grows, politicians argue it was due to favorable geography and cheap labor, but when their own country's economy grows they credit smart policy and national work ethic. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A coach whose team wins credits the players' talent and hard work, but when the opposing team wins the same coach attributes it to favorable scheduling and lucky breaks. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
Experimental participants told that a person from a disliked group helped someone in need explained the helpful act as self-interest or an exception, while the same act by an in-group member was seen as genuine kindness. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A hiring manager dismisses a strong interview from a candidate of a different background as the candidate just being well-rehearsed, but gives full credit for the same performance to a candidate from a familiar background. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A news commentator explains a crime committed by a member of an immigrant community as evidence of cultural values, but explains the same crime committed by a native-born person as a result of personal hardship. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
When a study found that students from one racial group scored lower on a test, some observers immediately attributed it to inherent ability differences rather than to systemic educational disadvantages. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A voter whose candidate loses an election concludes the voters who chose the other side were manipulated by media, but when their own candidate wins they say the public made a smart and informed decision. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A parent assumes that when a child from their neighborhood gets in trouble at school it was because of peer pressure and a tough week, but when a child from a poorer part of town gets in trouble they blame the family. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
Members of one religious group who read about a charity donation made by their own group saw it as genuine generosity, while the same donation made by a rival religious group was dismissed as a publicity stunt. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A doctor who is told a patient from a lower-income area did not follow a treatment plan assumes they are irresponsible, while attributing the same noncompliance in a middle-class patient to complicated life circumstances. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
When a university run by one group receives poor ranking scores, rivals say it confirms the group lacks academic rigor, but when the university improves its scores the same rivals attribute the change to grade inflation. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
column6:
Acknowledging that both groups face similar external pressures.
 Judging individuals from another group by their specific context.
 Admitting your own group can be at fault internally too.


A judge who applies a consistent sentencing standard explicitly reviews whether situational factors were considered equally for defendants from all backgrounds before issuing a ruling. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A teacher who notices she is harder on students from certain backgrounds deliberately blind-grades papers to make sure her assessments are based on the work itself rather than who produced it. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A sports analyst reviewing two teams' losses correctly applies the same framework to both, examining coaching decisions and player fatigue as situational causes regardless of which team is being discussed. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A researcher who studies inequality explicitly trains themselves and their team to apply the same causal explanation standards to positive and negative outcomes across all groups in their study. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A manager who receives two similar performance reports from employees of different backgrounds applies the same evaluation criteria to both and reaches the same conclusion about the causes of each outcome. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A journalist covering two communities affected by the same economic downturn applies the same structural analysis to both, avoiding the tendency to explain one community's struggles as cultural and the other's as situational. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A coach who reflects on a loss correctly identifies a tactical mistake her own team made rather than attributing the defeat entirely to referee bias or bad luck. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A hiring panel that uses structured scoring rubrics applied equally to all candidates avoids drawing on group membership to explain why a particular candidate performed well or poorly in the interview. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A parent who catches both their own child and a neighbor's child misbehaving at the same time holds both equally accountable and applies the same explanation for the behavior to each child. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A voter who reflects carefully acknowledges that both their preferred candidate and the opposing candidate have had successes driven by favorable conditions and failures driven by bad decisions, without attributing this asymmetrically. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A social psychology student correctly explains to classmates that the ultimate attribution error involves applying different causal rules to in-group and out-group behavior, and gives examples of what it would look like to reason without that bias. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A doctor reviewing patient noncompliance data across a hospital correctly identifies that structural barriers like transportation and cost explain missed appointments equally across patient demographic groups. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A news editor reviewing coverage of crime stories notices that situational context is being provided for suspects from one background but not another, and revises the style guidelines to require consistent framing. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A student who loses a debate competition correctly attributes the loss to being less prepared and having weaker arguments rather than blaming the judges or assuming bias against his team. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
An executive who reads about a competitor's company succeeding acknowledges that the competitor made smart strategic decisions rather than attributing the success entirely to luck or an unfair advantage. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A community organization working across cultural groups explicitly teaches members to ask the same questions about cause and context when evaluating the actions of any group, including their own. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A political scientist correctly points out in a paper that both the party being studied and their opposition have won and lost elections due to a mix of strategic choices and external circumstances rather than fixed group traits. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686
A diversity trainer who runs a workshop on attribution errors asks participants to apply the same explanatory lens to a failure story about their own group that they just applied to a failure story about an out-group. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A parent who watches two children from different backgrounds argue at the playground waits to hear both sides before drawing any conclusions about why the conflict started, applying equal curiosity to both. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
An athlete who wins a competition correctly credits both their preparation and the favorable conditions of that day rather than attributing the win entirely to superior natural talent. (Pettigrew, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.10.1686

column3: Assigning traits to individuals based solely on group membership.
column4: Assuming all group members act the same
column5:
Assuming a programmer likes video games.
 Believing artists are emotional.
 Thinking tall people play basketball.
 Assuming older adults dislike technology.
 Believing scientists are introverted.

A job recruiter spends less time reading resumes with names that sound like they belong to a minority group, assuming before even looking at the qualifications that those candidates are less likely to be a good fit. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A teacher calls on boys more often during science class because she unconsciously expects them to be better at the subject, even though the girls in the class perform equally well on tests. (Sadker & Sadker, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1177/003172171409500413
A store security guard follows a young Black man around the store without any reason to suspect him, acting on an assumption based entirely on race and age rather than actual behavior. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A nurse assumes an elderly patient does not want detailed information about their treatment options because she believes older people prefer to just follow doctor's orders rather than make their own decisions. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A teenager at a party avoids talking to a group of kids wearing leather jackets because he assumes they must be troublemakers based on how they look, even though he has never met any of them. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A human resources manager assumes a female candidate applying for a senior leadership role will eventually want to take time off for family reasons, and passes her over for someone less qualified. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
Research found that people expected Asian students to be good at math before ever seeing their grades, and that this expectation affected how teachers and peers interacted with those students. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A doctor spends less time explaining pain management options to a Black patient than to a white patient with the same condition, reflecting an assumption that Black patients tolerate pain differently or will be less compliant. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A bank loan officer rates a business application less favorably after learning the applicant is from a low-income zip code, assuming the person is a financial risk based on address rather than the actual business plan. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
An interviewer assumes a candidate who speaks with a regional accent is less educated and less professional, and rates them lower on a job suitability scale before they have even answered a single question. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A gym member assumes the person in the plus-size body next to them on the treadmill must be new to exercise and out of shape, not considering that the person could be a marathon runner who simply has a larger build. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
Studies found that people rated identical essays as less intelligent when told the author was a woman compared to when told the author was a man, showing how gender stereotypes affect even objective-looking judgments. (Sadker & Sadker, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1177/003172171409500413
A parent assumes their son is not interested in dance class because boys do not typically enjoy that kind of activity, and does not even ask him if he wants to try it. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A police officer pulls over a car driven by a young Latino man in an expensive vehicle, assuming the car must be stolen because the driver does not fit the stereotype of someone who could afford it. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A college advisor steers a first-generation student away from applying to competitive universities, assuming without evidence that the student would not fit in or succeed in a demanding academic environment. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A person at a networking event spends the night talking only to people who seem to match their idea of what a successful person looks like, and walks past others whose appearance does not fit the mental template. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
An employer assumes a job applicant with a disability will need excessive accommodation and special treatment, and decides not to call them for an interview before asking a single question about their abilities. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A student assumes the quiet classmate who recently moved from another country must not speak English well and does not try to start a conversation, when in fact the classmate is perfectly fluent. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
Research participants shown identical customer service complaint letters rated the person as more aggressive and less reasonable when told the writer was Black compared to when they were told the writer was white. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A real estate agent unconsciously spends more time showing properties in certain neighborhoods to white buyers and different neighborhoods to Black buyers, steering clients based on race rather than their stated preferences. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
column6:
Asking someone about their interests instead of assuming them.
 Recognizing that group labels don't predict personality.
 Hiring based on skills and evidence rather than group traits.

A hiring panel that uses blind resume review removes all names and demographic information before evaluating candidates, ensuring that assessments are based only on skills and experience rather than assumptions about group membership. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A teacher who notices she calls on boys more often in class deliberately uses a random name-picker for the rest of the semester to give all students an equal chance to participate regardless of gender. (Sadker & Sadker, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1177/003172171409500413
A loan officer who reviews an application evaluates only the credit history, income documentation, and business plan provided rather than drawing any conclusions based on where the applicant lives or what their name sounds like. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A doctor who treats patients from many different backgrounds uses the same detailed pain assessment protocol with every patient, ensuring no group receives less thorough care based on assumptions about tolerance or compliance. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A gym member introduces themselves to the person next to them on the treadmill without making any assumptions about their fitness level or experience based on body size or appearance. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A college advisor encourages a first-generation student to apply to competitive schools after reviewing their grades and test scores, without assuming the student's background predicts how they will perform academically. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A parent asks their son if he wants to sign up for dance class the same way they would ask about any other activity, without assuming his gender means he would not enjoy it. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A security guard who notices genuinely suspicious behavior in the store investigates based on what the person is doing rather than what they look like, and applies the same standard to every person in the store. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A student who joins a new class introduces themselves to a classmate who recently moved from another country by simply asking about their interests, without assuming anything about their language ability. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
An employer reads through an applicant's entire portfolio and work samples before forming any opinion about their capabilities, not allowing the applicant's disability status to influence the evaluation before seeing the evidence. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A real estate agent who shows a buyer several neighborhoods asks the buyer directly what features matter most to them and uses only those stated preferences to guide the search. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A police officer who observes a car commits a traffic violation pulls the car over for that specific infraction and interacts with the driver based on the situation rather than the driver's appearance. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
An interviewer who catches themselves making an early judgment about a candidate based on their accent deliberately pauses, resets, and focuses only on the content of the answers for the rest of the interview. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A nurse who is about to explain treatment options to an elderly patient stops and first asks how much detail the patient would like to know, rather than assuming the level of information appropriate for them. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
Participants in a study who were given training on recognizing stereotypes showed significantly reduced bias when evaluating identical resumes from candidates of different backgrounds compared to those who received no training. (Bertrand & Mullainathan, 2004) https://doi.org/10.1257/0002828042002561
A person at a networking event makes a point of introducing themselves to people whose backgrounds and appearances vary widely, deliberately avoiding the habit of gravitating only toward people who look like them. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A student who reads a review of a book before knowing the author's name forms a genuine opinion of the writing quality, and does not revise that opinion after learning the author is a woman. (Sadker & Sadker, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1177/003172171409500413
A manager evaluating team performance reviews each employee's output, attendance record, and client feedback before drawing any conclusions, without letting assumptions about any employee's background shape the assessment. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466
A social worker who is assigned a new client family reads the case notes and meets the family before forming any view of their situation, rather than drawing conclusions from the neighborhood they live in or their last name. (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0065-2601(08)60358-5
A journalist writing a story about a community affected by a policy change interviews residents across a wide range of ages, incomes, and backgrounds before drawing any conclusions, rather than assuming all members of the community share the same experience. (Allport, 1954) https://doi.org/10.2307/2089466

column3: Believing groups have inherent, unchangeable characteristics.
column4: Believing groups have fixed qualities that cannot change.
column5:
Thinking creativity is something people are born with.
 Believing certain cultures are naturally better at math.
 Assuming personality traits are fixed from birth.
 Thinking gender determines career ability.
 Believing intelligence is predetermined.

A parent tells their daughter that girls are naturally more emotional and less suited for careers in engineering, treating these traits as built-in features of being female rather than the result of culture and upbringing. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A teacher assumes that a student who struggles in math simply does not have the math gene, treating ability as a fixed biological trait rather than something that can grow with effort and practice. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A person argues that people from a particular country are naturally more aggressive because of their history, treating a complex social behavior as if it were an inherited biological characteristic of that group. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
An employer refuses to consider a job applicant for a leadership role because he believes introverts are naturally not cut out to be leaders, treating introversion as a fixed limit on what a person can do. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A teenager tells their friend that certain people are just born creative and others are not, believing that artistic talent is something you either have in your genes or you do not. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
Research found that when children were told that a group had a hidden biological essence that made them the way they are, they became more resistant to updating their beliefs about individual members who broke the group stereotype. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A coach tells a young player that speed is something you are born with and cannot be trained, leading the player to stop working on agility drills because they believe their potential is already determined. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A person insists that men and women think completely differently because of biology, using this as a reason to dismiss any evidence that socialization and culture might explain most of the observed differences. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
Children in a study were more likely to assume that a baby adopted at birth would grow up to share the traits of its biological parents rather than its adoptive parents, reflecting an essentialist belief that traits are carried in the blood. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A politician argues that poverty in a certain community is caused by that group's inherent lack of ambition, treating a complex economic situation as if it were the natural result of who those people are inside. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A student gives up on learning a second language after struggling for a few months because she believes language ability is something you are naturally wired for or not, and she has decided she simply does not have it. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A manager tells a nervous new employee not to worry about improving their public speaking because some people are just natural communicators and others will never be comfortable in front of a crowd. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A person who learns someone is adopted assumes that the adopted child will eventually turn out just like their biological parents regardless of how they were raised, because they believe nature overrides nurture. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A coach refuses to try a new training method because she believes athletic greatness is mostly genetic and that training can only do so much to change someone whose DNA is not elite-level. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A person argues that criminals cannot be rehabilitated because crime is driven by something deep inside certain people that therapy and programs cannot change, treating criminal behavior as a fixed internal trait. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A grandmother insists that her grandchildren who show musical ability got it from the family's musical blood, treating a complex skill shaped by practice and exposure as if it were passed down through genes like eye color. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
Research showed that adults who held essentialist beliefs about racial groups were significantly more likely to endorse racial stereotypes and less willing to update those beliefs when presented with counter-evidence. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A school counselor tells a student with dyslexia that reading will always be a struggle for her because of how her brain is wired, rather than encouraging evidence-based reading interventions that have been shown to work. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
Young children who were told that members of an unfamiliar group shared a hidden biological property were more likely to expect those members to all behave the same way, even after seeing evidence of individual differences within the group. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A person meets someone from a country they have negative stereotypes about and, even after a pleasant conversation, continues to believe the stereotype holds because they assume the person they met is an exception to an otherwise essential group nature. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
column6:
Accepting that people can change over time.
 Recognizing the role of environment and learning.
 Encouraging growth through practice and feedback.

A coach tells a struggling athlete that speed and technique are skills that improve significantly with the right training program, and designs a specific practice plan to help the athlete develop over the next season. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A teacher whose student is struggling in math tells them that mathematical ability grows through practice and persistence, and provides extra support rather than treating the difficulty as a permanent fixed trait. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A researcher studying gender differences in career outcomes correctly attributes the gap to structural barriers, social expectations, and unequal access to opportunity rather than to biological differences in ability. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A parent who notices their child struggling to read arranges for a literacy tutor, believing that reading is a skill that can be developed rather than a fixed ability the child either has or does not have. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A counselor helps a client work on social anxiety through therapy and gradual exposure, treating social confidence as something that can be learned and built over time rather than a personality trait that cannot change. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A person who meets someone from a country they had negative stereotypes about updates their view after the conversation, recognizing that their initial expectations were shaped by overgeneralizations rather than the reality of who that person is. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A teacher explains to her class that intelligence is not fixed at birth, and shares research showing that students who believe they can grow their abilities through effort actually perform better over time. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A hiring manager interviews candidates from backgrounds that do not match the typical profile for the role because she believes capability is shaped by experience and training rather than by fixed group traits. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A criminologist argues in a report that crime rates in a community are better explained by poverty, unemployment, and lack of educational access than by anything inherent to the people who live there. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A student who failed an exam decides to change their study strategy and seek tutoring rather than concluding that they are just not a math person and giving up on the subject entirely. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A parent tells their introverted child that leadership is a skill that can be developed in many different styles, and that being quieter does not mean they cannot become an effective leader one day. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A developmental psychologist correctly explains to a parent that a child's early temperament is not destiny, and that the environment, relationships, and experiences they have will shape who they become far more than any fixed biological essence. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A school administrator reviewing low test scores in one demographic group recommends an audit of teaching resources and support systems, treating the performance gap as a product of unequal inputs rather than fixed student traits. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A language learner who has been told they are not naturally gifted at languages decides to try a new method and practices daily for three months, eventually achieving conversational fluency and disproving the essentialist belief they had internalized. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A researcher conducting a study on creativity finds that it increases significantly with specific types of training and environmental support, publishing results that challenge the idea that creative ability is a fixed trait some people are simply born with. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A grandmother who notices her grandchildren differ widely in musical ability despite sharing the same family genes concludes that practice and early exposure must be the main drivers of musical skill. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097
A coach who attends a sports science seminar revises her belief that speed is purely genetic after learning that training can produce significant improvements in reaction time and acceleration even in adult athletes. (Dweck, 2006) https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.013
A politician responding to a question about poverty in a struggling community explains that decades of underfunding in education and housing, not any inherent trait of the residents, is the primary driver of the economic situation. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A social worker helping a client with a criminal record focuses on building new skills, expanding their social network, and addressing housing stability rather than treating the person's past as evidence of a fixed inner character. (Haslam et al., 2000) https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2000.18.2.113
A person who discovers that their sibling who was adopted early in life has very different personality traits from their biological family correctly concludes that environment and upbringing play a much bigger role in shaping who we are than shared biology alone. (Gelman, 2003) https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674038097

column3: Seeing objects only in terms of their traditional uses.
column4: Wheny you can't see how an object can be used in multiple ways.
column5:
Using a mug only for drinking instead of as a pen holder.
 Not realizing a shoe can hammer a nail.
 Failing to use a scarf as a makeshift rope.
 Ignoring that a phone flashlight can light a room.
 Not thinking to use a book as a doorstop.

A person whose glasses screw is loose cannot think to use a coin as a screwdriver to tighten it, because in their mind a coin is only ever money. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
In the classic candle problem experiment, most participants struggled to figure out that the small cardboard box holding the thumbtacks could be emptied and used as a shelf to mount the candle on the wall. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A person locked out of their car cannot think to use the wire from a notebook spiral as a slim jim tool, because in their mind wire is only for binding paper. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A camper who runs out of kindling cannot think to use the pages of an old paperback book as fire starter, because in their mind books are for reading and it feels wrong to use one differently. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
In an experiment where participants needed to connect two strings hanging from a ceiling that were too far apart to grab both at once, most people failed to realize they could tie a heavy pair of pliers to one string to make it swing like a pendulum. (Maier, 1931) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071938
A child trying to weigh down a paper airplane cannot think to use a paperclip as ballast even though there is a stack of them on the desk, because in their mind paperclips are only for holding paper together. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A nurse trying to open a sealed medication bottle without the correct tool cannot think to use the edge of her ID badge to pop the cap, because in her mind the badge is for identification only. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A student working on a science project cannot think to use a rubber band as a pulley anchor even though there are dozens in the supply box, because they only associate rubber bands with holding stacks of things together. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
Research found that participants who were shown the thumbtack box already full of tacks solved the candle problem far less often than participants who were shown the box empty and separate from the tacks, because the full box triggered only its storage function. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A person trying to prop open a window in a hot room cannot think to use the thick dictionary on the table as a window stopper, because in their mind a dictionary is only for looking up words. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
An office worker whose monitor stand breaks cannot think to use a thick three-ring binder to raise the screen to the right height, because binders are for filing documents and that function feels fixed and exclusive. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A hiker whose boot lace snaps cannot think to use the drawstring from their jacket hood as a replacement lace, because in their mind the drawstring serves only to tighten the hood opening. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A person who needs to measure something does not think to use a dollar bill, which is almost exactly six inches long, because in their mind money is for spending and not for measuring. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A designer trying to quickly illustrate proportions on a whiteboard cannot think to use the business card in their pocket as a scale reference, because they only think of business cards as contact-sharing tools. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
Studies of engineering students found they consistently failed to suggest using the materials available in novel ways during problem-solving tasks, defaulting instead to solutions that required tools not present, because they could only see each object in terms of its labeled function. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A teacher trying to keep papers from blowing off a desk in a breezy room does not think to use the stapler as a paperweight, because in their mind a stapler is a machine for fastening things and not a weight. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A person who needs to hang something on the wall temporarily cannot think to use a strip of masking tape folded back on itself as a hanger, because in their mind tape is for sticking two surfaces together and not for hanging objects. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A researcher who needed to keep a sliding laboratory drawer shut during an experiment did not think to use the rubber tip of a pencil eraser as a wedge, because pencils are for writing and not for mechanical tasks. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A person trying to press a restart button recessed inside a device cannot think to use a toothpick even though there is one nearby, because in their mind toothpicks are only for teeth. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A cook who runs out of a rolling pin cannot think to use a wine bottle filled with cold water to roll out pastry dough, because in their mind a bottle is a container for liquid and that is all. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
column6:
Using a paperclip to pick a lock in an emergency.
 Turning a box into a temporary table.
 Using a scarf as a bag strap when one breaks. 

A camper who runs out of lighter fluid immediately thinks to use hand sanitizer from their first-aid kit as an accelerant, because they focus on the functional properties of what they have rather than its label. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
In the candle problem experiment, participants who were given the thumbtacks presented separately from the box solved the problem much more often because the box's alternative use as a shelf was easier to see when it was not already playing its storage role. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A child asked to solve a puzzle with only the materials in front of them quickly suggests using a book as a ramp because they are focused on what they need rather than on what the object is normally called. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A nurse who cannot find the proper tool to hold a patient's IV line in place folds a piece of medical tape into a loop to create a makeshift clip, thinking past the tape's standard use. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
An engineer on a camping trip whose tent pole snaps uses a thick branch from a nearby tree as a replacement support, recognizing the physical properties needed rather than fixating on what a tent pole is supposed to look like. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A student in a design course who is taught to first list the physical properties of each object before trying to solve a problem comes up with significantly more creative solutions than students who are not given that instruction. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A cook who does not have a rolling pin immediately reaches for an empty wine bottle because they are thinking about what they need, which is a smooth cylinder, rather than the name of the tool they are missing. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
An office worker whose chair wobbles uses a folded piece of cardboard to stabilize the leg rather than waiting to find a proper furniture pad, thinking flexibly about what she has on hand. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A researcher who studies functional fixedness correctly explains that the bias is not inevitable and that it can be reduced by training people to think about what materials can do rather than what they are called. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A traveler who needs to prop a hotel door open uses their shoe as a doorstop without hesitation, easily moving past the shoe's primary function because their need is concrete and immediate. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A person trying to level a crooked picture frame immediately uses a small folded piece of paper as a shim behind the frame, thinking about the physical task at hand rather than what paper is normally used for. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A hiker whose boot lace breaks uses the drawstring from their jacket to replace it without having to think very hard, because the situation makes the physical need obvious and they focus on matching that need to what is available. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A teacher who leads a creative problem-solving workshop gives participants an exercise where they must list fifteen uses for a paper clip before tackling a challenge, and finds that participants who complete the exercise show significantly less functional fixedness in the main task. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A child who needs something heavy to hold down a tent corner during a windstorm immediately picks up a rock without needing to be told, because the problem frames what is needed so clearly that they think about the rock's weight rather than any other attribute. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A professional designer who regularly works with unconventional materials has no trouble suggesting that a binder clip could serve as a cable organizer on a desk, because years of creative work have weakened the fixed associations she might otherwise have with common objects. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A repair technician who needs a small wedge to hold two parts in position uses a folded matchbook without hesitating, because years of working with limited tools in the field have trained him to see physical properties before functions. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
Research found that people who were asked to generate multiple non-standard uses for objects before a problem-solving task were significantly more likely to solve that task creatively than those who were not given the warm-up activity. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
A parent helping their child build a cardboard fort immediately suggests using a clothes peg to hold two flaps together when they cannot find tape, seeing the clip's gripping function clearly because the need is right in front of them. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599
A person who needs to mark a page in a book and has no bookmark tears off a small corner of a receipt in their pocket to use as a marker, easily shifting their perception of the paper from something to be kept to something to be used functionally. (McCaffrey, 2012) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797612439593
An architect who needs to demonstrate a scale concept to a client on the spot uses their own hand as a reference object, pointing out that their palm width represents approximately ten centimeters, because the problem demands a solution and they focus on what will serve that need. (Duncker, 1945) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0093599

column3: Feeling licensed to act less morally after doing something moral.
column4: Thinking one good deed is enough.
column5:
Donating once and then feeling justified in ignoring future charity.
 Helping a friend and then being rude to a stranger.
 Recycling and then wasting energy later.
 Volunteering once and then judging others harshly.
 Making one ethical choice and then indulging in selfish behavior.

A person who donates to charity in the morning feels justified skipping the door when a collection box appears that afternoon, using the morning's good deed as a reason to do less later in the day. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
In a study, participants who had the chance to express a non-prejudiced opinion earlier in the experiment were significantly more likely to make a biased choice later, as if the earlier act had earned them permission to behave less fairly. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A manager who gave an employee a glowing public compliment earlier in the week felt comfortable delivering a harsher-than-usual performance review at the end of the month, reasoning unconsciously that the compliment had balanced things out. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who recycled their bottles and cans in the morning felt less guilty about leaving the lights on all evening, treating the eco-friendly act as a kind of environmental credit they could spend later. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
Research found that people who purchased an environmentally friendly product made a less ethical choice in a subsequent unrelated task, as if the first purchase had made them feel like a good person who had already done their part. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A voter who chose a candidate from a minority background felt more comfortable making a negative comment about that group later, reasoning that their vote proved they were not prejudiced. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A company that announced a large sustainability pledge then lobbied quietly against environmental regulations the following quarter, as if the pledge had given them credibility to balance against their ongoing behavior. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A person who spent an hour volunteering at a food bank felt entitled to eat an unhealthy meal afterward, treating the volunteer work as a wellness credit they could apply to their diet. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A study found that participants who were first asked to write about a time they had acted fairly were more willing to make a biased hiring recommendation afterward, using the memory of past virtue as a license for current bias. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A politician who had voted for a popular civil rights bill used that vote as a defense when criticized for later supporting a policy that harmed the same community, pointing to the old vote as proof of good character. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A person who helped a stranger with directions in the morning felt they had already been kind enough for the day and walked past a person who dropped their groceries without stopping to help. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
An employee who had stayed late to finish a project for a colleague felt that this act of generosity gave them the right to be short and dismissive in a team meeting the next week. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who had been particularly patient and kind during a stressful family visit allowed themselves to be rude to customer service staff on the drive home, feeling that the earlier effort at patience justified a little venting. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
Research showed that people who wore a shirt displaying a charity logo were less likely to donate money to a fundraiser immediately afterward, as if the public display of support had already fulfilled their sense of moral obligation. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A student who turned in a thoughtful assignment about social justice felt she had done enough for equity that week and did not bother to push back when a classmate made an exclusionary comment in the hallway. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who had exercised in the morning felt they had earned a larger lunch than they needed, treating the physical effort as a direct license to consume more food even though the two things are unrelated in a health sense. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A company executive who had publicly championed a diversity hiring initiative felt comfortable ignoring a complaint about a discriminatory comment from a colleague, reasoning that her track record on diversity had established her credentials. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A parent who had spent the whole morning being patient and engaged with their child felt justified in being distracted and dismissive for the rest of the afternoon, banking the morning's effort as permission to coast. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
Participants in a study who were allowed to recall a past act of bravery before a fear-inducing task rated themselves as less afraid than those who could not recall such an act, using the memory of past courage as a kind of emotional credential. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who had given up their seat on a crowded bus for an elderly passenger felt they had already done their good deed for the commute and ignored a pregnant woman who boarded at the next stop. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
column6:
Continuing to act kindly after doing a good deed.
 Reflecting on past good actions as motivation to do more good.
 Avoiding using past morality as an excuse for bad behavior.


A person who donated to charity in the morning sees another fundraiser that afternoon and donates again, because their giving is driven by consistent values rather than a sense that the first donation balanced their moral ledger. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A company that publicly commits to sustainability treats that commitment as the beginning of ongoing accountability rather than a credential that gives them room to behave less carefully in other areas. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A manager who gave an employee a public compliment continues to offer fair and consistent feedback in subsequent reviews, not treating the kind word as something that offsets harder feedback or excuses less careful evaluation later. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who recycled their bottles in the morning turns off the lights when they leave a room that evening because their environmentally friendly behavior reflects a genuine ongoing commitment rather than a daily quota they have filled. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A researcher who has documented their own past unbiased hiring decisions still uses a structured rubric for every new hire, not treating their good track record as a license to skip the fairness checks going forward. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A parent who was patient and engaged with their child all morning continues to be present and attentive in the afternoon because their parenting choices come from a stable set of values rather than a sense that they have used up their daily kindness quota. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A politician who voted for a civil rights bill feels no greater license to support harmful policies afterward because they understand that one good vote does not balance ongoing obligations to the communities affected. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A student who turned in a thoughtful paper about equity still intervenes when a classmate makes an exclusionary remark, because she sees advocacy as something that continues rather than something she has already completed for the week. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
Research found that participants who thought about their past good deeds but were then asked to explain specifically how those deeds were relevant to the current situation showed significantly less moral licensing than those who were allowed to rely on a vague sense of virtue. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
An executive who championed a diversity initiative continues to take complaints about discriminatory behavior seriously, viewing the initiative as one component of an ongoing responsibility rather than a credential that excuses future inaction. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A person who gave up their seat for an elderly passenger also stops to help a pregnant woman who boards at the next stop, because their willingness to be kind is not limited by a sense of having already met a daily obligation. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A voter who chose a candidate from a minority background does not take that choice as proof they cannot be biased, and continues to reflect on whether their assumptions and decisions treat people from that group fairly. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A person who exercised in the morning still chooses a nutritious lunch because their health choices come from long-term goals rather than a system of rewards where one good behavior cancels out a less healthy one. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
An employee who stayed late to help a colleague with a project continues to be collaborative and generous in meetings the following week because their work culture is built on consistent support rather than a tit-for-tat credit system. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
A study found that participants who were encouraged to think of their past moral behavior as the result of who they are rather than actions they had performed showed significantly reduced moral licensing effects, suggesting that identity-based framing reduces the credential effect. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who wore a charity logo shirt earlier in the day donates money at a fundraiser that evening, because wearing the shirt reflected genuine values rather than a substitute for real action. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
An employee who has a strong track record of fair and inclusive behavior at work continues to apply the same care to a new team member, not treating the track record as an excuse to be less attentive now. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who helped a stranger with directions in the morning helps another person later that day without thinking of themselves as having already used up their generosity for the day. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213
Research showed that participants who were reminded that their past good deeds happened in a different context than the current situation did not show the typical moral licensing pattern, suggesting that people can be prompted to avoid using unrelated past virtue as permission for current behavior. (Monin & Miller, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.1.33
A person who had been patient and thoughtful during a difficult family visit continues to treat customer service staff respectfully on the drive home, because their kindness does not operate on a budget that runs out after being spent. (Merritt et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797610371213

column3: Believing people get what they deserve, leading to victim-blaming.
column4: Thinking people get what they deserve.
column5:
Assuming a successful person must have worked hard.
 Believing good things happen to good people.
 Thinking misfortune reflects personal flaws.
 Assuming kindness guarantees good outcomes.
 Believing effort always leads to success.

A bystander who hears that someone was mugged assumes the victim must have been walking in an unsafe area late at night, reasoning that bad things happen to people who make bad choices rather than accepting that random misfortune exists. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A student who fails an exam is told by a classmate that she probably did not study hard enough, even though the classmate has no idea how much she studied, because it feels more comfortable to assume the outcome was deserved. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
Participants in an experiment who watched a person receive electric shocks and could not stop it began to rate the victim as less likable and less moral over time, finding it easier to believe the person deserved the pain than to accept that an innocent person was suffering. (Lerner & Simmons, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023562
A coworker who is laid off is told by colleagues that he probably was not putting in enough effort, even though the layoff was driven by company-wide budget cuts that had nothing to do with individual performance. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A person who gets very sick believes they must have done something to bring the illness on themselves, such as not eating well enough or not resting enough, because accepting that they got sick for no reason feels unbearable. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A community member who hears about a house fire assumes the homeowner must not have checked their smoke detectors, because believing the fire was purely random would make them feel vulnerable too. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
Jurors in a rape trial rated the victim as more responsible for what happened to her when she was described as having been at a party, even though the legal and moral responsibility lay entirely with the perpetrator. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A person who watches a documentary about poverty assumes that the people featured must have made poor financial decisions, rather than considering that structural inequality and lack of opportunity played a larger role. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
Research found that people who were told a lottery winner had won a large prize began to rate that person as smarter and more hardworking than before, as if winning the lottery was evidence of good personal qualities. (Lerner & Simmons, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023562
A patient recovering from cancer treatment is told by an acquaintance that she must have a strong will to live and a positive attitude, implying that patients who do not recover must not have tried hard enough. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A voter assumes that someone who has been imprisoned must be guilty because the justice system would not imprison an innocent person, making it psychologically easier to believe the system works fairly. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A teenager who hears that another student was bullied assumes the bullied student must have done something to bring the attention on themselves, because it is easier than accepting that bullying can happen to anyone. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A person who is passed over for a promotion at work tells themselves that the colleague who got it must have worked harder and been more deserving, rather than considering that favoritism or bias may have played a role. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
Participants shown photos of people described as having experienced misfortune rated those people as less attractive than they had before learning about the misfortune, as if looking unlucky was itself evidence of a flaw. (Lerner & Simmons, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023562
A child who watches another child get hurt on the playground tells a friend the injured child must not have been paying attention, even though they did not see what happened, because they need to believe they can avoid the same thing by being more careful. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A person who hears a news story about a car accident assumes the driver must have been speeding or distracted, because accepting that careful drivers sometimes get hit by others is more frightening than believing the victim was at fault. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
An employee who is unfairly treated by their manager tells a friend it is probably because she must have done something to annoy the manager, even though the manager's behavior was unjust and unprovoked. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
Research found that observers who could not help a suffering person tended to devalue the person's worth to reduce their discomfort, rating the victim as deserving of their fate as a way to restore psychological balance. (Lerner & Simmons, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023562
A person who hears that a friend's relationship ended assumes the friend must have been doing something wrong in the relationship, because believing a healthy relationship can simply fall apart without cause feels too random and threatening. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A wealthy person attributes their financial success entirely to their own hard work and intelligence, refusing to acknowledge the role of luck, family connections, or being born into better circumstances than others. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
column6:
Recognizing that bad things can happen to good people.
 Acknowledging the role of luck and systemic factors.
 Supporting victims without blaming them for their situation.

A social worker who helps a client who has been evicted correctly identifies the structural causes of the housing crisis rather than assuming the client must have made bad choices that brought the situation on themselves. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A juror who hears a rape case correctly focuses on the evidence and legal standards rather than assigning blame to the victim based on where she was or what she was wearing when the assault occurred. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A person who hears about a random mugging in a safe neighborhood correctly acknowledges that crimes can happen to anyone regardless of how careful they are, rather than concluding the victim must have done something to deserve it. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A doctor who treats a patient with a serious illness correctly explains that the disease has multiple complex causes and does not imply that the patient's lifestyle choices were the primary factor responsible. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A teacher who hears that a student was bullied focuses on stopping the bullying and supporting the student rather than wondering what the targeted student did to attract the negative attention. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A journalist covering a story about poverty correctly explains the structural and historical factors that concentrate economic hardship in certain communities rather than framing the story around the personal failures of the people affected. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A friend who hears that someone was passed over for a promotion acknowledges that workplace bias and internal politics can affect outcomes, rather than immediately assuming the person must not have worked hard enough. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A researcher studying wrongful convictions correctly explains that innocent people are sometimes convicted due to flawed evidence and systemic failures, without assuming that imprisonment is itself proof of guilt. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
Participants in a study who were allowed to help a person being harmed immediately stopped the suffering rather than devaluing the victim, showing that the ability to take action removes the motivation to believe the victim deserves the outcome. (Lerner & Simmons, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023562
A wealthy person who reflects honestly on their success acknowledges that being born into a stable family and having access to good education gave them significant advantages that others in their industry did not have. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A community member who hears about a house fire expresses sympathy for the family and helps organize donations rather than looking for a reason to believe the fire was the family's fault. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A person who gets sick accepts that illness sometimes happens to healthy people who do everything right, rather than searching for a personal choice or behavior to blame for their condition. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A student who fails an exam correctly reflects on how much time they actually put into studying and acknowledges that this time was the likely cause, rather than blaming the teacher or the test. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A coworker who hears about a colleague being laid off correctly recognizes that budget cuts and restructuring decisions are usually made for organizational reasons rather than as accurate reflections of individual performance. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
An advocacy organization fighting for criminal justice reform correctly explains to the public that being wrongly imprisoned is a real and documented phenomenon rather than proof that all those convicted must be guilty. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A person who hears that a careful driver was hit by a drunk driver expresses sympathy and focuses entirely on the other driver's recklessness, without looking for any way in which the victim could have prevented the accident. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
A school counselor who works with a bullied student focuses on the bullying behavior and the system that allowed it to continue rather than examining anything about the targeted student that might explain why it happened to them. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A person reflecting on a friend's relationship ending tells the friend they are sorry and listens without searching for something the friend must have done wrong, accepting that not all relationship endings can be traced to a clear personal failure. (Lerner & Miller, 1978) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.85.5.1030
