An economics professor correctly teaches students that wealth distribution is shaped by structural and historical factors that create unequal starting points, rather than being a straightforward reflection of individual effort and talent. (Lerner, 1980) https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4899-0448-5
A person who wins a lottery prize correctly recognizes that their win was the result of chance and does not take it as evidence of any special personal quality or effort on their part. (Lerner & Simmons, 1966) https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023562

column3: Assuming that if an argument contains a fallacy, its conclusion must be false.
column4: Rejecting a valid idea because of bad reasoning.
column5:
Rejecting a claim because someone argued it poorly.
 Dismissing a point due to a flawed analogy.
 Ignoring evidence because one example was weak.
 Rejecting a conclusion because a speaker misspoke.
 Assuming a belief is wrong because someone defended it badly.


A student argues that the theory of evolution must be wrong because she caught her teacher making a logical error while explaining it, assuming that a flawed argument for a claim automatically means the claim itself is false. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A debate student dismisses his opponent's conclusion that climate change is serious because the opponent committed an appeal to authority in their speech, reasoning that the bad argument proves the conclusion is incorrect. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A politician tells voters that because her opponent used a misleading statistic when arguing for a new tax policy, the policy itself must be bad, even though the underlying evidence for it may be solid. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A teenager tells his parents that their rule about curfews must be wrong because their reason for the rule did not make sense to him, not realizing that a bad explanation does not automatically mean the rule has no good basis. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A juror decides a defendant must be innocent because the prosecutor made an emotional appeal during closing arguments rather than presenting pure logic, treating the flawed argument as proof that the prosecution has no real case. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A reader online sees someone poorly argue in favor of a health intervention and concludes that the intervention cannot be effective, even though many well-designed studies actually support it. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A philosophy student argues that free will must exist because her professor's argument against it contained a false premise, not realizing that disproving one argument for a position does not establish the opposite position. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A manager rejects a proposal to improve team communication because the employee who presented it used a false analogy in their pitch, deciding the idea itself is worthless rather than evaluating it on its own merits. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A voter decides a ballot measure to fund public schools must be a bad idea because one of its supporters used a slippery slope fallacy in a speech, treating the flawed argument as evidence that the measure itself is flawed. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A scientist rejects a colleague's research finding because the colleague made a strawman error when defending it at a conference, not considering that the study's results might still be valid regardless of how poorly the colleague argued for them. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A child tells a parent that eating vegetables cannot really be important because the parent gave a bad reason for why vegetables are healthy, concluding that the recommendation is wrong because the explanation did not hold up. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
An employee dismisses a new workplace safety rule because the HR manager who introduced it used a misleading comparison to justify it, deciding the rule must be unnecessary rather than checking whether independent evidence supports it. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A social media user posts that vaccines cannot be safe because a pro-vaccine account made a logical error in a thread about them, treating the poor reasoning as proof the conclusion is wrong rather than looking at the scientific evidence directly. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A student tells his class that the theorem they are studying cannot be correct because the teacher's proof had a gap in it, not understanding that theorems can be true even when a particular proof attempt is flawed. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A journalist writes that a government report's conclusions must be wrong because the minister who released it made a circular argument at the press conference, incorrectly treating the bad presentation as evidence that the report's findings are false. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A person on a panel argues that since the person who proposed a budget cut used a false dilemma to justify it, the budget must not need to be cut at all, ignoring that the financial situation may genuinely require action regardless of how badly it was argued. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A book club member argues that a novel cannot have literary value because the person who recommended it gave a fallacious reason for why it was great, not recognizing that the quality of the book is independent of how well someone argued for it. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A patient decides not to take a medication because the pharmacist made a hasty generalization while explaining side effects, concluding that the drug must not be safe rather than seeking better information from other sources. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A politician argues that since his opponent used a red herring to defend a foreign policy position, the policy itself must be wrong, using the logical error in the defense as evidence against the position rather than examining the policy independently. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A student tells her study group that a historical claim their textbook makes cannot be accurate because the textbook author's reasoning in the surrounding paragraph was circular, not recognizing that a factual claim can be correct even when the argument given for it is poor. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
column6:
Separating the quality of reasoning from the truth of the conclusion.
 Re-examining a claim using better evidence.
 Accepting that a poorly argued claim can still be true.

A philosophy professor correctly explains to students that identifying a fallacy in an argument only tells you the argument is bad, and that you still need to look at evidence independently to decide whether the conclusion is true or false. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A debate coach tells her team that winning a round by pointing out a fallacy in the opponent's argument does not mean the opponent's position is wrong, just that the opponent argued for it poorly. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A scientist who hears a colleague make a logical error while defending a study result goes to read the study itself before forming an opinion about whether the result is valid. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A juror correctly notes that the prosecutor's emotional appeal was a logical fallacy but still evaluates the physical evidence and witness testimony independently before reaching a verdict. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A student who catches a gap in her teacher's proof correctly identifies it as an error in the proof rather than evidence that the theorem itself is false, and goes to look up a valid proof. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A voter who notices that a ballot measure's supporter used a slippery slope argument reads the independent fiscal analysis and public health research before deciding how to vote, not treating the bad speech as a verdict on the measure. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A reader who sees someone poorly argue in favor of a health intervention looks up the systematic reviews and clinical trials on the topic rather than using the bad argument as a reason to dismiss the intervention entirely. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A journalist who catches a minister making a circular argument at a press conference correctly describes the logical error in her article but notes that the underlying report's conclusions are supported by external data. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A manager who hears an employee use a false analogy to pitch an idea asks follow-up questions to evaluate the proposal on its merits rather than rejecting it outright because the analogy did not work. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A parent whose child says the curfew rule must be wrong because the explanation did not make sense correctly tells the child that the rule has other justifications and offers to explain them, rather than conceding the rule is wrong simply because one argument for it was weak. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A social media user who notices a logical error in a vaccine safety post looks up the original clinical trial data and public health records before forming an opinion about vaccine safety, not allowing the bad post to substitute for real evidence. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
An employee who hears a safety rule introduced with a misleading comparison asks their union rep to review the rule's basis in workplace safety regulations rather than dismissing it because the HR presentation was poorly argued. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A patient who hears a pharmacist make a hasty generalization about side effects asks the doctor for a more detailed review of the clinical evidence before deciding whether to take the medication. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A book club member who disagrees with a flawed argument for why a novel is great still reads the book before deciding whether they agree with the conclusion that it has literary value. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A student correctly explains to her study group that their textbook's claim about a historical event needs to be verified with primary sources regardless of whether the textbook's surrounding argument was circular. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A politician who identifies a red herring in an opponent's defense of a foreign policy still engages with the policy on the merits in their rebuttal, rather than treating the logical error as a complete refutation. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A scientist who hears a paper criticized for having a weak theoretical justification goes to examine the data and methodology independently before deciding whether the findings hold up. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A logic teacher correctly tells their class that pointing out a fallacy is always just the beginning of the analysis, not the end, because the truth of a conclusion has to be evaluated separately from the quality of the argument used to support it. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842
A teenager who catches a bad reason behind a house rule asks their parent for additional reasons before deciding whether the rule makes sense, recognizing that one weak justification does not prove a rule is groundless. (Engel, 1994) https://archive.org/details/withgoodreasonin0000enge_w6p5
A panel member who points out that a budget proposal was defended with a false dilemma asks for a detailed financial review of the actual numbers before recommending whether to cut or maintain the budget. (Damer, 2009) https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315664842

column3: Overtrusting automated systems and ignoring contradictory human judgment.
column4: Trusting a computer's answers more than your own.
column5:
Trusting GPS directions even when the road is closed.
 Accepting spellcheck suggestions without reviewing.
 Believing a medical device's reading without question.
 Letting software choose the best photo automatically.
 Relying on autopilot settings without checking.

Airline pilots who trusted an autopilot system that was giving incorrect altitude readings failed to catch the error in time because they had stopped actively monitoring the instruments themselves. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A radiologist reviewing scans with an AI assistant missed a tumor that was visible on the image because the AI did not flag it and the radiologist trusted the software's judgment over their own careful inspection. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A driver using a GPS navigation app followed its route directly into a closed road because the app had not been updated with the road closure and the driver did not question the instruction. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A nurse administered the wrong dose of a medication because the electronic health record system auto-populated a value and the nurse assumed the system had calculated it correctly without verifying manually. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
An accountant reviewing a budget report trusted the spreadsheet formula results without checking whether the underlying data had been entered correctly, missing a significant error because the computer output looked authoritative. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A soldier in a military exercise accepted the automated threat identification system's classification of an aircraft as hostile without independently verifying the signal, leading to a simulated friendly fire incident. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A student submitting a paper trusted the spelling and grammar checker to catch all errors and did not read through the paper themselves, missing several context errors that the software flagged as correct. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
An online shopper trusted the recommendation engine's top result without reading reviews or comparing alternatives, assuming the algorithm had already found the best product for their needs. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
Research found that workers in automated environments were significantly slower to detect system failures when automation was performing well most of the time, because they had reduced their independent monitoring of the system. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A warehouse manager approved a shipment without physical inspection because the automated inventory system confirmed the item count, not realizing the barcode scanner had counted one item twice. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A financial trader placed a large order without questioning it because the trading algorithm flagged it as optimal, even though market conditions had changed in ways the algorithm's training data had not anticipated. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A hiring manager rated a candidate higher after an AI screening tool gave them a high match score, even though the manager had not yet reviewed the candidate's actual work samples or references. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A self-driving car passenger failed to take control of the vehicle when the system began drifting toward a lane line because they assumed the system would correct itself, not realizing it had entered a scenario outside its operating parameters. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A teacher accepted the plagiarism detection software's clean report as definitive proof a student had not cheated, not realizing the student had paraphrased closely enough to avoid detection by the algorithm. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A doctor followed an electronic clinical decision support tool's recommendation for a treatment protocol without noting that the patient's allergy history, which was visible in another part of the record, contraindicated the suggested medication. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
An engineer cleared a mechanical system for operation because the automated safety diagnostic returned no warnings, without conducting a hands-on physical check that would have revealed a worn component not sensed by the diagnostic tool. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A journalist published a story that included a factual error because the automated fact-checking tool marked the claim as verified and the journalist did not independently confirm it with a primary source. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A parent believed a content filtering app had blocked all inappropriate material and stopped monitoring their child's online activity, not realizing the filter had failed to catch several categories of harmful content. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A border security officer waved a traveler through after the automated passport scanner cleared them, not noticing that the traveler's face did not closely match the passport photo because they trusted the machine's identification over their own visual check. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
Participants in a study were significantly more likely to follow an incorrect instruction given by a computer interface than the same incorrect instruction given verbally by a person, showing that automated sources are granted more trust than human ones even when they are wrong. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
column6:
Double-checking GPS directions against road signs.
 Questioning a suspicious medical reading with a manual check.
 Overriding an automated system when it clearly malfunctions.

A pilot who notices the autopilot is suggesting an unusual heading cross-checks it against the navigation chart and the air traffic control feed before following the instruction, rather than trusting the automated system without verification. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A radiologist who uses an AI flagging tool also personally reviews the full scan themselves before signing off, not relying solely on what the software highlighted or cleared. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A driver using GPS navigation who sees a sign indicating the road ahead is closed pulls over and checks the map manually rather than following the app's instruction to continue. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A nurse who sees that the electronic health record has auto-populated a medication dose manually recalculates it based on the patient's current weight and renal function before administering. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
An accountant who receives a spreadsheet from a colleague runs a manual spot-check on the key formulas before using the figures in the final report, not assuming the automated calculations are error-free. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A student who runs their paper through a grammar checker still reads the full document carefully before submitting, knowing that automated tools can miss context-dependent errors. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A hiring manager who receives an AI-generated candidate ranking reviews all of the top candidates' actual portfolios and references before forming a hiring recommendation, treating the algorithm as a starting point rather than a final answer. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A doctor who receives a clinical decision support suggestion checks whether it conflicts with any of the patient's documented allergies or other active prescriptions before following it. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A warehouse supervisor who receives a clean count from the automated inventory system still physically checks a random sample of items before approving the shipment. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A teacher who receives a plagiarism detection report showing no matches still reads through the student's paper for signs of unusual phrasing or ideas that do not reflect the student's prior work. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
An engineer who receives a clean automated safety diagnostic still performs a physical walkthrough of the system to check for anything the sensors might have missed before clearing it for operation. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A border security officer who receives a passport scanner clearance still looks carefully at the traveler's face and asks a follow-up question before waving them through, treating the automated result as one input rather than a final decision. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A journalist who receives a verified flag from a fact-checking tool still looks up the primary source themselves before including the claim in the published story. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A financial trader who receives an optimal trade recommendation from the algorithm reviews current market conditions manually before executing, making sure nothing has changed since the system was last updated. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
Research found that workers who received periodic training reminders about the limits of automated systems maintained significantly better independent monitoring habits than those who received no such training. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A parent who uses a content filter to restrict online access still regularly checks their child's browsing history and has open conversations about what they are watching, not assuming the filter has caught everything. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A self-driving car passenger stays alert and ready to take manual control throughout the trip, treating the automation as assistance rather than a replacement for their own attention and judgment. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
A military operator who receives a hostile classification from the automated threat identification system still follows the protocol of requesting a second human confirmation before authorizing any response. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3
A shopper who sees the algorithm's top recommendation still reads through several independent reviews and compares the product against alternatives before buying. (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010) https://doi.org/10.1177/0018720810376055
Participants in a study who were trained to treat automated outputs as one source of information among many rather than as authoritative verdicts showed significantly better error detection rates than untrained participants when the system gave incorrect results. (Mosier & Skitka, 1996) https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327108ijap0601_3

column3: Adopting beliefs or behaviors because many others do.
column4: Believing/Doing someting just because its popular.
column5:
Buying a product because it's trending.
 Supporting a sports team because everyone else does.
 Joining a social media challenge.
 Following a fashion trend without preference.
 Agreeing with a popular opinion to fit in.

A person who had no opinion on a political candidate changes their mind in favor of that candidate after seeing them consistently described as the frontrunner in the polls, wanting to be on the winning side. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A student who is on the fence about which extracurricular to join picks the one with the longest waitlist, reasoning that so many people wanting to join must mean it is the best option. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
Research found that when people were shown that a majority of their peers had donated to a charity, they were significantly more likely to donate themselves compared to when they were given no information about what others had done. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A teenager starts listening to a music artist she previously disliked after noticing that all of her friends are talking about the artist, deciding that so many people liking something must mean she was wrong about it. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
An investor puts their money into a stock that has been rising sharply, assuming that the large number of buyers must know something worth following, even though no new fundamental information has come out about the company. (Shiller, 2015) https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc7778s
A restaurant diner chooses the most popular item on the menu based on the note that says it is the house favorite ordered by most customers, even though they had been more interested in a different dish before seeing that label. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A small business owner adopts a new software platform not because it fits their specific needs but because everyone else in their industry seems to be switching to it, not wanting to be the only one left behind. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
Experiments found that when participants were told a list of statements had been endorsed by a large number of people, they rated those statements as more accurate and credible than identical statements without endorsement information. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A voter decides to support a constitutional amendment after seeing news coverage showing that public support for it has crossed 70 percent, switching from undecided to in favor based on the crowd rather than on the policy details. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A person downloads an app primarily because it is listed as the number one most downloaded app in the store that week, trusting the crowd's collective choice over their own assessment of whether the app suits their needs. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A fashion trend spreads rapidly not because most early adopters genuinely love it but because each new adopter sees others wearing it and assumes it must be good, creating a cascade driven by social proof rather than individual preference. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
During a financial bubble, ordinary investors buy into an overvalued asset because they see prices rising and conclude that the growing crowd of buyers must know something, only to lose money when the bubble bursts. (Shiller, 2015) https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc7778s
A scientist submits their paper to a journal that has recently become the most cited in their field, not because it is the best fit for the work but because submitting where everyone else wants to be published feels like the right move. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A parent enrolls their child in the tutoring program that all the other parents in the school seem to be using, assuming that widespread adoption by the community is evidence of the program's quality even though no independent evaluation has been done. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A community member begins to support a new neighborhood development project after a local leader announces that the majority of residents have already signed a petition backing it, changing their previously skeptical view in response to the apparent consensus. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A job applicant lists a popular framework on their resume primarily because it appears on nearly every other resume in their field, not because they have strong expertise in it, wanting to fit in with what the crowd is signaling. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A new employee immediately agrees with the dominant opinion in their first team meeting after noticing that everyone else in the room seems to share that view, not wanting to be the only dissenter even though they privately have reservations. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
Research found that hotel guests who were told most guests in the same room had reused their towels were significantly more likely to reuse their own towels than those who received only a general environmental message, showing that knowing what the crowd does directly influences behavior. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A musician releases a song that gets an early burst of streams from a promotional push, and the increased popularity ranking then attracts many more listeners who choose the song primarily because it appears to be trending, regardless of its actual quality. (Shiller, 2015) https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc7778s
A country adopts a new education policy primarily because several neighboring countries have already implemented it, with policymakers citing widespread adoption as the main argument for change rather than independently evaluating whether the policy fits their own context. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
column6:
Choosing a product after independent research despite its unpopularity.
 Supporting an unpopular but well-reasoned position.
 Refusing to join a trend that doesn't match your values.

An investor who notices that a stock is rising sharply reviews the company's fundamentals and earnings data before deciding whether to buy, concluding the price run is not supported by the underlying business and choosing to stay out. (Shiller, 2015) https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc7778s
A voter who hears that a ballot measure is leading in the polls reads the full text of the measure and reviews independent fiscal analyses before deciding how to vote, not changing their position based on what others seem to be doing. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A scientist who sees that a particular journal has become the most popular submission destination in their field still evaluates which venue provides the best peer review process and audience fit for the specific paper before submitting. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A restaurant diner who notices the most popular item on the menu still orders the dish that matches their dietary preferences and taste, recognizing that crowd popularity does not predict whether they personally will enjoy it. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A student who sees a long waitlist for one extracurricular activity still signs up for the activity that most closely matches their genuine interests and goals rather than letting the crowd's demand determine their choice. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A small business owner who notices competitors switching to a new software platform researches whether the platform actually meets their own business requirements before adopting it, rather than switching just because everyone else has. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A teenager who notices her friends all listening to a new artist gives the music a listen and decides it is genuinely not her style, maintaining her own preference rather than adopting the crowd's taste. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A new employee who has reservations about the team's dominant opinion raises their concern respectfully in the meeting rather than going along with the crowd, providing a different perspective based on their own analysis. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
Participants in a study who were explicitly told to evaluate a list of statements based on their own knowledge and reasoning showed significantly less influence from crowd endorsement information than those who were not given that instruction. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A hotel guest who reads the towel reuse message notes that they always reuse towels when traveling regardless of what other guests do, making their behavior driven by a personal environmental commitment rather than social proof. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A policy analyst who is asked to evaluate an education reform that several countries have already adopted independently reviews the outcome data from those countries before making a recommendation, not treating widespread adoption as sufficient evidence of effectiveness. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A person who sees a trending app in the top download chart reads through the reviews and checks whether the app addresses a need they actually have before downloading, not using its popularity alone as a reason to get it. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A job applicant lists only the frameworks they have genuine expertise in on their resume, not adding popular terms simply because they appear frequently on other people's profiles. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A community member who hears that most residents have signed a petition supporting a development project goes to a public meeting to hear the details before deciding whether to add their name, treating the majority's action as a prompt to investigate rather than a signal to follow. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A musician who receives a modest initial streaming boost continues to invest in improving their songwriting craft rather than tailoring their next release to match whatever is currently trending on the charts. (Shiller, 2015) https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc7778s
A parent who hears about a popular tutoring program looks up its independent evaluation results and asks to speak with parents whose children have completed it before enrolling, not treating its widespread use as proof of quality. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
A person who sees a fashion item appearing everywhere still decides not to buy it because it does not fit their personal style, distinguishing between what is popular and what is right for them. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104
A charity donor who sees that many peers have given to a particular organization still researches the organization's effectiveness rating and financial transparency before deciding whether to give, not letting the crowd's behavior substitute for their own evaluation. (Cialdini, 2001) https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.56.4.320
An investor who sees a stock trending on social media correctly identifies that the price spike is driven by momentum and speculation rather than fundamentals, and chooses not to participate in what they recognize as a crowd-driven bubble. (Shiller, 2015) https://doi.org/10.2307/j.ctvc7778s
A scientist reading a paper that has already accumulated thousands of citations evaluates its methodology and conclusions on their own merits rather than treating the high citation count as a reason to accept its findings without scrutiny. (Sunstein, 2003) https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X03000104

column3: Experiencing real changes due to belief in a treatment rather than the treatment itself.
column4: feeling better from a treatment even if it didn't actually do anything.
column5:
Feeling pain relief after taking a sugar pill.
 Sleeping better after drinking 'relaxation tea' with no active ingredients.
 Improving mood after a fake vitamin.
 Believing a workout supplement boosts energy when it doesn't.
 Feeling calmer after a 'stress patch' with no chemicals.

Patients who took a sugar pill they were told was a powerful painkiller reported significantly less pain than patients who received no treatment at all, even though the pill contained no active ingredient. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A runner who was given a sports drink and told it would improve their endurance ran measurably longer before exhaustion than a runner given the same drink but told it was plain water. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
Patients with irritable bowel syndrome who were openly told they were receiving a placebo still showed clinically significant symptom improvement compared to a no-treatment control group, even when fully aware the pill had no active ingredient. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A person who was told their cup of coffee contained a double shot of espresso reported feeling noticeably more alert and energized than when drinking the same amount of coffee without that information, even when the caffeine content was actually identical. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
Patients with Parkinson's disease showed measurable improvements in motor function after receiving saline injections they were told were an effective new drug, with brain imaging confirming increased dopamine release in response to the expectation of treatment. (de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1060937
A student who was told the energy bar they ate before a test was specially formulated to improve focus and memory scored higher on the subsequent exam than students who ate the same bar without that framing. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
Patients who received fake acupuncture with retractable needles that did not penetrate the skin reported similar levels of pain relief to patients who received real acupuncture, because both groups expected the treatment to work. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A child who was given a brightly colored vitamin C tablet and told it would make them feel better recovered from a cold more quickly than expected, with parents noting the child seemed more motivated to rest and take care of themselves after receiving the treatment. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
Research found that patients who received more elaborate and attentive interactions with their doctor before taking a placebo reported significantly greater symptom relief than patients who received the same placebo with minimal interaction, showing that context shapes the placebo response. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A person who rubbed a branded name-brand cream onto their arm after a minor burn reported that the area felt cooler and healed faster than when they used an unbranded version of the identical formula, reflecting the expectation of quality attached to the familiar brand. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
Patients who were told they were receiving a new expensive medication showed significantly greater improvement in depression symptoms than those told they were receiving a cheap generic version, even though both groups were actually given the same placebo pill. (Waber et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1001/archinternmed.2007.72
An athlete who was given a placebo that they believed was a legal performance-enhancing supplement lifted more weight in a strength test than in a previous session without the supplement, showing that the belief in the treatment was sufficient to change the outcome. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A person with chronic headaches who was treated with a blue placebo pill reported faster relief than one treated with a red placebo pill, showing that even the color of an inert treatment can affect its perceived effectiveness. (de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1060937
Research on surgical placebo found that patients who underwent a sham knee surgery in which only small incisions were made without any actual repair reported the same levels of pain relief and functional improvement as patients who had the real surgical procedure. (Moseley et al., 2002) https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa013259
A person who drank dealcoholized beer they were told was a regular beer reported feeling more relaxed and socially confident, even though no alcohol was actually consumed, demonstrating that expectations about a substance can produce its psychological effects. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
Patients in pain who pressed a button they believed would administer extra painkiller through their IV reported lower pain scores than those who had no button, even though in some conditions pressing the button delivered no additional medication. (Waber et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1001/archinternmed.2007.72
A student who was told that the chair they were sitting in had been used by top performers in previous years felt more confident and scored higher on a creativity test than students who were given no such information about the chair. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
Patients who saw a doctor wearing a white coat and speaking with authority reported better outcomes from a placebo treatment than patients who received the same treatment from someone dressed casually and speaking hesitantly, showing that the ritual of medicine itself drives part of the response. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A person with insomnia who was given a placebo sleeping pill and told it was a highly effective new sleep aid fell asleep faster and reported sleeping more soundly than in previous nights when they had gone to bed with no treatment at all. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
Research found that patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy who were given saline drips but told it might cause nausea actually reported nausea in response to the false expectation, demonstrating a nocebo effect that is the mirror image of the placebo response. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
column6:
Experiencing no change after taking an inert pill you don't believe in.
 Improving only after receiving an active, evidence-based treatment.
 Showing symptoms that don't respond to fake treatments but do respond to real ones.

A patient with a bacterial infection who takes a real antibiotic recovers because the drug directly kills the bacteria, not because they believed it would work, and a control group given a placebo in the same study did not recover at the same rate. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A person with a broken bone heals because of the mechanical process of bone regeneration, which occurs regardless of whether the patient believes their cast is effective, meaning expectation is not driving the recovery. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A runner given a sports drink containing actual electrolytes and carbohydrates during a long race performs better than a runner given plain water, with the improvement attributed to the drink's real physiological effects rather than to expectation. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A patient with a severe vitamin D deficiency who starts taking real vitamin D supplements sees their blood levels return to normal, a measurable biological change that cannot be explained by expectation alone. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A researcher conducts a blinded trial in which both groups improve similarly after a new drug, but biological markers show actual changes in the drug group that are not present in the placebo group, confirming that the drug is producing real effects beyond expectation. (de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1060937
A diabetic patient whose blood sugar remains high after taking a sugar pill that they believe is insulin demonstrates that expectation cannot substitute for the biological action of actual insulin, and the condition continues to deteriorate without real medication. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A student who drinks actual caffeine and studies for a test shows improved alertness and attention compared to a student who drinks decaffeinated coffee without being told, demonstrating that the performance benefit came from the drug's pharmacological action. (Waber et al., 2008) https://doi.org/10.1001/archinternmed.2007.72
A patient who is clearly informed that the pill they are receiving is an inert sugar tablet and that no placebo effect has been observed for their specific condition shows no change in symptoms compared to a no-treatment group. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A child with a strep throat infection that requires antibiotics does not recover from taking a vitamin C tablet their parent describes as medicine, because the infection's physical cause cannot be resolved by expectation or belief. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A clinical trial finds that a new cancer drug outperforms a placebo not just on patient-reported symptoms but on objective tumor reduction measured by imaging, confirming that the drug is producing biological effects that cannot be attributed to expectation. (de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1060937
A person who takes a genuine over-the-counter antihistamine stops sneezing and has reduced nasal congestion, with the improvement confirmed by objective allergy testing, distinguishing the response from a belief-driven placebo outcome. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A runner given a carbohydrate gel during a race outperforms a runner given a taste-matched placebo gel on objective time measures, with the difference attributed to the fuel provided by the real gel. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A patient who undergoes real knee repair surgery shows significantly greater improvement in cartilage integrity on follow-up MRI than a patient who underwent the sham surgery, demonstrating that the physical repair produced an objective benefit beyond expectation. (Moseley et al., 2002) https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa013259
A Parkinson's patient who receives a real dopamine agonist shows sustained neurological improvement over months, while the patient who received the saline injection in the placebo condition showed improvement only briefly before returning to baseline, distinguishing the real treatment effect from the placebo response. (de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1060937
A double-blind randomized trial confirms that a new blood pressure medication reduces systolic blood pressure significantly more than a placebo, with objective measurements showing that the drug is producing a real physiological effect independent of patient expectations. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A person who takes real insulin for type 1 diabetes maintains stable blood sugar levels, while a person of the same diagnosis who takes only a placebo experiences dangerous glucose spikes, confirming that the drug's effect is biological rather than expectation-driven. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A patient who is given a sedative for a medical procedure becomes drowsy and loses consciousness, demonstrating a pharmacological effect that cannot be produced by expectation alone, since patients given a saline placebo in equivalent conditions remain alert. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011
A clinical trial of a vaccine finds that participants who received the real vaccine show measurable antibody production while those who received the placebo injection do not, confirming that immune protection came from the vaccine's biological action rather than from belief. (de la Fuente-Fernández et al., 2001) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1060937
A child who is given a real antibiotic for an ear infection recovers within three days while a child given a placebo in a blinded comparison recovers more slowly, with the difference confirmed by a follow-up exam showing bacterial clearance only in the antibiotic group. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316
A researcher correctly notes in a paper that the improvement seen in patients after a new intervention exceeds what would be expected from placebo response rates in prior studies and attributes the additional improvement to the intervention's specific mechanism of action. (Beecher, 1955) https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1955.02960340031011

column1: More fond of what we are familiar with

column3: Letting one positive trait influence overall judgment of a person.
column4: Thinking if someone has one good trait it means they are entirely a good person.
column5:
Assuming someone is smart because they are attractive.
 Thinking a friendly coworker is also highly competent.
 Believing a well-dressed applicant is more qualified.
 Rating a student higher because they participate often.
 Trusting a charismatic speaker more than the evidence warrants.

A teacher assumes a neatly dressed student is also smarter and gives them extra benefit of the doubt on a borderline grade. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
Voters who find a candidate physically attractive also tend to rate that candidate as more competent and trustworthy on policy issues. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A hiring manager who likes a candidate's firm handshake assumes the candidate is also highly skilled at the actual job. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
Customers believe a product must be higher quality simply because the company has a likable, famous founder. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A juror who finds a defendant good looking unconsciously assumes the defendant is less likely to have committed the crime. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
Sports fans assume a high scoring athlete must also be a kind and generous person off the field. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A patient trusts a doctor's medical advice more simply because the doctor speaks in a confident, polished tone. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
An employee who is friendly and well liked gets rated as more competent on a performance review even though their actual output is average. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
Consumers assume a phone is more secure and reliable simply because the brand has a sleek, attractive design. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
People assume a well spoken news anchor must be more knowledgeable about world events than a less polished one. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
College students rate an instructor as more skilled and likable across unrelated traits like appearance and mannerisms after just hearing a warm introduction. (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11614318/
People assume attractive social media influencers are also more trustworthy when they recommend a product. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
Investors assume a charismatic CEO in interviews must also be running the company's finances well. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
A manager assumes an employee who is always punctual must also be more honest in unrelated areas of work. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
People rate a smiling job applicant as more competent than a neutral faced applicant with the exact same resume. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A restaurant's nice interior design makes customers assume the food will taste better before they even order. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
Parents assume a well behaved child at school must also be doing well academically without checking the report card. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
People assume a celebrity who publicly supports a charity must also be a more moral person in their private life. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A scientist with a prestigious university affiliation gets their weaker study trusted more than a stronger study from an unaffiliated researcher. (Thorndike, 1920) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11614318/
Online shoppers assume a website with a professional looking layout is more trustworthy with their payment information. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
column6:
Evaluating someone based on detailed performance metrics.
 Separating appearance from ability when judging.
 Recognizing strengths and weaknesses independently.

A teacher gives a sloppy looking student a lower grade after carefully checking the actual math and finding real errors. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A hiring manager dislikes a candidate's handshake but still rates them highly because their coding test scores were objectively the best. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A juror finds a defendant unattractive but still votes not guilty after reviewing the alibi evidence point by point. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
A patient double checks a confident sounding doctor's diagnosis with lab results and a second opinion before trusting it. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A manager rates a friendly employee lower on punctuality after pulling the actual attendance records. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
An investor ignores a CEO's charisma and bases the investment decision entirely on audited financial statements. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
A consumer dislikes a brand's logo but still buys the phone after reading independent security test results. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A professor grades a liked student's vague essay answer the same as a disliked student's identical answer, both receiving a lower score for lacking detail. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A scientist's prestigious university affiliation gets ignored once peer reviewers find errors in the actual data analysis. (Thorndike, 1920) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11614318/
A voter dislikes a candidate's appearance but votes for them anyway after researching their voting record on key issues. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
Fans criticize a high scoring athlete's character after seeing news reports of poor sportsmanship, regardless of his stats. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
A customer assumes a beautifully designed website is trustworthy, then changes their mind immediately after reading reviews about stolen payment information. (Thorndike, 1920) https://reference.jrank.org/psychology/Halo_Effect.html
A parent checks the actual report card instead of assuming good behavior at school means good grades. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect
An employer rates a punctual worker as average on honesty after catching them in an unrelated lie. (Thorndike, 1920) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halo_effect

column3: Underestimating travel time on familiar routes and overestimating unfamiliar ones.
column4: Thinking a familiar task/route is shorter than it actually is.
column5:
Thinking your usual commute is shorter than it is.
 Assuming a new route will take much longer.
 Believing a familiar path is always faster.
 Choosing the same route because it feels quicker.
 Estimating unfamiliar travel times conservatively.

A traveler overestimates the time it took to reach an unfamiliar hotel even though it actually took less time than their usual commute. (Block & Zakay, 1997) https://www.montana.edu/rblock/documents/papers/BlockZakay1997.pdf
A parent thinks the walk to their child's familiar school felt short, even though it covers the same distance as an unfamiliar walk that felt much longer. (Block & Zakay, 1997) https://www.montana.edu/rblock/documents/papers/BlockZakay1997.pdf
A delivery driver consistently underestimates the time needed for routes they drive every day compared to new routes of equal distance. (Block & Zakay, 1997) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well_travelled_road_effect
A person planning a road trip picks the familiar highway over a shorter unfamiliar back road because the familiar route feels faster. (Block & Zakay, 1997) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well_travelled_road_effect

A driver leaves later than they should for a routine doctor's appointment because the familiar drive there always feels quick. (Block & Zakay, 1997) https://www.montana.edu/rblock/documents/papers/BlockZakay1997.pdf
A hiker on a regularly walked trail underestimates how long the hike took compared to an unfamiliar trail of the same length. (Block & Zakay, 1997) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well_travelled_road_effect

Using GPS estimates instead of intuition.
 Timing routes to compare objectively.
Become well-prepared before go to an unfamiliar place.

column3: Seeing out-group members as more similar than they really are.
column4: Believing people outside your group are the same.
column5:

 Assuming a rival team's fans share identical traits.
 Thinking another department's employees all behave the same.
 Believing an out-group has uniform preferences.
 Assuming individuals from another group vary widely.

column3: Devaluing proposals simply because they come from an opposing group.
column4: Disliking an idea because an opponent suggested it.
column5:
Rejecting a good idea because a rival suggested it.
 Assuming a negotiation offer is bad due to its source.
 Dismissing a policy because it came from another party.
 Undervaluing a suggestion from a competing team.
 Rejecting a compromise because of who proposed it.

A student dismisses constructive feedback on an essay simply because it came from a classmate they dislike. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation

A parent agrees to a teenager's curfew compromise after discussing it calmly and finding the reasoning sound. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation
A committee member rates a proposal the same regardless of which colleague authored it, evaluating only the data presented. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation
An athlete follows coaching advice from an assistant coach they have clashed with after seeing it actually improves their performance. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation
A city council member approves a developer's proposal after an independent environmental review confirms it meets all standards. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation
A student government officer supports a rival officer's budget plan after reviewing the actual numbers and finding them sound. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation
A negotiator rejects a counterpart's concession because it genuinely fails to address the core issue, not because of who offered it. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://law.stanford.edu/index.php?webauth-document=child-page%2F370999%2Fdoc%2Fslspublic%2FReactive+Devaluation.pdf
A consumer accepts a product recall offer from a disliked brand after confirming with an independent safety review that it is legitimate. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation
Pedestrians rated the same arms reduction proposal consistently regardless of who they were told proposed it, once the proposal's actual text was the focus of the study. (Ross & Stillinger, 1991) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_devaluation

column3: Older adults tending to focus more on positive than negative information.
column4: Focusing on positive information more than negative information.
column5:
Remembering pleasant events more than unpleasant ones.
 Paying more attention to uplifting news.
 Choosing to spend time with positive people.
 Recalling positive traits of others more easily.
 Focusing on optimistic interpretations.

An older adult remembers more positive details from a family gathering than negative ones, while a younger adult remembers both equally. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
In eye tracking studies, older adults spent more time looking at happy faces and less time looking at angry faces compared to younger adults. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A grandmother recalls her wedding day mostly through warm, happy memories, leaving out most of the stressful planning details. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
Older participants in a memory study recalled a larger proportion of positive words from a list than negative words, unlike younger participants. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired teacher looks back on her career and mostly remembers the encouraging moments with students rather than the difficult ones. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An elderly patient describes their recent hospital stay by focusing on the kind nurses rather than the painful procedures. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
In a working memory task, older adults performed better remembering positive images than negative ones, while younger adults showed no such gap. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older employee describes their entire career mostly in terms of accomplishments, downplaying the setbacks more than a younger employee would. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A grandfather's autobiographical stories about raising his children leave out most of the stressful arguments and focus on happy milestones. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
Older adults in a decision making study weighted positive product reviews more heavily than negative ones compared to younger shoppers. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult reflecting on a recent vacation recalls the beautiful sunsets vividly but barely remembers the flight delays. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A senior citizen describes a difficult medical diagnosis by emphasizing the supportive friends who helped rather than the fear they felt. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
In an autobiographical memory study, older adults rated their past life events more positively in hindsight than they had rated them at the time. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired nurse who endured tough hospital shifts now mostly remembers the patients she helped rather than the exhausting hours. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult choosing which photos to keep from an old album favors the smiling, joyful pictures over the awkward or sad ones. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A grandmother telling stories about her youth mostly highlights the fun adventures, glossing over financial hardships she faced. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An elderly man recalling his military service focuses more on the camaraderie with friends than on the frightening combat experiences. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
Older adults asked to recall a recent argument with a family member tend to remember the eventual resolution more than the heated exchange itself. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired coach looks back on a losing season and remembers the team's effort and bonding rather than the losses themselves. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult rates their overall life satisfaction higher than a younger adult with a similar life history, partly due to selectively recalling positive events. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
column6:
Remembering negative and positive events equally.
 Evaluating information without emotional filtering.
 Giving equal weight to neutral, positive, and negative cues.
A young adult remembers a stressful exam day in vivid detail, including every frustrating moment, much more than any positive parts of that day. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A grandmother forgets the details of her wedding day entirely because of unrelated memory loss, not because of any positive bias. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult vividly remembers a painful injury from years ago because it required ongoing medical treatment, not because of any memory bias. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A college student remembers more positive details from a party than negative ones simply because the party was overwhelmingly fun with no negative moments. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired teacher remembers a former student's misbehavior clearly because it led to a major school policy change still discussed today. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An elderly patient recalls a frightening medical emergency in sharp detail because the hospital later used the case in a training video. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A young adult chooses only smiling photos to keep from an old album simply because the other photos were blurry, not because of age related bias. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult remembers a recent argument with a family member in painful detail because the conflict remains unresolved. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A grandfather's stories about raising his children include plenty of stressful arguments because he is specifically asked to describe the hardest parts of parenting. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired nurse remembers the exhausting overnight shifts clearly because she is writing a memoir specifically about workplace burnout. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A younger adult rates a recent vacation overwhelmingly positively because nothing went wrong on the trip, not because of any selective memory. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult accurately recalls both the highs and lows of a recent job evaluation because they specifically reread their performance notes. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A senior citizen describes a difficult diagnosis by focusing on the fear they felt because they are speaking to a support group about coping with fear. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An elderly man recalling his military service focuses on the combat experiences because he is being interviewed for a historical documentary about the battles. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired coach remembers a losing season's failures in detail because he is analyzing what went wrong for a coaching certification course. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult and a younger adult both recall a car accident with equally vivid, distressing detail because the event was highly traumatic for both. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A grandmother shares both fun adventures and financial hardships from her youth equally because she wants her grandchildren to understand the full picture. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older adult in a memory study performs equally well recalling positive and negative words, showing no measurable bias toward the positive. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
An older shopper weighs negative product reviews just as heavily as positive ones when deciding whether to buy something. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/
A retired employee recounts their career with an even mix of accomplishments and setbacks because they are writing an honest professional memoir. (Mather & Carstensen, 2005) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3459016/

column3: Treating money differently depending on arbitrary categories.
column4: Treating equal amounts of money differently by category.
column5:
Saving a tax refund while overspending from a paycheck.
 Refusing to spend gift money on necessities.
 Splurging with 'vacation money' but being frugal at home.
 Treating casino winnings as disposable.
 Separating budgets for groceries and entertainment rigidly.
A person spends a $50 lottery windfall on a fancy dinner but would never dip into their regular paycheck for the same meal. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A shopper happily uses a tax refund to buy something fun, even though they would call that same amount from their checking account too important to spend on fun. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A traveler keeps separate envelopes labeled "vacation fund" and "bills fund," refusing to use vacation money to pay an overdue bill even when it makes more financial sense. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A gambler treats winnings from an earlier bet as "house money" and takes bigger risks with it than they would with their original paycheck. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A customer uses a $10 off coupon to justify buying extra snacks at the grocery store that they would not normally purchase. (Thaler & Shefrin, 1981) https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/mental_accounting_and_small_windfalls_3cef0fc5-f8f0-4490-b284-3932dd90ab05.pdf
An investor refuses to sell a losing stock from their "retirement account" but would readily sell the same stock if it were in their "fun money" account. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person who finds $30 in an old jacket pocket spends it frivolously, even though they would never spend $30 of their regular salary the same way. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A family keeps a separate "emergency fund" account and will not touch it for a fun purchase, even when their regular checking account is briefly overdrawn. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person pays off a credit card slowly while keeping money sitting in a low interest savings account, treating the two accounts as completely separate even though combining them would save money. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A diner who already paid for a non-refundable meal forces themselves to keep eating even after they are full, because they mentally separate the cost of the meal from how they feel. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person treats their annual work bonus as "extra" money to splurge on, even though it is mathematically identical to the rest of their yearly income. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A student labels part of their budget as "food money" and refuses to use leftover food money to cover a textbook expense, even though both come from the same bank account. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A homeowner takes out a high interest personal loan for a kitchen remodel while keeping a separate "house fund" savings account untouched, treating the two pots of money differently. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
In an online grocery study, customers who received a small unexpected coupon spent more on impulse items than customers who received the same discount built into regular prices. (Thaler, 1999) https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/mental_accounting_and_small_windfalls_3cef0fc5-f8f0-4490-b284-3932dd90ab05.pdf
A person feels fine spending a casino's free chips but would feel guilty spending the same amount of their own cash at the same casino. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A couple budgets separate "his" and "hers" spending categories, refusing to dip into one category to cover a shortfall in the other, even when it would be more efficient. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person sets aside birthday gift money in a separate mental category and spends it more freely than they would spend an equivalent amount from their regular checking balance. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A worker treats their tax refund as "free money" for a vacation, even though it is really just an interest free loan they gave the government throughout the year. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A shopper buys a $200 jacket without hesitation while shopping but agonizes over a $20 delivery fee for the same purchase, mentally weighing the two costs very differently. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person spends their entire holiday cash gift on something impractical, treating it as separate from their normal monthly budget. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A shopper insists a $150 coat was "basically free" because they saved $150 during a 50% off sale, even though they still spent $150. (Richard H. Thaler, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.4.3.199
A woman returns a $90 dress and tells her friend she "made $90 today," treating the refund as income rather than simply recovering money she had already spent. (Richard H. Thaler, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.4.3.199
A college student buys an expensive concert ticket months in advance and later says the concert is "free" because the payment happened so long ago. (Drazen Prelec & George Loewenstein, 1998) https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.17.1.4
A shopper spends an entire $50 gift card on unnecessary items because it "isn't real money." (Nicholas Reinholtz et al., 2015) https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucv045
A person buys another $20 item they did not need because spending $20 more qualifies them for free shipping. (Richard H. Thaler, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.4.3.199
A shopper justifies buying $250 boots by saying they will only cost about $1 every time they wear them over several years. (Cost-per-wear framing; based on mental accounting and framing.) (Richard H. Thaler, 1985) https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.4.3.199
A customer buys an extra sweater because the store advertises "Buy one, get one 50% off," even though they only intended to purchase one item. (Amos Tversky & Daniel Kahneman, 1981) https://doi.org/10.1126/science.7455683
A person spends far more using a mobile wallet than they would with cash because tapping a phone feels less like giving up money. (Drazen Prelec & George Loewenstein, 1998) https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.17.1.4
In the 21st century in U.S. this is also called "girl math"
column6:
Viewing all money as interchangeable.
Making decisions based on total financial picture.
Combining funds instead of labeling them emotionally. 
A person treats a $50 lottery windfall exactly the same as their regular paycheck, depositing it straight into savings without any special spending plan. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A shopper calculates that a purchase is unaffordable and skips it, regardless of whether the money would come from a tax refund or their regular paycheck. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
An investor sells a losing stock as soon as the fundamentals turn bad, regardless of which account it sits in. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A gambler treats winnings from an earlier bet with the same caution as their original stake, refusing to take on extra risk with it. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
