A family moves money freely between their "vacation fund" and "bills fund" whenever it makes the most financial sense to do so. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person who finds $30 in an old jacket pocket deposits it directly into their savings account just like any other income. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A diner stops eating a non-refundable meal the moment they feel full, regardless of how much money was already spent on it. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A worker pays off their high interest credit card immediately using savings, recognizing that keeping both separate would cost them more in interest. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A student uses leftover food budget money to cover a textbook expense without hesitation, since it all comes from the same bank account. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A homeowner pays for a kitchen remodel directly from savings instead of taking out a high interest loan, since they treat all their money as one combined pool. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person feels exactly as guilty spending casino chips as spending their own cash, since they recognize both represent real money. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A couple pools all their income into one joint account and makes spending decisions based on the total balance rather than separate categories. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person spends a birthday gift exactly as cautiously as they would spend the same amount from their regular paycheck. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A shopper weighs a $20 delivery fee with the same scrutiny as a $200 purchase, treating both as equally important costs. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person uses their entire holiday cash gift to pay down debt, treating it no differently than any other income they receive. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
An online grocery shopper spends the same amount whether a discount comes as a surprise coupon or as a lower listed price. (Thaler, 1999) https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/mental_accounting_and_small_windfalls_3cef0fc5-f8f0-4490-b284-3932dd90ab05.pdf
A worker treats their annual bonus as part of their total yearly income and budgets it the same way as their regular salary. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A person declines a free upgrade at a hotel because they genuinely do not need it, regardless of whether it would have cost separate "vacation money." (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A family keeps one single combined emergency fund and freely uses part of it for an unexpected fun expense when the budget allows. (Thaler, 1999) https://www-apache.anderson.ucla.edu/faculty_pages/keith.chen/negot.%20papers/Thaler_MentalAccounting99.pdf
A customer ignores a coupon entirely and buys only the items already on their grocery list, regardless of the small discount offered. (Thaler, 1999) https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/mental_accounting_and_small_windfalls_3cef0fc5-f8f0-4490-b284-3932dd90ab05.pdf

column3: Underestimating the possibility or impact of disasters.
column4: Assuming a disaster will not happen.
column5:
Ignoring evacuation warnings because 'storms always pass.'
 Assuming a pandemic won't affect daily life.
 Believing a financial crash won't happen again.
 Staying home during an approaching wildfire.
 Dismissing early signs of system failure.

Residents stayed in their homes as Hurricane Katrina approached New Orleans, assuming the situation would turn out fine like past storms had. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
Office workers in the World Trade Center on September 11 gathered their belongings and finished tasks before evacuating instead of leaving immediately. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A family ignores a tornado warning siren because severe storms have always passed by their town safely before. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
Studies show many people check with several other sources before deciding whether to evacuate ahead of a disaster, delaying their response. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A company ignores early signs of a cybersecurity breach because nothing like that has ever happened to them before. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
A community continues building homes on a known floodplain because no major flood has occurred there in living memory. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A passenger on a ship ignores the captain's early warning about rough seas, assuming the trip will go as smoothly as every previous voyage. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
Disaster planning research finds that effective warnings must be designed to overcome people's tendency to assume an unfolding crisis is not as serious as it actually is. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
A small business owner delays preparing for an approaching wildfire because previous fire seasons never reached their property. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
An employee ignores a fire alarm and keeps working at their desk because previous alarms have always turned out to be false. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A homeowner refuses to buy flood insurance because their neighborhood has never flooded in the decades they have lived there. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A government delays issuing a pandemic response plan because early case numbers seem similar to past outbreaks that fizzled out. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A camper ignores a park ranger's warning about an approaching storm because the weather has always cleared up before. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A factory manager dismisses an unusual machine noise as nothing serious because the machine has always worked fine in the past. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A coastal town's residents delay evacuating ahead of an approaching tsunami warning because the area has not seen a major tsunami in generations. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A school administrator decides not to update an outdated emergency response plan because no major incident has occurred at the school before. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
An airline passenger ignores a flight attendant's serious safety briefing because every other flight they have taken has landed without incident. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A driver continues down a road despite flood warning signs because the road has always been passable during past storms. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A nursing home delays its evacuation plan during a hurricane warning because past hurricanes have weakened before reaching their area. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A city government underfunds earthquake preparedness because the region has not experienced a major earthquake in many decades. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
column6:
Preparing emergency supplies proactively.
Responding quickly to unusual warning signs.
Accepting that rare events can still occur.
Residents immediately evacuate ahead of a hurricane after seeing satellite images showing the storm is far stronger than any previous storm in the area's history. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A family leaves their home the moment a tornado siren sounds because they had just completed a safety class teaching them to act immediately. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
An employee evacuates the building right away when a fire alarm sounds because their company runs realistic surprise drills that train fast responses. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A homeowner buys flood insurance immediately after a neighboring town floods for the first time, even though their own town has never flooded. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A government rapidly issues a pandemic response plan as soon as early case numbers show signs of unusually fast spread. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A coastal town evacuates immediately after a tsunami warning because the town conducts mandatory annual evacuation drills. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A camper packs up and leaves a campsite the moment a park ranger issues a storm warning, trusting the ranger's expertise over past experience. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A factory manager shuts down a machine immediately after hearing an unusual noise because the maintenance team had warned this specific sound indicates failure. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A school administrator updates the emergency response plan every year regardless of whether any incident has occurred. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
A driver turns around immediately after seeing a flooded road, regardless of whether the road has been passable in the past. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A nursing home begins evacuation procedures as soon as a hurricane warning is issued, without waiting to see how the storm develops. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A city government invests heavily in earthquake preparedness immediately after seismologists report new fault line activity in the region. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A small business owner who lives in a high fire risk area installs sprinklers and clears brush every year regardless of past fire seasons. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
An airline passenger pays close attention to the safety briefing every single flight because they take air travel safety seriously as a rule. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A community relocates new construction away from a floodplain after a hydrology study identifies clear future flood risk. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A company quickly contains a cybersecurity breach because its staff are trained to treat every unusual login attempt as a serious threat. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
A passenger on a ship requests a life jacket the moment the captain mentions rough seas, regardless of how smooth past trips have been. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
Office workers leave the building immediately when an alarm sounds because their employer holds unannounced fire drills that reward fast evacuation. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias
A disaster planning agency successfully designs warnings that get most residents to evacuate quickly during a real emergency. (National Research Council, 2006) https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/11671/chapter/6
A resident moves out of a floodplain neighborhood after researching the area's actual flood risk data, despite no flood ever occurring there. (Normalcy bias, n.d.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normalcy_bias

column3: The idea that working memory holds about 5'9 items.
column4: Remembering only about five to nine items at once.
column5:
Remembering about seven digits without effort.
 Keeping a short grocery list in mind.
 Recalling a sequence of simple instructions.
 Holding several ideas in mind during conversation.
 Remembering a handful of new vocabulary words.

A student can easily remember a seven digit phone number but struggles to recall a twelve digit number without writing it down. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A waiter can hold about seven items of a complex order in memory but starts forgetting items once the order grows past nine or ten. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A website designer limits a navigation menu to about seven options because users start struggling to remember more choices than that. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
In Miller's classic experiments, participants could repeat back about seven random digits immediately after hearing them, but accuracy dropped sharply beyond that. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A grocery shopper without a list can usually remember around seven items they need to buy before forgetting some. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A teacher limits a multiple choice question to about seven answer options because more choices overwhelm students' short term memory. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A pilot can hold roughly seven checklist items in working memory before needing to glance back at the printed list. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A musician memorizing a new song can hold about seven measures in their head before they need to look at the sheet music again. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A call center worker can remember about seven steps of a troubleshooting script without needing to check their notes. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A user interface designer breaks a long form into sections of about seven fields each because longer sections overwhelm users' working memory. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A person memorizing a credit card number breaks it into chunks of four digits because remembering all sixteen digits at once is much harder. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A trivia game show contestant can hold about seven multiple choice options in mind while deciding on an answer. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A driver glancing at a list of seven turn by turn directions can recall most of them, but a list of fifteen directions quickly becomes unmanageable without GPS. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A presentation coach advises speakers to limit a slide to about seven bullet points because audiences cannot hold more in working memory. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A new employee can remember about seven new coworkers' names after a single introduction round before names start blurring together. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A chess novice can track about seven possible moves ahead in their head before losing track of the board state. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A radio DJ memorizes a station's phone number easily because it is seven digits long, similar to a typical local phone number. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A software developer limits a dropdown menu to roughly seven categories so users can scan and remember the options easily. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A patient can recall about seven instructions a doctor gives verbally during a checkup but forgets details from a longer list. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A flight attendant explaining safety procedures keeps the list to about seven key steps so passengers can actually remember them. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
column6:
Using external tools to track many items.
 Chunking information to exceed memory limits.
 Recognizing that memory capacity varies by task.

A chess grandmaster can recall an entire board position with over thirty pieces because years of practice let them "chunk" the layout into a few meaningful patterns. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A student forgets a seven digit phone number moments after hearing it because they were distracted by a loud noise, not because of any inherent memory limit. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A waiter remembers a fifteen item order perfectly because he writes it down immediately rather than relying on memory. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A musician memorizes an entire forty measure song easily because they grouped the notes into a few familiar chord patterns rather than memorizing each note individually. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A driver follows twenty turn by turn directions without trouble because a GPS app reads them aloud one at a time as needed. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A patient forgets a doctor's three simple instructions because they were anxious and not paying attention, unrelated to memory capacity limits. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A trivia contestant struggles with even three answer choices because the question topic is completely unfamiliar to them, not because of memory overload. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A new employee forgets a coworker's name immediately after one introduction because they were distracted checking their phone. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A software developer adds twenty categories to a dropdown menu and finds users navigate it just fine because the categories are organized into clear nested groups. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A person memorizes a sixteen digit credit card number with ease because they have repeated it to themselves hundreds of times over months. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A pilot misses a checklist step because of a sudden mechanical alarm distracting them, not because the list exceeded memory capacity. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A teacher writes a thirty option matching quiz and finds students perform well because they can look back and forth between the columns rather than memorizing them. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A radio DJ forgets a seven digit station phone number because she rarely needs to use it and has not rehearsed it. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A presentation with twenty bullet points is well received because the speaker reads each one aloud slowly rather than asking the audience to memorize them. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A grocery shopper forgets two items on a five item list because they were rushing, not because the list exceeded memory capacity. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A call center worker reads a script word for word off the screen, so the script length has no effect on their performance. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A flight attendant explains a fifteen step procedure successfully because passengers follow along with a printed safety card while she talks. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A website with twelve menu items tests well with users because the items are grouped under three clear labeled headings. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A person fails to recall a short three item list because they have early stage memory impairment, not because the list size exceeded normal capacity. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two
A user interface form with twenty five fields tests fine with users because it is broken into five clearly separated pages of five fields each. (Miller, 1956) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two

column3: The humorous idea that 'anything that can go wrong will go wrong.'
column4: Believing that everything will go wrong.
column5:
Expecting tech to fail during a presentation.
Assuming traffic will be worst on important days.
Believing a dropped toast will land butter-side down.
Expecting delays when you're already late.
Predicting complications in a simple task.

A driver forgets their umbrella on the one day it unexpectedly pours rain, then remembers every other rainy day they forgot it too, while forgetting the dry days they left it at home unused. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A computer crashes and deletes unsaved work moments before a major deadline, the kind of vivid, painful event that sticks in memory far longer than the many times saving went fine. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
The phrase originated when sixteen accelerometers in a 1949 Air Force rocket sled test were all installed backwards, giving a zero reading and prompting engineer Edward Murphy's frustrated remark. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A toddler spills juice on the exact moment a guest sits down on the new white couch, an event so distinctive that it gets retold for years while ordinary spill-free visits are forgotten. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A flight gets delayed for hours on the one day a passenger absolutely cannot afford to be late, and that single bad experience colors their whole impression of the airline far more than dozens of on-time flights. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A person notices that the grocery store checkout line they pick always seems to move slower than the other lines, vividly remembering the slow waits while forgetting the many times their line was actually fastest. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A printer runs out of ink on the morning of an important job interview when a resume needs to be printed, a stressful coincidence that feels meaningful even though printers run low on ink at random times regardless of how important the day is. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A car gets a flat tire on the one day the driver is running late for a critical meeting, and the frustration of that single bad-timing event outweighs years of routine, trouble-free commutes in memory. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A backup generator fails during the exact storm it was installed to protect against, an upsetting coincidence that gets repeated as a cautionary tale far more than the many storms it worked through. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A wireless connection drops in the middle of an important video call presentation to clients, an embarrassing memory that lingers much longer than the routine calls that went smoothly. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
The military's investigation into the failed 1949 rocket sled test traced the accelerometer wiring error back to the technician who had installed all sixteen sensors in the same incorrect orientation. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A person buys an umbrella because rain is forecast, and the forecast turns out wrong, a frustrating and memorable miss that overshadows the many times the forecast was actually right. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
The only day someone forgets their work badge happens to be the day security is doing a strict ID check, an unlucky pairing that becomes a vivid story retold at work for months. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A washing machine breaks down right after the warranty expires by a single week, a sharply remembered injustice compared to the many years of trouble-free use before it. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A wedding's outdoor ceremony gets rained out despite a sunny weather forecast all week leading up to it, leaving the couple with a far more vivid memory of that one bad day than of the week of good weather. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A student's alarm fails to go off on the one morning of their final exam, an intensely stressful and memorable failure compared to the hundreds of mornings the alarm worked perfectly fine. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A key project file becomes corrupted the day before a major client presentation is due, an event so disruptive it gets remembered as proof that "things always go wrong," despite being a rare occurrence. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
Colonel John Paul Stapp, who led the rocket sled testing program at Edwards Air Force Base, later popularized the saying at a press conference after the failed accelerometer test. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
The bus arrives early the one day a commuter is running a few minutes behind schedule, a frustrating coincidence that feels significant even though bus arrival times vary randomly day to day. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A toast slice lands butter side down on the floor the one time someone forgets to wipe up a spill first, a small but memorable mishap that gets treated as confirmation of a pattern rather than ordinary bad luck. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
column6:
Acknowledging that many things go right.
 Recognizing that outcomes depend on probability.
 Planning based on realistic risk, not pessimism.

A frequent flyer reviews the airline's actual on-time performance data and notes that the vast majority of flights they've taken arrived on schedule, with the one delay being a rare exception rather than the rule. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
An engineer assessing equipment failure rates plans maintenance schedules around the actual, low statistical probability of breakdown rather than assuming failure is inevitable at the worst possible moment. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A driver keeps a log of their commute times and finds that traffic delays happen only a small fraction of the time, so they plan a reasonable buffer instead of assuming the worst every day. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A project manager reviews completion data from past projects and budgets a realistic contingency based on the actual historical rate of delays, neither assuming smooth sailing nor assuming certain disaster. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A homeowner consults their insurer's claims data and recognizes that major appliance failures are statistically rare events, so they budget modestly for repairs rather than living in dread of constant breakdowns. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A public health official explains that a small percentage chance of a side effect does not mean the side effect is likely, helping patients weigh real probabilities instead of fearing the worst outcome. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A team reflecting on a finished product launch notes that most steps went smoothly and only one minor issue came up, giving them a fair, balanced account of how the project actually went. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A traveler recalls that, of the dozens of trips they've taken, only a couple involved any real mishap, and deliberately keeps that ratio in mind instead of remembering only the bad ones. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A small business owner reviewing a full year of operations recognizes that the business ran smoothly on the overwhelming majority of days, with only a handful of genuine problems standing out in memory. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A parent keeping a simple log of school mornings finds that the alarm, the car, and the schedule all worked fine almost every day, with the one chaotic morning being the rare exception worth remembering accurately. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A pilot training program teaches that mechanical failures are statistically rare and prepares crews with calm, procedure-based responses rather than a fatalistic expectation that something will always go wrong. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
An engineering team investigating the original 1949 accelerometer failure identified one specific, fixable wiring mistake, showing that the mishap had an ordinary cause rather than reflecting some inevitable law of failure. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A safety officer plans equipment checks based on actual failure statistics for that specific machine type, calibrating effort to the real level of risk instead of preparing for catastrophe at every turn. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A person who tends to assume the worst keeps a weekly journal and discovers that most of their predicted disasters never actually happened, helping them recalibrate their expectations toward realistic odds. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A retail manager reviewing register data finds that long lines happen only during a few predictable peak hours, so staffing is planned around that real pattern instead of around a vague sense that things always go wrong at checkout. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A couple planning an outdoor wedding checks regional weather statistics for that date over the past twenty years and finds a low historical chance of rain, allowing them to plan with realistic confidence rather than dread. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A frequent commuter notices that their bus is on time roughly nine days out of ten and plans their schedule around that real probability instead of assuming lateness is the norm. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/
A technician reviewing server uptime logs finds the system has run reliably almost continuously for the past year, with only brief, well-understood outages, giving an accurate rather than gloomy picture of its dependability. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A new pilot is taught during training that the original "Murphy's Law" mishap traced back to a single avoidable installation error, reinforcing that careful procedure, not fate, determines whether equipment works. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A risk analyst presents a balanced report showing both the likelihood of project success and the smaller chance of setbacks, helping stakeholders plan around realistic probabilities rather than either blind optimism or assumed doom. (Gigerenzer et al., 2007) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2733256/

A driver checks the weather forecast, packs an umbrella accordingly, and stays perfectly dry during a predicted rainstorm, a routine success that, true to the negativity bias, barely registers in memory compared to days things went wrong. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A computer with automatic cloud backup loses no work at all when it unexpectedly crashes before a deadline, demonstrating that careful preparation, not fate, determines the outcome. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A toddler spills juice on an old kitchen rug that the family no longer cares about, causing no real inconvenience and quickly forgotten rather than becoming a retold story. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A flight departs and arrives exactly on schedule, allowing a passenger to make their connecting flight with time to spare, an unremarkable outcome that fades from memory precisely because nothing went wrong. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A driver who left an hour early for a critical meeting hits no traffic at all and arrives comfortably ahead of time, an outcome that reflects good planning rather than any cosmic tendency toward mishap. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A printer with a fresh ink cartridge prints a resume perfectly on the morning of an important interview, a mundane success too unremarkable to be remembered later. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A backup generator works flawlessly during a storm, keeping the power on the entire time, an outcome attributable to proper maintenance rather than luck. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A car with new tires drives smoothly without any flats during a long road trip, the predictable result of routine vehicle upkeep rather than any pattern of fate. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A wireless connection holds steady throughout an important client video call with no interruptions, an unremarkable success that, consistent with the negativity bias, is unlikely to be specifically remembered later. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A student's alarm goes off right on time, giving them plenty of time to prepare calmly for their final exam, a routine outcome that fails to stand out in memory the way a failure would. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A person's phone with a fully charged battery lasts the entire day, including an unexpected need to call for roadside assistance, an uneventful outcome with no story-worthy coincidence attached. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A washing machine continues working reliably for years past its warranty period without any issues, an outcome quickly taken for granted rather than remembered as notable. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A wedding's outdoor ceremony enjoys clear sunny skies exactly as the week-long forecast had predicted, an unremarkable match between expectation and outcome with no illusory pattern to notice. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A grocery store checkout line a shopper picks happens to move the fastest out of all the available lines, an instance that, true to the bias, is far less likely to be remembered than a slow line would be. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A key project file saves correctly and opens without any problems the day before a major client presentation, an ordinary, forgettable success rather than a notable event. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A commuter's bus arrives exactly when scheduled, matching perfectly with the commuter's own arrival time at the stop, an outcome too mundane to be retold as a story later. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
An engineer reviewing the original 1949 accelerometer failure determined the cause was a specific, correctable wiring error rather than any inherent tendency of machines to fail at the worst moment. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law
A toast slice is caught mid-fall and never even touches the floor, an uneventful save that, unlike a dramatic mishap, is unlikely to be remembered or retold afterward. (Chapman, 1967) https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-5371(67)80066-5
A driver who left exactly on time for a meeting hits a few normal lights but still arrives precisely on schedule, an ordinary commute that leaves no strong impression in memory either way. (Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Finkenauer & Vohs, 2001) https://assets.csom.umn.edu/assets/71516.pdf
A team's product launch goes exactly according to plan, with no last-minute technical issues at all, a smooth outcome attributable to thorough testing rather than to chance favoring or disfavoring them. (DoD News, n.d.) https://www.dvidshub.net/video/513892/dod-news-focus-murphys-law

column3: Judging the probability of a whole as less than the sum of its parts.
column4: Thinking something is more likely because you listed many ways it could happen.
column5:
Estimating the chance of 'death by natural causes' as lower than its components.
 Believing specific travel risks add up to more than general travel risk.
 Thinking detailed scenarios are more likely than broad ones.
 Overestimating probabilities when broken into parts.
 Judging multiple small risks as larger than the overall category.

A manager thinks there's a 30% chance a project will be delayed.
But when asked separately about delays due to software problems, staffing issues, supplier delays, and budget cuts, they assign probabilities that add up to 60%.
A homeowner estimates a 10% chance their house will be damaged this year.
But when asked separately about fire, flooding, theft, storms, and vandalism, their estimates total 25%.
A student estimates a 15% chance of doing poorly on an exam.
When asked separately about forgetting material, running out of time, misreading questions, and test anxiety, the combined estimates become much higher


People estimated separately that death from cancer was 18%, heart attack was 22%, and other natural causes was 33% likely, yet rated death from any natural cause overall as only 58% likely, even though these add up to 73%. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
Search and rescue planners who broke down the possible reasons a missing hiker left the search area into five separate scenarios gave a higher combined probability than when asked for one overall estimate. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A patient asked to estimate the chance their chest pain is caused by a heart attack, panic, indigestion, or a pulled muscle separately gives a higher combined total than when simply asked the chance it has "any medical cause." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A survey respondent rates support for "improving roads, schools, and hospitals" separately higher in total than support for the broad combined category of "improving public infrastructure." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
In a wilderness search, planning team members who listed each possible escape route from a search zone individually assigned higher summed probabilities than colleagues who judged the escape question as one combined event. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A juror who separately estimates probabilities for several specific ways a crime could have happened ends up with a higher combined likelihood than when asked simply how likely the crime is overall. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A doctor estimating the chance of death from car accidents, falls, and drowning separately produces a higher combined total than when asked for the chance of death from "any accident." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A voter who is asked their support for specific tax cuts on groceries, gas, and clothing rates the sum higher than their support for a single combined "tax cut on consumer goods" policy. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
Experienced search planners showed just as much subadditivity bias as less experienced planners when estimating the odds that a missing person had left the designated search area. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A student estimates the chance of failing due to a missed deadline, poor grade, or attendance issue separately, and the sum exceeds their estimate of failing for "any reason." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
An insurance underwriter separately estimates the likelihood of fire, flood, and theft damage to a property, and the sum is higher than their estimate of "any property damage" occurring. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A search and rescue coordinator who first listed individual scenarios for where a lost hunter might be found later gave a higher overall probability estimate for that location than colleagues who skipped the breakdown step. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A researcher polling public opinion finds that breaking a broad policy into specific sub-policies and asking about each one separately raises the total measured support compared to asking about the broad policy as a whole. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A patient's family separately estimates chances of recovery, partial recovery, or full recovery with therapy, and the combined estimate exceeds their single estimate for "any improvement." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A project manager who separately estimates delay risk from supply issues, staffing issues, and weather ends up with a combined estimate higher than their single estimate of "any delay." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A scientist separately estimates probabilities that a chemical spill harmed soil, water, or air quality, and the sum is greater than their estimate for "any environmental harm." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A search team that breaks a wooded search zone into five smaller sections and rates the chance the missing person is in each one separately ends up with a combined total well above 100 percent. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A teacher separately estimates the chance a student struggles due to reading, math, or attention issues, and the sum exceeds the estimate for the student struggling "for any reason." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A travel agent separately estimates flight delay risk from weather, mechanical issues, or staffing shortages, and the combined total is higher than the single estimate of "any delay." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A city planner separately estimates traffic accident risk from speeding, distracted driving, or poor signage, and the sum exceeds the single estimate for "any cause of accidents." (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
column6:
Evaluating probabilities using consistent categories.
 Comparing whole vs. part probabilities logically.
 Recognizing that details don't increase likelihood.

A statistician carefully checks that probabilities for cancer, heart attack, and other natural causes sum to exactly the same number as the combined "natural causes" estimate. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A search planning team uses standardized mapping software that automatically calculates probabilities for each search segment so they sum correctly to 100 percent, eliminating manual estimation error. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A doctor's separate estimates for several causes of chest pain happen to add up to the same total as their estimate for "any medical cause," because they used a calculator to ensure consistency. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A pollster finds that breaking a policy into sub-policies does not change total measured support at all, because respondents are shown the math behind the categories. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A search coordinator overestimates the overall probability a missing hiker is in a specific zone because of a credible witness sighting there, unrelated to how the search areas were broken down. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A juror underestimates the likelihood of a crime occurring because they distrust the prosecution's evidence, unrelated to how the scenarios were broken down. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
An insurance underwriter's separate fire, flood, and theft estimates total the same as the combined property damage estimate because the company uses a standardized actuarial formula. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A student overestimates their chance of failing simply because they are anxious about an upcoming exam, regardless of how the risks are categorized. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A search and rescue trainer specifically teaches planners to cross-check their segment probabilities against the overall total, successfully eliminating the subadditivity pattern in training exercises. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A bank loan officer underestimates default risk overall because the applicant has an unusually strong credit history, unrelated to how risk categories are listed. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A project manager's delay risk estimates for supply, staffing, and weather sum to exactly match the single combined estimate because all three estimates were calculated using the same spreadsheet formula. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A travel agent quotes the same flight delay probability whether asked about specific causes or about delays in general, because the airline provides one official statistic. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A scientist's separate environmental harm estimates match the combined estimate exactly because all figures come from one peer-reviewed environmental impact report. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A search team using GPS-tracked probability density mapping finds their segment estimates sum correctly to the total search area probability, unlike teams using manual judgment. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A teacher's estimates for why a student struggles total correctly because the school's standardized assessment system calculates each percentage from the same underlying data. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A city planner's traffic accident estimates broken down by cause sum to the same total as the city's overall accident statistic because both come from the same official database. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A patient's family accurately estimates a single recovery probability without ever being asked to break it down into separate scenarios. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A voter supports a broad tax policy strongly simply because they trust the politician proposing it, regardless of how the policy is described or broken down. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547
A research team replicating the search and rescue probability study with professional statisticians instead of field planners found the subadditivity effect was eliminated. (Hill, 2012) https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/cognition-in-the-woods-biases-in-probability-judgments-by-search-and-rescue-planners/EF44B5DEF980D0B8ADE23620AFA467B4
A doctor underestimates a patient's overall risk because of an outdated chart, an error unrelated to how the risk categories were presented. (Tversky & Koehler, 1994) https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.101.4.547

column3: Focusing on successful examples while ignoring failures.
column4: Only focusing on your sucesses.
column5:
Studying only successful startups to learn business strategy.
 Believing a workout routine works because influencers use it.
 Assuming old buildings prove construction was better in the past.
 Thinking famous artists succeeded purely through talent.
 Believing investors always profit because winners are visible.

WWII analysts initially wanted to reinforce the areas of returning bomber planes with the most bullet holes, ignoring that planes hit in other areas never made it back to be examined. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
Mutual fund performance studies that only include funds still operating today tend to overstate historical returns because poorly performing funds were shut down and dropped from the data. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A business book studies only highly successful companies to find "secrets to success," ignoring the many companies that did the exact same things and failed. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
An investor judges a mutual fund family's track record using only funds still operating, ignoring all the funds that performed poorly and were quietly closed and merged away. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A person believes "everyone who works hard becomes a millionaire" because they only hear inspiring stories from the few who succeeded, not the many who worked hard and failed. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
Wald's wartime analysis showed that the empty, undamaged sections of returning bombers were actually the most vulnerable, since planes hit there never survived to be counted. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A finance researcher who studies only currently listed stocks on an index overstates historical average returns because failed and delisted companies were removed from the index over time. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A startup founder studies only famous successful startups for inspiration, ignoring the much larger number of similar startups that failed using the same strategies. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A diet program advertises only its successful before and after customers, ignoring the larger group of people who tried the diet and quit. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
Probit analysis of mutual fund data shows that poor performance significantly increases the probability that a fund disappears from the database, skewing later studies that only look at survivors. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A researcher studying centenarians concludes that a certain habit causes long life, without considering people who had the same habit and died young. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A college only highlights graduates who became famous or wealthy in its alumni magazine, ignoring the much larger group of graduates with average careers. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
Military aircraft survivability work originally classified for decades found that combat damage data collected only from surviving planes systematically misrepresented which parts of an aircraft were truly vulnerable. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A restaurant chain assumes a certain menu strategy works because they only look at their surviving locations, ignoring locations that closed using the same strategy. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A teacher concludes a teaching method is effective by only following up with students who stayed in the program, ignoring students who dropped out. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A finance textbook example shows that a sample of "winning" mutual funds with high volatility looks like it predicts future success, when in fact the pattern is an artifact of failed funds disappearing from the data. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A gambler believes a betting system works because they only remember the times it paid off, forgetting the many times it failed and they stopped using it. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A publisher concludes self published books can be hugely profitable by only studying the rare bestsellers, ignoring the vast majority that sold almost nothing. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A historian studying ancient artifacts concludes a certain material was common because it survived better over time, even though other materials may have been just as common but decayed. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A hiring manager assumes a certain interview question predicts success because they only follow up with employees who are still at the company, not those who were hired and later left. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
column6:
Including failures in analysis.
 Asking what didn't survive and why.
 Evaluating full datasets instead of visible successes.

A statistician studying aircraft damage deliberately requests data on planes that were shot down, not just the ones that returned, to avoid skewing the survivability analysis. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A finance researcher specifically constructs a survivorship-bias-free dataset that includes defunct and merged mutual funds, correcting for the inflated returns found in earlier studies. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A business researcher studies both successful and failed companies that used similar strategies before drawing conclusions about what actually predicts success. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
An investor evaluates a mutual fund family's performance using a database that explicitly includes funds that were shut down, not just the ones still operating. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A college advisor surveys all graduates from a major, including those who are unemployed or changed careers, before concluding how valuable the major is. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
An engineer studying old buildings accounts for the fact that poorly built structures from the same era have since collapsed, adjusting their conclusions accordingly rather than only examining what's left standing. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A startup founder studies a representative sample of both successful and failed startups before deciding which strategies actually matter. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A diet program publishes results from all participants, including those who did not lose weight or dropped out, alongside its success stories. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A finance professor explicitly corrects for survivorship bias in classroom data by adding back delisted companies before teaching students how to interpret historical index performance. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A researcher studying centenarians also studies people with the same habits who died young, to properly test whether the habit actually causes longevity. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A military analyst correctly concludes that armoring the undamaged areas of returning planes, not the damaged ones, will improve survival, properly accounting for the missing aircraft. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A teacher evaluates a new teaching method by tracking outcomes for every student who started the program, including those who dropped out. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A publisher studies the financial outcomes of all self published authors, including the many who sold very few copies, before describing typical earnings. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A hiring manager tracks outcomes for every employee hired through a certain interview question, including those who later left the company. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A fund-of-funds manager uses an industry database specifically designed to retain records of closed funds, ensuring performance comparisons aren't skewed toward survivors. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf
A restaurant chain reviews data from both open and closed locations before deciding whether a menu strategy actually works. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A gambler tracks every single bet placed with a system, including all the losses, before concluding whether the system actually works. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A historian studying ancient artifacts accounts for differential material decay rates before concluding how common a certain material actually was in the original population of objects. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
A book author interviews both successful and unsuccessful CEOs with the same morning routine before drawing conclusions about its effectiveness. (Mangel & Samaniego, 1984) https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478038
An asset management firm reports its track record using a survivorship-bias-free benchmark, deliberately including the returns of funds it has since closed. (Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, 1992) https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~wermers/ftpsite/FAME/Brown_Goetzmann_Ibbotson_Ross.pdf

column3: Assuming one person's gain must be another's loss.
column4: Thinking one person must lose when another wins.
column5:
Believing a coworker's promotion harms your chances.
 Thinking economic growth benefits one group at another's expense.
 Assuming shared resources always create competition.
 Believing cooperation reduces personal advantage.
 Viewing negotiations as win-lose by default.

A coworker assumes that if a colleague gets a promotion, it must mean fewer promotions are left for everyone else, even though the company is actively growing and creating new positions. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A student assumes a classmate's high grade on a curve-free assignment must somehow make their own grade lower, even though grades are not limited or compared. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
In an experiment, participants predicted that a strong grade on a presentation would be followed by a weaker one, even when grades were not curved or limited in any way. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A worker believes that if immigrants get jobs in their industry, it must mean fewer jobs for native born workers, even when the industry is expanding overall. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A person believes one group's gain in social status must come directly at the expense of another group's status, even when both groups can rise together. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A trade negotiator assumes any deal that benefits the other country must be hurting their own country, even when research shows the trade benefits both sides. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A sibling believes their parents' affection is a fixed resource, assuming more attention given to a new baby means less love left for them. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A small business owner assumes a new competitor opening nearby must directly steal their customers, even though the increased foot traffic could grow the whole market. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A person believes economic success is inherently zero-sum, assuming that for them to get richer, someone else must get poorer. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A team member assumes giving credit to a teammate for a successful project somehow takes credit away from their own contribution. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A homeowner assumes new affordable housing built nearby must lower their own property value, even when studies show mixed or even positive effects. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A parent assumes that praising one child for good behavior must come at the cost of praising the other child less. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A voter assumes another racial group's progress toward equality must mean their own group is losing ground, even when both groups' opportunities can expand. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A scientist assumes a rival lab's research funding success must directly reduce their own lab's chances, even when the total research budget is growing. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
An employee assumes a coworker's flexible work schedule must mean less flexibility available for everyone else, even when policies are not limited in number. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A friend assumes that a close friend making a new best friend somehow reduces the friendship the friend has with them. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A nation assumes that another country's technological advancement directly weakens its own, even when shared innovation can benefit both. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A student athlete assumes a new player joining the team must reduce their own playing time, even though the coach is expanding the roster's overall minutes. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A consumer assumes a company's profits must come directly out of their own wallet, ignoring that the company could be creating new value rather than just redistributing existing wealth. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A manager assumes giving one department more resources must mean taking resources directly from another department, even when the overall company budget is increasing. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
column6:
Recognizing win-win outcomes.
 Understanding resources can expand.
 Seeing collaboration as mutually beneficial.

A coworker recognizes that a colleague's promotion does not reduce their own chances, since the company is actively creating new leadership roles as it grows. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A student understands that a classmate's high grade has no effect on their own grade, since the class uses a non-curved grading system. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A worker recognizes that immigrants entering a growing industry create new businesses and demand, which can expand the total number of jobs rather than reduce them. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A trade negotiator points out actual data showing both countries' economies grew after a trade deal, correctly recognizing the relationship as mutually beneficial. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A sibling understands that their parents' love for them did not decrease after a new baby was born, since both children receive plenty of attention. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A small business owner welcomes a new competitor nearby after noticing it actually increases foot traffic and grows the customer base for everyone. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A person correctly recognizes that their own financial success does not require anyone else to become poorer, since new value can be created through innovation. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A team member happily credits a teammate for a successful project, recognizing that shared credit does not diminish their own contribution. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A homeowner supports new affordable housing nearby after reviewing local studies showing it has no negative effect on property values in their neighborhood. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A parent praises both children generously, recognizing that encouragement is not a limited resource that runs out. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A scientist celebrates a rival lab's funding success, recognizing that a growing national research budget benefits the whole scientific community, including their own lab. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
An employee supports a coworker's flexible schedule, recognizing that the company offers flexible policies to every employee who requests them. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A friend is happy when their close friend makes a new best friend, recognizing that friendship is not a limited resource that gets divided up. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A nation invests in collaborative research with another country after recognizing that shared technological advancement benefits both economies. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A student athlete welcomes a new player joining the team after the coach explains that team practice time and game minutes are both expanding this season. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A consumer recognizes that a company's profits come from creating a product people want, not from directly taking money out of any one customer's pocket. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A manager increases funding for one department without cutting any other department's budget, since the company's overall revenue grew this quarter. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A voter supports policies that expand opportunity for multiple racial groups at once, recognizing that progress for one group does not require setbacks for another. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A negotiator structures a business deal so that both companies genuinely profit, designing the agreement to expand the total value rather than just split a fixed pie. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full
A researcher confirms that older adults in their study held fewer zero-sum beliefs than younger adults, correctly identifying many situations as mutually beneficial. (Meegan, 2010) https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2010.00191/full

column3: Spending small denominations more readily than large ones.
column4: Finding smaller amounts of money easier to spend than big amounts (even when they equal to the same amount).
column5:
Using small bills freely but avoiding breaking a large bill.
 Tipping more with coins than with a large note.
 Buying snacks with loose change but not with a $50.
 Feeling reluctant to spend a crisp large bill.
 Preferring to use small denominations for impulse buys.

A shopper hesitates to spend a single $20 bill but happily spends the same amount in four $5 bills. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A diner uses spare $1 bills from a tip jar to buy snacks faster than they would use one $20 bill of equal value. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person trying to save money asks to be paid in large bills specifically because large bills feel harder to break and spend. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A traveler holding a single 50 euro note hesitates to buy a snack but would spend the same amount easily if it were in 10 euro notes. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A gambler treats a stack of small chips as more spendable than the same dollar value in one large chip. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A student carrying loose coins and dollar bills spends them quickly on small purchases, while a single $20 bill in the same wallet stays untouched for days. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
In a field study, people given a $20 bill spent less of it at a snack bar than people given the equivalent amount in twenty $1 bills. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person deliberately asks a bank teller for large bills before a vacation specifically to curb their own impulse spending. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A child given one $10 bill for allowance saves it longer than a sibling given the same amount in ten $1 bills. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A vendor at a flea market notices customers spend pocket change more freely than they spend a single large bill of equal value. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person on a tight budget consciously withdraws cash in $50 bills instead of $10s because the larger bills feel harder to part with. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A festival-goer holding small bills tips street performers more often than someone holding only one large bill of the same total value. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person feels a stronger pang of loss breaking a single $100 bill for a small purchase than spending the equivalent in smaller bills. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A casino visitor cashes out winnings in large denomination chips specifically to make it harder to keep gambling. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A commuter spends loose change on a vending machine snack without hesitation but thinks twice before breaking a $20 bill for the same item. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A parent gives a teenager spending money in small bills specifically because it tends to get spent faster than the same amount in a single large bill. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A street vendor notices tourists carrying small foreign currency notes spend more freely than those carrying large denomination notes of equal value. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person who wants to stop impulse buying exchanges all their small bills for one large bill before going shopping. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A waiter notices customers leave bigger tips in scattered small bills than when paying the same tip amount with one larger note. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person carrying a roll of $1 bills for laundry day ends up spending several of them on snacks instead, something they say they would never do with a $20 bill. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
column6:
Spending based on need rather than bill size.
 Using digital payments to avoid denomination bias.
 Treating all money as equal regardless of form.

A shopper spends exactly $20 on groceries regardless of whether they are paying with one $20 bill or four $5 bills, because they calculated the total in advance. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person refuses to buy an item entirely because it is outside their budget, regardless of what denomination of cash they are holding. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A traveler spends the same amount on souvenirs whether they are holding a single large bill or several smaller ones, since they use a fixed daily spending limit. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
