A gambler sets a strict loss limit and stops playing at that limit regardless of whether their chips are large or small denominations. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person who pays exclusively by card shows no difference in spending behavior based on bill denominations, since they never handle cash. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A student tracks every purchase in a budgeting app and spends consistently whether carrying a $20 bill or twenty $1 bills. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A vendor finds that customers spend the same total amount at their stall regardless of what denomination of cash they are carrying that day. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person breaks a $100 bill without hesitation for an emergency purchase, since the urgency of the need outweighs any reluctance about the bill's size. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A child saves their entire allowance regardless of whether it is given as one large bill or several small ones, because they are saving for a specific goal. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A festival-goer tips performers the same average amount whether carrying small bills or a single large bill, based on how much they enjoyed the performance. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A commuter avoids vending machine snacks entirely as a health choice, regardless of whether they have loose change or a large bill. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person exchanges currency at the airport and spends the same percentage of their trip budget regardless of which denominations they receive. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A waiter receives the same average tip percentage from customers regardless of whether they pay with small bills or large ones, since tips are calculated as a fixed percentage of the bill. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A casino visitor who has a strict self-imposed betting limit stops at that limit regardless of whether their winnings are in large or small chips. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person feels equally reluctant to spend $100 whether it's in one bill or five $20 bills, since they have a strong general aversion to spending money right now. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A teenager spends their allowance the same way every week regardless of bill denomination, since they always save half and spend half on a fixed rule. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A tourist spends the same amount on souvenirs in a foreign country whether holding large or small denomination notes, because they convert everything to their home currency before deciding. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person sets aside a single $20 bill specifically as "emergency cash" and would treat any other $20, regardless of denomination mix, the same way. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A shopper carrying a roll of $1 bills for laundry sets that cash aside in an envelope and refuses to spend it on anything else, regardless of temptation. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/
A person exchanges all their cash for one large bill before a trip, but this has no effect on their spending since they track everything digitally instead. (Raghubir & Srivastava, 2009) https://blogs.pugetsound.edu/econ/2018/04/13/the-denomination-effect/

column3: Assuming something will happen simply because it can happen.
column4: Believing if it could happen it will happen.
column5:
Believing a car accident will occur because it's possible.
 Assuming a business idea will succeed because it could.
 Thinking a rare disease will strike because it exists.
 Expecting a lottery win because someone must win.
 Believing a rumor is true because it might be.

A person concludes "something will eventually go wrong on this trip" simply because mishaps are statistically possible on any trip. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A gambler insists they are certain to win eventually just because winning is mathematically possible with enough spins. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A student assumes they will definitely fail the exam because failing is a real possibility for anyone who didn't study much. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A business owner assumes a product launch is doomed to fail simply because most new products could fail. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A driver assumes they will definitely get into an accident on a long road trip because accidents are always a possibility. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A news commentator claims a recession is certain to happen because economic downturns are always a possibility at some point. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A worried parent assumes their child will definitely get hurt at the playground because injuries are always possible there. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A juror assumes a defendant is guilty simply because it's possible they committed the crime, treating possibility as proof. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A tech forecaster claims artificial intelligence will definitely cause mass unemployment because that outcome is at least conceivable. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A homeowner assumes their house will definitely be burglarized because burglary is always a possibility in any neighborhood. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A marketer claims a new ad campaign is guaranteed to go viral simply because viral success is technically possible for any ad. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A coach tells the team that since an upset win is possible, it is essentially a sure thing heading into the championship game. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A traveler assumes their flight will definitely be delayed because flight delays are always a possibility somewhere in the system. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A scientist's claim that a rare genetic mutation will certainly appear in the next generation, just because mutation is biologically possible, ignores actual probability. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
An investor assumes a small startup stock is guaranteed to make them rich because huge stock gains are technically possible. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A politician argues that a policy will definitely lead to disaster simply because that outcome falls within the range of possible effects. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A person buying a lottery ticket tells friends they are basically guaranteed to win since winning is, after all, possible. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A patient assumes a rare side effect of a medication will definitely happen to them because the side effect is listed as a possibility. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A social media user claims a conspiracy theory must be true because the scenario it describes isn't technically impossible. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
An engineer assumes a bridge will definitely fail because structural failure is always a theoretical possibility in any design. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
column6:
Evaluating likelihood based on evidence.
 Rejecting claims without probability support.
 Recognizing that possibility does not imply certainty.

A meteorologist states there is a 90% chance of rain and packs an umbrella, correctly treating high probability as likely rather than certain. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A statistician calculates the actual probability of a coin flip streak and reports the precise number instead of assuming any outcome is guaranteed. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A doctor tells a patient that a rare side effect is possible but statistically unlikely, correctly distinguishing possibility from probability. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
An engineer calculates the actual failure rate of a bridge design using real stress data instead of assuming failure is inevitable. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A juror requires concrete evidence before reaching a guilty verdict, refusing to convict based merely on the possibility that the defendant could have done it. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
An investor reviews a startup's actual financial data and concludes the chance of a huge payout is very low, despite it being technically possible. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A traveler checks a flight's actual on-time performance statistics and concludes a delay is unlikely, rather than assuming one is certain. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A scientist tests a hypothesis with controlled experiments before concluding a rare mutation is likely to occur, rather than assuming it from mere possibility. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A coach reviews the actual statistics from the season and tells the team an upset win is unlikely but not impossible, giving an honest assessment. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A homeowner reviews local crime statistics and installs security measures proportional to the actual burglary rate in their neighborhood. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A marketer runs a small test campaign and uses the actual engagement data to predict the odds of the bigger campaign's success. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A driver acknowledges that accidents are possible but does not change their travel plans because the actual statistical risk on their route is low. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A news commentator cites actual economic indicators, such as unemployment and inflation trends, before forecasting the likelihood of a recession. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A parent calculates the actual injury rate at a specific playground and decides it is safe enough based on real data. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A lottery player buys a ticket for fun while clearly stating that winning is extremely unlikely despite being technically possible. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A tech analyst reviews adoption trends and historical data before estimating how likely AI is to displace a specific number of jobs. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A student calculates their actual chance of passing based on their study hours and past test scores rather than assuming failure is certain. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A business owner conducts market research to estimate the realistic odds of a product's success before launching it. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A social media user fact-checks a conspiracy theory against verified evidence instead of accepting it simply because it isn't impossible. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html
A politician cites peer-reviewed economic studies estimating the actual likely effects of a policy rather than claiming any possible bad outcome is certain. (Fallacy Files, n.d.) https://www.fallacyfiles.org/probfall.html

column3: Difficulty imagining what it's like not to know something you know.
column4: Forgetting how confusing something is to a beginner.
column5:
Explaining a concept using jargon without realizing others don't understand.
 Assuming a beginner knows the steps you skipped.
 Teaching a skill too quickly because it feels obvious.
 Being surprised someone doesn't know a common shortcut.
 Giving unclear instructions because the task feels intuitive.

A college professor uses advanced jargon while explaining a basic concept, forgetting that freshmen do not yet know those terms. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A software engineer writes documentation that assumes the reader already understands technical terms a beginner would not know. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A doctor explains a diagnosis using complex medical terminology, forgetting the patient has no medical training. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A parent gets frustrated that their child doesn't understand a math concept that seems obvious, forgetting how long it took them to learn it themselves. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A well-informed seller in a market experiment cannot ignore their private information about a product's true value, even when it hurts their negotiating strategy to reveal it. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A chef writes a recipe assuming home cooks already know basic techniques like how to properly dice an onion. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A manager assumes new hires understand internal company acronyms without ever explaining what they stand for. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A tour guide who knows a city well gives directions using landmark names tourists have never heard of. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A musician teaching a beginner skips over basic notation, assuming the student already understands what the symbols mean. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A lawyer drafts a client letter full of legal terminology, forgetting the client cannot interpret it without help. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A video game designer creates a tutorial that is too fast paced because they forget what it was like to play the game for the first time. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A scientist writing a press release uses technical language that confuses a general audience, forgetting most readers lack a science background. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A tech support worker gives instructions assuming the customer knows what "clear your cache" means without explaining it. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
An experienced employee writes a training manual that skips steps they consider obvious but that confuse a new employee. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A financial advisor explains an investment strategy using terms like "amortization" without realizing the client has never heard the word. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A teacher creates an exam question that seems clear to them but is confusing to students because they forgot which parts of the material are genuinely tricky. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A coder leaves no comments in their code because the logic seems self-evident to them, though it baffles a teammate reading it later. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A real estate agent uses industry terms like "contingency" with first time home buyers without checking whether they understand. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A grandparent assumes a grandchild knows an old historical reference that was once common knowledge in their own generation. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A product manager writes user instructions that skip a key setup step because it feels too obvious to mention. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
column6:
Explaining a topic from the ground up.
 Checking for understanding before moving on.
 Remembering what it felt like to be a beginner.

A college professor pauses to define every new term clearly before using it, remembering what it was like to be a confused freshman. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A software engineer writes documentation specifically aimed at total beginners, testing it with someone unfamiliar with the system first. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A doctor deliberately explains a diagnosis in plain language and checks that the patient understands before moving on. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A parent patiently breaks a math concept into small simple steps, remembering exactly how confusing it was to learn at first. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A chef writes a recipe with detailed step-by-step instructions for basic techniques, assuming no prior cooking knowledge. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A manager creates an onboarding guide that defines every company acronym the first time it appears. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A tour guide gives directions using simple, universally recognizable landmarks instead of obscure local names. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A musician teaching a beginner starts with the absolute basics of notation and checks understanding before moving forward. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A lawyer rewrites a client letter in plain English and offers to explain any remaining unfamiliar terms. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A video game designer tests the tutorial extensively with brand-new players and slows the pacing based on their feedback. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A scientist writing a press release works with a science communicator to translate technical findings into accessible language. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A tech support worker walks a customer through each step slowly, defining technical terms like "cache" along the way. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
An experienced employee has a new hire shadow them and asks regularly whether any steps need more explanation. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A financial advisor checks in with a client after each term to make sure concepts like "amortization" are clearly understood. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A teacher pilot-tests exam questions with a colleague unfamiliar with the course material to catch confusing wording. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A coder writes thorough comments throughout their code specifically so future teammates can follow the logic easily. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A real estate agent stops to explain unfamiliar terms like "contingency" the moment a first-time buyer looks confused. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A grandparent explains the full context of an old historical reference, recognizing the grandchild has no prior familiarity with it. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A product manager has a new user test the instructions and adds in the missing setup step that the testers got stuck on. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651
A well-informed seller in a market deliberately discloses key private information about a product, leading to a fair negotiation outcome for both sides. (Camerer, Loewenstein & Weber, 1989) https://doi.org/10.1086/261651

column3: Overestimating how much others can read your thoughts or emotions.
column4: Thinking others can read your thoughts.
column5:
Believing others can tell you're nervous during a speech.
 Thinking your frustration is obvious when it isn't.
 Assuming people know you're joking without clarifying.
 Believing your intentions are clear when they're not.
 Thinking your discomfort is visible to everyone.

A liar overestimates how obviously their nervous behavior reveals that they are lying during a conversation. (Gilovich, Savitsky & Medvec, 1998) https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.75.2.332

column3: Overestimating how much others are motivated by external rewards.
column4: Believing that everyone is driven by getting rewards.
column5:
Assuming coworkers only work hard for bonuses.
 Believing students only study for grades.
 Thinking volunteers only help for recognition.
 Assuming athletes train only for trophies.
 Believing employees care only about salary.

MBA students predicted that customer service representatives were primarily motivated by pay, while the representatives themselves ranked pay near the bottom of their actual motivations. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A manager assumes employees mainly work hard for their salary, while employees themselves report being motivated more by meaningful work and learning. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A teacher assumes students are mostly motivated by grades, while many students report being motivated more by genuine curiosity about the subject. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A nonprofit director assumes volunteers are mostly motivated by building their resumes, while volunteers report being driven primarily by a desire to help others. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A parent assumes their child does chores only for the allowance, while the child reports enjoying the sense of contributing to the household. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A coach assumes athletes train hard mainly for trophies and rankings, while athletes report being driven more by personal improvement and team bonds. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A company executive assumes salespeople are motivated mostly by commission, while top salespeople report valuing the challenge and relationships more highly. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A recruiter assumes job candidates care most about starting salary, while many candidates rank growth opportunities and company mission higher. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A professor assumes graduate students pursue research mainly for prestige and publications, while many students report being driven by intellectual curiosity. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A bank manager designs an incentive plan around bonuses, assuming tellers care most about money, while tellers actually report valuing customer relationships most. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A startup founder assumes early employees joined mainly for stock options, while employees report joining mostly because they believed in the mission. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A hospital administrator assumes nurses are motivated primarily by overtime pay, while nurses report being motivated more by patient care satisfaction. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A landlord assumes a handyman does quality repair work only for the payment, while the handyman reports taking pride in doing the job well regardless of pay. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A music teacher assumes students practice mainly to please their parents, while students report practicing because they genuinely enjoy playing music. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A game studio executive assumes developers crunch overtime mainly for bonus pay, while developers report being driven by passion for finishing the game well. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A city official assumes firefighters mainly value hazard pay, while firefighters report a sense of duty and community service as their top motivator. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A restaurant owner assumes cooks stay late mostly for overtime pay, while cooks report staying because they take pride in their craft. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A scholarship committee assumes applicants pursue community service mainly to boost their applications, while many applicants report genuine personal investment in the cause. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A factory manager designs piece-rate pay assuming workers want maximum output for money, while workers report caring more about safe, steady conditions. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A grant reviewer assumes scientists pursue research mainly for funding, while scientists report being driven mostly by curiosity about unanswered questions. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
column6:
Recognizing intrinsic motivation like curiosity or pride.
 Asking people what motivates them.
 Designing incentives based on actual preferences.

A manager surveys employees directly about their motivations and accurately designs a pay structure based on what employees actually report valuing. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A company executive correctly predicts that commission-based salespeople are mainly motivated by money, since exit interviews consistently confirm pay is their top concern. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A recruiter accurately identifies that a specific candidate cares most about salary, because the candidate explicitly says so during negotiations. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A teacher conducts a class survey and correctly finds that most students in this particular class are indeed motivated mainly by grades. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122

A coach reviews athlete feedback forms and correctly identifies that several athletes are indeed mainly motivated by trophies and rankings. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A professor checks in with graduate students and accurately learns that a particular student really is focused mainly on publication count for career advancement. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A bank manager runs an anonymous survey and correctly finds that the majority of tellers really do rank pay as their top concern this year. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A hospital administrator interviews nurses directly and correctly identifies overtime pay as their top stated priority during a current staffing shortage. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A startup founder asks early employees in exit interviews and correctly confirms that stock options were indeed their primary reason for joining. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A music teacher asks a student directly and correctly learns that this particular student really is practicing mainly to please their parents. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A landlord asks a handyman directly about his motivation and the handyman openly admits he only does the work for the paycheck. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A factory manager surveys workers and accurately discovers that, in this specific factory, pay really is the top stated motivator. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A game studio executive conducts exit interviews and correctly learns that overtime bonus pay really was the deciding factor for several developers. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A city official surveys firefighters and finds hazard pay genuinely is ranked as their top motivator this particular year, confirmed by the data. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A restaurant owner asks a cook directly and the cook confirms they only stay late for the extra overtime pay, nothing more. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A scholarship committee interviews an applicant who openly admits the community service was done mainly to strengthen the application. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A grant reviewer interviews a scientist who explicitly states the research direction was chosen mainly to secure continued funding. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122
A recruiter accurately matches a benefits package to what an entire department says they want most, based on a formal internal survey. (Heath, 1999) https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-012420-091122

column3: Overestimating your ability to resist temptations.
column4: Thinking you are good at resisting temptations.
column5:
Believing you can keep junk food at home without overeating.
 Thinking you can study near your phone without distraction.
 Assuming you can stop after one episode of a show.
 Believing you can browse social media briefly.
 Thinking you can resist impulse purchases easily.

A recovering smoker who feels confident about their self-control puts themselves in tempting situations like parties with other smokers, leading to higher relapse rates. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A dieter who feels sure they can resist dessert keeps tempting snacks in the house, only to give in repeatedly. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
In an experiment, participants given false feedback suggesting they had high impulse control chose to expose themselves to greater temptation and gave in more often. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf

column6:
Removing temptations to avoid overconfidence.
 Setting limits because self-control fluctuates.
 Planning ahead to reduce exposure to triggers.

A recovering smoker who recognizes their own limited self-control avoids parties with other smokers entirely, successfully staying smoke-free. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A dieter who knows their own weaknesses removes all tempting snacks from the house and successfully avoids dessert. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A student who realizes phones are too distracting puts their phone in another room while studying and stays focused as a result. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A recovering gambler avoids casinos altogether, accurately recognizing that proximity to temptation increases relapse risk. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A person on a budget skips the mall entirely, accurately predicting that window shopping would lead to impulse buys. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A person trying to quit drinking politely declines the wine tasting invitation entirely, correctly judging the temptation as too risky. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A person reducing screen time gives away their gaming console entirely, accurately recognizing that having it nearby would be too tempting. A person managing their temper avoids a known difficult topic with a relative entirely, correctly predicting they would lose their cool otherwise. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A person on a diet declines to bake cookies for the school event, accurately recognizing they would be tempted to eat the batter. A recovering shopping addict unsubscribes from all promotional emails, accurately recognizing their own vulnerability to deals. A person limiting junk food avoids buying chips at all, even for guests, correctly predicting they would eat them. (Nordgren, van Harreveld & van der Pligt, 2009) http://homepages.se.edu/cvonbergen/files/2013/01/The-Restraint-Bias_How-the-Illusion-of-Self-Restraint-Promotes-Impulsive-Behavior.pdf
A person trying to stay focused at work uses a website blocker to remove access to games entirely, successfully avoiding the temptation. A person managing road rage takes a longer but less congested route, accurately predicting that heavy traffic would test their patience too much. A person saving for a vacation unsubscribes from online shopping newsletters entirely, correctly predicting that browsing deals would lead to spending. A reformed procrastinator schedules early milestones with a accountability partner, correctly recognizing they need external structure rather than relying on willpower alone. A person accurately predicts they will struggle with self-control around a specific temptation and arranges their environment to remove that temptation entirely, succeeding as a result.
