column3: Assuming others share your current preferences or beliefs.
column4: Believing that others agree with you.
column5:
Believing a friend wants the same food you crave.
 Assuming coworkers prefer your work style.
 Thinking others enjoy the same hobbies you do.
 Believing someone is upset because you would be.
 Assuming others share your sense of urgency.

A person grocery shopping while hungry buys far more food than they actually need, overestimating how hungry they'll feel later. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying a winter coat in the freezing cold overestimates how much they will still want a heavy coat once warmer weather returns. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A car buyer who currently loves a flashy sports car overestimates how much they'll still enjoy it once they have kids and need more space. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying a house during a calm, sunny week underestimates how much a busy road's noise will bother them in the future. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person feeling angry during an argument overestimates how angry they will still feel about it the next day. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A patient deciding on long-term dialysis treatment while feeling unusually good that day overestimates their future quality of life on the treatment. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person signing up for a gym membership while highly motivated overestimates how motivated they will remain months later. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A shopper ordering food from a catalog while hungry overestimates how much food they will want once the order actually arrives weeks later. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A consumer buying noise-canceling headphones during a loud, stressful week overestimates how much they will still need them once life calms down. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person planning a vacation while exhausted from work overestimates how much rest and relaxation they'll still crave by the time the trip actually happens. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A teenager choosing a college major while excited about a current hobby overestimates how much that passion will still drive them years later. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying spicy snacks while craving spicy food overestimates how much they will still want spicy food the following week. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A car shopper buying a convertible during a beautiful sunny day overestimates how much they will enjoy it during a rainy winter months later. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person feeling deeply in love overestimates how strongly they will feel that same intensity of emotion years into the relationship. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person quitting a stressful job while burned out overestimates how relieved they will continue to feel months after leaving. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A homebuyer touring houses during pollen season overestimates how much the surrounding greenery will continue to appeal to them once allergy season passes. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying party supplies while feeling extroverted at a social event overestimates how much they'll still want to host parties when feeling more introverted later. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person committing to a New Year's resolution while highly inspired on January 1st overestimates how motivated they'll feel by February. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A shopper buying umbrellas during a rainy week overestimates how much they will still think about needing one once the weather clears up. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person ordering an expensive piece of exercise equipment while feeling highly motivated after a great workout overestimates how often they'll use it months from now. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
column6:
Asking others about their preferences.
 Recognizing that tastes differ widely.
 Avoiding assumptions about shared feelings.

A person grocery shopping after eating a full meal accurately buys only what they actually need for the week, unaffected by current hunger. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying a winter coat consults seasonal weather data and accurately predicts they will rarely wear it once summer arrives, buying a lighter jacket instead. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A car buyer planning for a growing family deliberately chooses a practical sedan instead of a sports car, accurately anticipating their future needs. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying a house visits the property at different times of day and accurately predicts how the road noise will bother them long term. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person feeling angry during an argument consciously waits a day before responding, correctly predicting their anger will fade by then. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A patient deciding on long-term treatment consults with other patients about their actual long-term experiences rather than relying on their own current mood. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person signing up for a gym membership accurately predicts their motivation will wane and chooses a flexible month-to-month plan instead of a long contract. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A shopper ordering food from a catalog accounts for the multi-week delivery delay and accurately orders an amount appropriate for that future date. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A teenager choosing a college major researches long-term career trends rather than basing the choice solely on a current passing hobby. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A car shopper test drives a convertible in both sunny and rainy conditions before buying, accurately weighing both scenarios. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person planning a vacation months in advance accurately predicts their future energy levels based on past travel experiences, not their current exhaustion. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person quitting a stressful job consults former colleagues about how relief levels typically change over time before making the decision. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A homebuyer tours houses in multiple seasons specifically to accurately judge how the property will feel year-round, not just during peak bloom. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person committing to a New Year's resolution builds in a flexible, gradually increasing plan, correctly anticipating that motivation naturally dips after the first few weeks. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A shopper buying an umbrella checks the long-term seasonal forecast and buys only what they'll realistically need throughout the year. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person ordering exercise equipment reviews their actual past usage patterns of similar purchases and accurately predicts they likely won't use it much. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying spicy snacks correctly predicts their craving is temporary, based on past experience, and buys only a small amount. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A couple discusses long-term relationship expectations early on, accurately preparing for how romantic intensity naturally changes over years rather than assuming it stays the same. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person buying noise-canceling headphones for a specific loud project accurately predicts they'll need them again for future similar projects, basing the purchase on real recurring need. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf
A person feeling extroverted at a party books a future social event based on their typical, average social energy rather than their current heightened mood. (Loewenstein, O'Donoghue & Rabin, 2003) https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/loewenstein/projectionbias.pdf

column3: Overvaluing new technologies and underestimating drawbacks.
column5:
Assuming a new app is better simply because it's new.
 Believing new teaching methods must outperform old ones.
 Adopting new gadgets without evaluating usefulness.
 Preferring new tools over proven ones.
 Assuming innovation always improves efficiency.

A school district adopts a brand new teaching app for every classroom, assuming it must be better than older methods simply because it is new technology. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A hospital administrator pushes for every doctor to switch to a new electronic records system, assuming the innovation is automatically an improvement for all departments. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A city government insists every farmer adopt a new irrigation technology, framing any reluctance to switch as simple backwardness rather than legitimate concern. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A tech company assumes its new app feature should be adopted universally, without considering that some users may genuinely prefer the simpler old version. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
Agricultural extension agents in early diffusion research promoted hybrid corn to all farmers as an unquestioned improvement, without examining whether it suited every farm's conditions. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A government agency promotes a new digital ID system as inherently good for everyone, dismissing privacy concerns raised by some citizens as mere resistance to progress. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A manager mandates new project management software for the whole office, assuming any employee who struggles with it is simply resistant to change. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A university rolls out a new grading platform for all departments, assuming the change must be beneficial without consulting professors about its drawbacks. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A public health campaign promotes a new screening technology to every clinic, assuming universal adoption is automatically the right goal regardless of cost or context. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A nonprofit assumes a new fundraising app should replace all traditional donation methods, viewing donors who prefer mailing checks as simply outdated. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A retailer assumes self-checkout kiosks are an unquestioned improvement for every customer, framing shoppers who prefer cashiers as resistant to modernization. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A company executive insists a new communication app should fully replace email for the entire organization, assuming the newer tool must be better in every case. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A government agriculture program promotes genetically modified seeds to all farmers as a clear advance, brushing aside concerns about cost and compatibility with local farming practices. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A library replaces all of its physical card catalogs with a digital system, assuming every patron will prefer it without testing usability for older visitors. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A city transportation department promotes electric scooters as a universal improvement to urban mobility, dismissing safety concerns raised by pedestrians and city planners. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A software company assumes that a major redesign of their popular app is inherently an upgrade, ignoring user complaints that the older version was easier to use. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A school board adopts a new standardized testing software for all schools, assuming it must improve outcomes simply because it is more technologically advanced. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A factory manager assumes new automated machinery is an unqualified improvement, without examining whether it actually fits the specific needs of the production line. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A bank pushes all customers toward a new mobile app, treating customers who prefer in-person banking as simply resistant to beneficial change. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A city council adopts smart streetlights citywide, assuming the new technology must be a universal improvement without piloting it in a smaller area first. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
column6:
Comparing new and old solutions objectively.
 Keeping legacy systems when they work better.
 Evaluating technology based on evidence, not novelty.

A school district pilots a new teaching app in a few classrooms first, carefully evaluating both its benefits and drawbacks before deciding whether to expand it. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A hospital administrator surveys doctors about a proposed records system and decides not to adopt it after learning it would slow down patient care in certain departments. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
Agricultural researchers study a new irrigation technology's actual costs and benefits for different farm types before recommending it only where it makes sense. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A tech company tests a new app feature with a small user group and chooses to scrap it after data shows most users actually preferred the older version. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A government agency pauses rollout of a new digital ID system after a privacy review reveals legitimate security concerns that need to be addressed first. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A manager lets employees choose between old and new project management tools based on what actually works best for their individual workflows. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A university consults professors before adopting a new grading platform and decides to keep the old system for departments where the new one creates more problems. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A public health agency tests a new screening technology in a pilot clinic and finds it less effective than existing methods for a specific population, so it does not expand it. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A nonprofit keeps traditional mail-in donation options alongside a new fundraising app, recognizing that some donors genuinely prefer the older method. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A retailer keeps staffed checkout lanes available alongside self-checkout kiosks after customer feedback shows many shoppers prefer the human option. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A company executive runs a trial period for a new communication app and decides to keep email for certain formal communications based on employee feedback. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A government program tests genetically modified seeds on a small set of farms and only recommends them to farmers whose conditions actually benefit from the technology. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A library keeps a physical card catalog available for older patrons after usability testing shows the digital system is difficult for some visitors to navigate. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A city transportation department studies pedestrian safety data before deciding to limit electric scooter zones rather than rolling them out everywhere. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A software company reverts a recent app redesign after user feedback and usage data clearly show the older version performed better. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A school board pilots new testing software in a few schools and finds no real improvement in outcomes, so it decides not to adopt it district-wide. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A factory manager evaluates new automated machinery against the specific needs of the production line and decides the old equipment is actually more efficient for this particular task. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A bank maintains in-person banking services after research shows a significant portion of customers, especially older ones, genuinely need that option. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A city council pilots smart streetlights in one neighborhood first, evaluating real performance data before deciding whether wider adoption makes sense. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/
A company researches a competitor's new technology thoroughly and decides not to adopt it after concluding it would not actually benefit their specific business model. (Rogers, 1962) https://open.ncl.ac.uk/theories/8/diffusion-of-innovations/

column3: Misjudging how much time can be saved by increasing speed.
column5:
Believing driving faster saves more time than it does.
 Thinking doubling typing speed halves task time.
 Assuming a faster route saves significant time when it doesn't.
 Overestimating time saved by small efficiency boosts.
 Believing multitasking while increasing efficiency saves time.

A driver believes that speeding up from 70 to 110 km/h saves more time than speeding up from 30 to 40 km/h, even though the lower speed increase actually saves more time. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A commuter chooses to push their highway speed from 70 to 80 mph for a long trip, overestimating how much time this will actually save compared to driving the speed limit. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A city planner overestimates how much driving time a road widening project will save for already fast-moving highways compared to slower city streets. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A factory manager believes that speeding up an already fast machine will save significantly more time than speeding up a slow one by the same percentage, despite this being inaccurate. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A delivery company assumes increasing driver speed on a highway route saves more total delivery time than increasing speed on a slower neighborhood route, even when the math says otherwise. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A parent rushing to drop off their kids speeds up significantly from a slow residential street, underestimating just how little time this actually saves. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A taxi driver believes pushing speed from 90 to 110 kph on a highway saves much more time than the math actually shows, leading to risky overtaking. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A road improvement plan is approved to raise the speed limit on an already fast rural highway, based on an overestimate of how much travel time the change will actually save commuters. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A runner believes that increasing their already fast pace slightly will save them more race time than the math actually supports, compared to a slower runner making the same percentage increase. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A cyclist speeding up from a high speed underestimates how little additional time they will actually save compared to a cyclist speeding up from a low starting speed. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A driver running late assumes weaving through traffic at high speed will save significant time, despite research showing such time savings are typically minutes, not the large amount imagined. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A transportation engineer overestimates the travel time benefit of increasing speed limits on a highway that is already fast moving, compared to improving slower side roads. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A bus company believes increasing bus speed on an already efficient express route will save much more rider time than increasing speed on a slower local route. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A long-haul trucker pushes highway speed up by 10 mph, overestimating how many minutes this will actually shave off a multi-hour trip. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A simulator study found that drivers who increased their speed from already high speeds judged the time saved to be far greater than it actually was. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A motorcyclist commuting in slow city traffic underestimates how much time can actually be saved by slightly speeding up, compared to their assumption it wouldn't matter much. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A school bus route planner overestimates how much time can be saved by raising the speed on an already efficient highway segment of the route. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A driver in stop-and-go traffic underestimates how much time could be saved by moving from a near standstill to a moderate speed, focusing more on the higher speed segments of their trip. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A logistics manager mistakenly prioritizes speeding up the fastest leg of a delivery route over the slowest leg, based on a flawed intuition about where the most time can be saved. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A study found that even professional taxi drivers, despite their experience, still overestimated the time saved by increasing speed from an already high starting point. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
column6:
Calculating actual time saved.
 Choosing tasks based on realistic time estimates.
 Recognizing diminishing returns in speed increases.

A driver uses a GPS app's real-time calculation to accurately see that speeding up from 30 to 40 km/h saves more time than speeding up from 70 to 110 km/h. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A transportation engineer runs the correct mathematical formula and accurately predicts that widening a slow city street saves more total travel time than widening an already fast highway. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A logistics manager uses route optimization software that correctly identifies the slowest leg of a delivery route as the one where speeding up saves the most time. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A factory manager consults an engineer who accurately calculates that speeding up the slow machine saves more total production time than speeding up the already fast one. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A commuter checks their actual arrival time data over several weeks and correctly concludes that driving faster on the highway barely changes their commute time. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A road planning committee reviews accurate traffic flow data and chooses to improve a slow rural road instead of an already fast highway, correctly predicting greater time savings. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A delivery company's dispatch software correctly calculates that increasing speed on the slow neighborhood route saves more total time than increasing speed on the fast highway route. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A runner uses a sports science coach's analysis to correctly understand that a pace increase at a slower point in the race yields more time savings than a similar increase at a faster point. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A bus company analyzes ridership and route data and correctly chooses to speed up the slower local route rather than the already efficient express route to save the most rider time. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A driver running late checks their navigation app's estimated arrival time and accurately realizes that speeding will only save two minutes, not justifying the added risk. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A cyclist uses a cycling computer that accurately displays projected time savings, correctly showing that speeding up from a low starting speed saves more time. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A long-haul trucking company uses fleet tracking software that correctly calculates minimal time savings from small speed increases on already fast highway segments. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A taxi driver trained on accurate trip-time calculations correctly judges that increasing speed on the slower portion of a route saves more time than the faster portion. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A school bus route planner uses route-optimization software that correctly identifies the slow city segment, not the fast highway segment, as where speed increases would help most. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A motorcyclist commuting in slow traffic accurately estimates time savings using a stopwatch comparison and adjusts their commute strategy based on the real numbers. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A parent rushing to drop off kids checks the actual time difference using a phone timer and realizes speeding only saves about thirty seconds, choosing to drive safely instead. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A city planner correctly uses the formula for time saved based on distance and speed to prioritize upgrading the slowest road segments in the city. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A driver in stop-and-go traffic correctly recognizes that moving from a near standstill to a moderate speed saves far more time than any further speed increase later in the trip. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A study participant trained on the correct time-saving formula accurately judges which of two road improvement plans would save more travel time. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html
A professional driver who has internalized the correct relationship between speed and travel time consistently makes accurate judgments about where speeding up actually helps. (Svenson, 2008) https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~baron/journal/13/13309/jdm13309.html

column3: Underestimating time, cost, or effort required for future tasks.
column5:
Believing a project will take a day when it needs a week.
 Underestimating how long homework will take.
 Thinking packing will take minutes but it takes hours.
 Assuming renovations will finish ahead of schedule.
 Believing you can finish a report quickly despite past delays.

A student predicts they will finish their thesis in about a month, even though similar projects have historically taken them three or four months. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A construction company estimates a building will be completed in one year, despite nearly every previous project of similar size running well over that estimate. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A government agency predicts a new transit tunnel will open on schedule and on budget, despite a long history of similar megaprojects running late and over cost. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A software team promises a new app feature will ship in two weeks, even though comparable features have historically taken closer to six weeks. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A homeowner estimates a kitchen renovation will take three weeks, despite knowing from a friend's experience that similar renovations usually take two months. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A wedding planner promises a couple their venue will be fully set up in four hours, even though every previous wedding of similar size has taken six hours. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A research team predicts they will finish data collection in two months, despite their last three studies all taking at least four months to complete. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A small business owner expects to break even within six months of opening, even though industry data shows most similar businesses take over a year. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A film production company schedules a six week shoot, despite nearly every comparable film in their portfolio having gone significantly over schedule. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A student confidently predicts they will study for a final exam starting two weeks in advance, despite consistently cramming the night before every previous exam. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A city government predicts a new bridge will be completed on the original timeline, despite their own department's track record of consistent delays on similar bridges. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A marketing team estimates a product launch campaign will take three weeks to prepare, even though past campaigns of similar scope have always taken closer to six. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A startup founder predicts the company will be profitable within its first year, ignoring industry statistics showing most startups take much longer if they succeed at all. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A graduate student plans to finish their dissertation in six months, even though their academic advisor has watched every previous student in the program take over a year. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A nonprofit estimates a fundraising gala will be organized in one month, despite every past gala taking closer to three months of preparation. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A software engineer commits to fixing a complex bug by tomorrow morning, despite similar bugs in the codebase consistently taking several days to resolve. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A homeowner predicts a DIY bathroom remodel will take one weekend, despite online forums full of similar projects taking multiple weekends. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A publisher schedules a new book's release for six months out, despite the author's previous two books both being delayed by several months. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A city council predicts a road repaving project will be done before winter, despite similar projects in past years consistently running into the cold season. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A surgeon estimates a complex operation will take three hours, despite their own logs showing similar operations have typically taken closer to five. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
column6:
Using past data to estimate timelines.
 Adding buffers to project plans.
 Acknowledging uncertainty in time predictions.

A student uses an outside view, looking at how long their last three similar papers took, and predicts a realistic two-month timeline for their thesis. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A construction company uses historical data from twenty similar projects to build in a realistic buffer, predicting completion within fourteen months instead of twelve. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A government agency hires an independent reference-class forecasting consultant who accurately predicts the transit project will take two extra years based on comparable projects. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A software team reviews past sprint data and accurately predicts six weeks for the new feature, based on how long similar features actually took before. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A homeowner asks several contractors for realistic timelines based on past similar renovations and budgets two months for the kitchen project. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A wedding planner builds in extra setup time based on data from past events of similar size, accurately scheduling six hours for venue setup. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A research team reviews their last three studies' actual timelines and accurately budgets four months for data collection this time. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A small business owner consults industry benchmarks and accurately plans for a fourteen-month path to profitability, in line with comparable businesses. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A film production company uses historical overrun data from its past five films to accurately budget an extra two weeks into the shooting schedule. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A student, based on past exam experience, accurately predicts they will cram the night before and plans their schedule around that reality rather than an idealized one. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A city government reviews its own department's delay history and accurately announces the bridge project will take eighteen months instead of the originally hoped-for twelve. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A marketing team reviews past campaign timelines and accurately schedules six weeks for the new product launch preparation. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A startup founder studies industry failure and success timelines and accurately tells investors profitability is unlikely before year three. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A graduate student's advisor shares data on every previous student's actual completion time, leading the student to accurately plan for fourteen months on their dissertation. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A nonprofit reviews timelines from its past three galas and accurately plans for three months of preparation this year. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A software engineer reviews the bug tracker's history of similar issues and accurately tells the team it will take three to four days to fix, not one. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A homeowner reads several detailed online accounts of similar DIY bathroom remodels and accurately plans for three full weekends of work. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A publisher reviews an author's past two books' delay patterns and accurately schedules the new release nine months out instead of six. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A city council reviews past years' repaving project data and accurately schedules the project to finish in early fall, well before winter weather typically causes delays. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf
A surgeon reviews their own surgical logs and accurately tells the patient's family the operation will likely take close to five hours, based on past similar cases. (Buehler, Griffin & Ross, 1994) https://web.mit.edu/curhan/www/docs/Articles/biases/67_J_Personality_and_Social_Psychology_366,_1994.pdf

column3: Overestimating the likelihood of negative outcomes.
column5:
Expecting a presentation to go poorly despite preparation.
 Believing a trip will be stressful before it begins.
 Assuming a new job will be overwhelming.
 Thinking a conversation will end badly.
 Expecting failure despite evidence of competence.

A person with depression consistently predicts they will fail an upcoming job interview, even though their qualifications are strong and similar past interviews have gone well. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A student expects to perform worse on a test than they actually end up performing, despite having studied just as much as for tests where they did well. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
In a study, participants with depression predicted fewer positive future events and more negative ones for themselves than nondepressed participants, regardless of their actual circumstances. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A patient assumes a minor medical procedure will go badly, despite statistics showing the vast majority of similar procedures have positive outcomes. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
An employee assumes an upcoming performance review will be negative, despite consistently positive feedback throughout the year. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A person predicts their blind date will go poorly, despite generally enjoyable past dating experiences and no specific red flags about this one. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
An athlete expects to lose an upcoming match despite a strong winning record against similar opponents. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A small business owner expects a new product launch to flop, despite positive early customer feedback and strong pre-orders. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A person consistently underestimates the likelihood of positive events happening to them, such as receiving good news or having a pleasant social interaction. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A parent expects their child's first day at a new school to be a disaster, despite the child being generally adaptable and the school having a strong support system. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A traveler assumes their flight will be canceled or delayed, despite the airline's strong on-time record for that specific route. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A person predicts a planned reunion with old friends will be awkward and disappointing, despite years of warm, easy friendship before the gap in contact. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A job seeker assumes they will not get a callback after submitting an application, despite having a strong resume well matched to the role. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A musician assumes an upcoming performance will go badly, despite weeks of confident, successful rehearsals. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A person predicts a planned vacation will be ruined by bad weather, despite favorable seasonal forecasts for the destination. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A college applicant assumes they will be rejected from their top choice school, despite having grades and test scores well within the school's typical accepted range. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A homeowner predicts a home inspection will reveal major problems, despite the house being relatively new and well maintained. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A salesperson expects a major client meeting to fall through, despite positive signals and strong rapport built over previous interactions. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A person assumes a long-distance friendship will fade away, despite both friends consistently making an effort to stay in touch. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
A new parent assumes their baby will have trouble at the pediatrician's checkup, despite the baby being healthy and developing normally according to all previous visits. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/
column6:
Evaluating risks realistically.
 Recognizing positive possibilities.
 Balancing concerns with evidence-based optimism.

A person accurately predicts a difficult job interview outcome after the interviewer explicitly tells them the position has already been filled internally. (Pyszczynski, Holt & Greenberg, 1987) https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3559896/

column3: Judging someone's morality based on outcomes they couldn't fully control.
column5:
Criticizing a good decision because it ended badly.
 Praising a risky choice because it succeeded.
 Judging a strategy solely by its outcome.
 Blaming a doctor for a rare complication.
 Rewarding a reckless gamble that paid off.

Two equally drunk drivers swerve dangerously, but only the one who happens to hit a pedestrian is judged as a criminal, while the other is judged far more leniently. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A doctor who skips a routine test and the patient happens to be fine faces no consequences, while another doctor who skips the same test and the patient has a rare allergic reaction is harshly blamed. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
Two employees who each cut the same safety corner are judged completely differently because one incident happened to result in an injury and the other did not. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A study found that participants assigned harsher punishment to someone whose reckless action happened to harm a family friend than to the same reckless action that happened to harm a burglar. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
Two students who both copy the exact same answer on a test are judged very differently because one happens to get caught and the other does not. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A revolutionary leader is hailed as a hero if their uprising succeeds, but condemned as reckless if the exact same plan fails, even though the decision making was identical. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A surgeon who takes a risky but reasonable approach is praised when the patient survives and harshly criticized when an identical case results in death. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A texting driver who happens not to hit anyone faces only a minor traffic fine, while another texting driver who happens to strike a pedestrian faces serious criminal charges, despite identical behavior. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
Two companies that both cut corners on product safety testing are judged very differently because one product happens to cause harm and the other does not. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/

Two chefs who both forget to wash their hands are judged completely differently because one customer happens to get food poisoning and the other does not. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A whistleblower who leaks information and the leak happens to prevent a disaster is celebrated as a hero, while the same action that happens to cause chaos is condemned as reckless. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A teenager who runs a red light and happens not to hit anyone gets a warning, while a teenager who runs the same red light and happens to hit a cyclist faces serious legal consequences, despite the identical violation. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A babysitter who briefly looks away and the child happens to be fine faces no consequences, while another babysitter who looks away for the same amount of time and the child happens to fall faces serious blame. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
A factory that skips a maintenance check and nothing goes wrong faces no scrutiny, while an identical factory that skips the same check and has an accident faces severe penalties. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
An investor who makes a risky bet that happens to pay off is praised for boldness, while the same risky decision that fails is condemned as reckless mismanagement. (Nagel, 1979) https://iep.utm.edu/moralluc/
